WR #31253711 11. First Readings 2026-151 An Order to authorize the Mayor to accept and expend a grant in the amount of $9,020.00 from the Massachusetts Emergency Management Agency to be used by the Amesbury Emergency Management Agency, which is managed by the Amesbury Fire Chief.-Mayor Sponsor Summary: These grant funds will be expended for the purpose of maintaining Amesbury’s Radiological Emergency Response Preparedness Program for the Operation Center for FY 2026. 2026-152 An Order to authorize the Mayor to accept and expend a grant award in the amount of $25,200 from the Massachusetts Executive Office of Public Safety and Security, Office of Grants and Research FY27 Municipal Road Safety (MRS) Grant Program. -Mayor Sponsor Summary: This grant award will be used to fund traffic enforcement. This funding will allow the Police Department to increase the number of hours spent conducting selective enforcement to combat the most problematic areas, which include distracted drivers, impaired driving, and speeding. This is a cost reimbursement grant program with an end date of September 15, 2026. 2026-153 An Order to approve payment from the FY27 general fund operating budget for the below listed prior year invoices. -Mayor Sponsor Summary: The listed invoices below are for operating expenses related to supplies or services rendered in prior fiscal years but for which funds were not encumbered by the corresponding city department at fiscal year-end. This order requests payment be made to the listed vendors from the corresponding department’s current year (FY27) operating budget in accordance with M.G.L. c. 44 s. 64. This vote requires two thirds approval of the City Council. 2026-154 An Order to authorize the Mayor to accept and expend an award amendment in the amount of $146,653 awarded to the Amesbury Council on Aging through the FY27 Behavioral Health Outreach for Aging Populations (BHOAP) program. -Mayor Sponsor Summary: The Executive Office of Aging and Independence administers the BHOAP program to provide home-based mental health and substance use support for adults aged 60 and older. This funding will support two LICSW positions and clerical staff to provide behavioral health services and support to older adults in Amesbury through the Senior Center and Department of Public Wellness. 2026-155 An Order to authorize the Mayor to accept and expend a Shared Streets Grant from the Massachusetts Department of Transportation (MassDOT). -Mayor Sponsor Summary: This $175,000 grant from MassDOT will help fund the replacement of the Upper Millyard Pedestrian Bridge. Earlier this summer, the bridge was closed following an inspection by structural engineers due to concerns about its condition. Previous engineering inspections had also identified the need for replacement, including a 2024 inspection that recommended the bridge be replaced within two years. Since the bridge was closed, the City has been working closely with MassDOT to coordinate next steps and move the replacement project forward. This grant will support that ongoing effort and help fund the replacement of the bridge and restoration of this important pedestrian connection. Specifically, this funding will fund surveying, geotechnical exploration, design and environmental permitting. 12. Correspondence a. Communications from Mayor, City Staff, other Elected Officials, and Representatives of City Boards and Committees 2026-147 Warrant for the November 3, 2026 State Election b. Council Communications c. Council Committee Reports 13. Act on Minutes • September 22, 2026 14. Adjournment

and WHEREAS, domestic violence affects individuals and families of all ages and backgrounds and can take many forms, including physical, emotional, psychological, sexual, and financial abuse; and WHEREAS, survivors demonstrate tremendous courage and resilience, and every survivor deserves to be heard, believed, supported, and treated with dignity and without judgment; and WHEREAS, October 5th is the Day of Unity that calls upon communities to stand together in solidarity with survivors, remember victims whose lives have been lost, and recognize the advocates, service providers, law enforcement officers, and community members working to create safer communities; and WHEREAS, organizations such as REACH Beyond Domestic Violence, which provides free and confidential services to survivors and serves Billerica among its Massachusetts communities, play an important role in providing safety, advocacy, shelter, education, and support; and WHEREAS, ending domestic violence requires all of us to listen, learn, recognize warning signs, support healthy relationships, and ensure that those experiencing abuse know that help and resources are available; and WHEREAS, the Town of Billerica recognizes that every person deserves to live with safety, dignity, respect, and freedom from fear and violence; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT PROCLAIMED, that the Billerica Select Board hereby recognizes October 5, 2026, as Domestic Violence Awareness Day of Unity in the Town of Billerica, and calls upon our residents, businesses, organizations, schools, and community leaders to stand together in support of survivors and in opposition to domestic violence. BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED that the Town of Billerica encourages everyone to use this Day of Unity to listen, learn, support survivors, remember those we have lost, and help build a community where everyone can live free from fear and violence. and WHEREAS, domestic violence affects individuals and families of all ages and backgrounds and can take many forms, including physical, emotional, psychological, sexual, and financial abuse; and WHEREAS, survivors demonstrate tremendous courage and resilience, and every survivor deserves to be heard, believed, supported, and treated with dignity and without judgment; and WHEREAS, October 5th is the Day of Unity that calls upon communities to stand together in solidarity with survivors, remember victims whose lives have been lost, and recognize the advocates, service providers, law enforcement officers, and community members working to create safer communities; and WHEREAS, organizations such as REACH Beyond Domestic Violence, which provides free and confidential services to survivors and serves Billerica among its Massachusetts communities, play an important role in providing safety, advocacy, shelter, education, and support; and WHEREAS, ending domestic violence requires all of us to listen, learn, recognize warning signs, support healthy relationships, and ensure that those experiencing abuse know that help and resources are available; and WHEREAS, the Town of Billerica recognizes that every person deserves to live with safety, dignity, respect, and freedom from fear and violence; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT PROCLAIMED, that the Billerica Select Board hereby recognizes October 5, 2026, as Domestic Violence Awareness Day of Unity in the Town of Billerica, and calls upon our residents, businesses, organizations, schools, and community leaders to stand together in support of survivors and in opposition to domestic violence. BE IT FURTHER PROCLAIMED that the Town of Billerica encourages everyone to use this Day of Unity to listen, learn, support survivors, remember those we have lost, and help build a community where everyone can live free from fear and violence. and WHEREAS, Head Start and Early Head Start programs serve children and families throughout Massachusetts, including families in the City of Chicopee and surrounding communities, providing critical early learning opportunities and support services to children and families who may otherwise face barriers to accessing high-quality early childhood education; and WHEREAS, Head Start programs operate under the federal Head Start Act and comprehensive program standards addressing early learning, teacher qualifications, classroom quality, child health and development, family engagement, mental health, nutrition, transportation, and services for children with disabilities; and WHEREAS, On August 6, 2026, the United States Department of Health and Human Services introduced a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that would substantially reduce existing Head Start program standards, including standards related to teaching and learning and state licensing requirements; and WHEREAS, Significant changes to Head Start standards and funding requirements could have a direct impact on the availability, quality, and accessibility of early childhood services for children and families in Chicopee and across Massachusetts; and WHEREAS, Reductions in staffing, changes to classroom requirements, elimination of specialized positions, increased class sizes, or reductions in family support services could place additional burdens on children, families, educators, and early childhood providers; and WHEREAS, High-quality early childhood education plays an important role in preparing children for kindergarten and future academic success while also supporting working families and strengthening the overall health and economic well-being of our community; and WHEREAS, The City of Chicopee recognizes that children and families deserve access to safe, high-quality early education and comprehensive support services, regardless of the challenges facing federal programs; and WHEREAS, The Chicopee City Council believes that protecting strong standards for early childhood education, child health, safety, family engagement, and developmental services is in the best interest of Chicopee children and families; NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That the Chicopee City Council hereby expresses its strong support for Head Start and Early Head Start programs and for maintaining strong standards that promote the education, health, safety, development, and welfare of children and families served by these programs; and that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the Massachusetts Congressional delegation, the Governor of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, the Massachusetts Legislature, the Massachusetts Head Start Association, and appropriate federal and state agencies for their consideration. text: TOWN OF COLRAIN Commonwealth of Massachusetts Special Town Meeting Warrant Fiscal Year 2027 FRANKLIN SS: To either of the Constables of the Town of Colrain in the County of Franklin. GREETINGS: In the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, you are hereby directed to notify and warn the inhabitants of said town, qualified to vote on town affairs, to meet at the Colrain Central School, located at 22 Jacksonville Road at 6:00 PM in said town on Tuesday the twentieth day of October 2026, there and then to act on the following articles: ARTICLE 1. To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, or otherwise provide a sum of money for the demolition of the partially collapsed former schoolhouse located at 101 Heath Road, and all costs incidental and related thereto, or pass any vote or votes in relation thereto. ARTICLE 2. To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, or otherwise provide a sum of money for the Town of Colrain’s share of the cost to replace the fire alarm control panel at Colrain Central School, including all costs incidental and related thereto, or pass any vote or votes in relation thereto. ARTICLE 3. To sce if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, or otherwise provide a sum of money for the Colrain Central School Weatherization Project, said amount representing the Town-funded portion of the project after application of the Eversource/Mass Save incentive and available Green Communities grant funds, or pass any vote or votes in relation thereto. ARTICLE 4. To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, ot otherwise provide a sum of money to provide the Town's contribution toward implementation of the FY27 Service Incentive Grant (SIG) Field Demonstration Project for Nutrition, including costs associated with program implementation, said project having received $20,000.00 in grant funding from the Massachusetts Association of Councils on Aging through the Massachusetts Executive Office of Aging & Independence, or pass any vote or votes in relation thereto. ARTICLE 5. To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, or otherwise provide a sum of money for costs associated with the removal or demolition of the unsafe structure located at 6 Greenfield Road, including demolition, removal and disposal, site work, professional services, and all other costs incidental and related thereto, or pass any vote or votes in relation thereto. ARTICLE 6. To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, or otherwise provide a sum of money for the purchase, implementation, configuration, and related costs of an electronic permitting system for the Town, including software, setup, training, integration, and other costs incidental and related thereto, or pass any vote or votes in relation thereto. ARTICLE 7. To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, or otherwise provide a sum of money to fund additional costs associated with the Town’s transition from its physical server environment to a cloud-based server environment, including migration, configuration, licensing, professional information technology services, and other costs incidental and related thereto, or pass any vote or votes in relation thereto. And to concurrently authorize the Town Accountant to make the adjustments within the FY 2027 General Fund Operating Budget (Schedule A) that are necessitated by this implementation and funding. Or take any other action relative thereto. Sponsor: Select Board ARTICLE 11: TOW SERVICE PROVIDER LICENSE To see if the Town will vote to amend Chapter 340 of the General Bylaws by adding a new Article IV as follows: Article IV Tow Service Provider Licenses § 340-11 Licensing requirements. No towing company shall be utilized by, or operate on behalf of, the Police Department in response to public safety situations unless it has first received a towing license from the Chief of Police. A. Scope of Applicability. For the purposes of this licensing requirement, and except as otherwise provided in Paragraph B, a public safety situation shall include any of the following: 1. A motor vehicle accident; 8 2. The determination by a police officer that a motor vehicle is in violation of any parking restriction; 3. The determination by a police officer that a motor vehicle cannot be lawfully operated by any person; and 4. Any other incident, occurrence or situation in which a motor vehicle is causing a safety hazard, obstructing or impeding the flow of traffic, or otherwise is inoperable but requires removal in the determination of a police officer. B. Nonapplicability. This Article IV, and the licensing requirements of the same, shall not apply to the following: 1. The towing of any motor vehicle of the Police Department; 2. The towing of any motor vehicle where the same or any contents thereof are considered to be criminal evidence; or 3. The towing of any motor vehicle at the direct request of the owner or operator of said motor vehicle, without communication by the Police Department, and regardless of whether said request is in response to any accident, incident, occurrence or situation for which the Police Department could have contacted a Licensee; provided, that nothing shall preclude the Police Department from determining that circumstances require the utilization of a Licensee even when said owner or operator would prefer to utilize a different towing company. § 340-12 Limitations on licenses. A. All towing licenses shall be issued annually, and each such license shall expire on December 31st of that year, regardless of the day on which it was issued. There shall be no automatic renewal of towing licenses. B. Applications for renewal of towing licenses shall be accepted not sooner than October 1st of the year preceding the start date of the renewed towing license. Applications for original towing licenses shall be accepted not sooner than November 1st of the year preceding the start date of the original towing license. Applications shall be reviewed and acted upon on a rolling basis. C. Not more than five towing licenses shall be issued and valid at any given time. Any application that is submitted when no towing licenses are available shall be denied without prejudice. D. The Chief of Police may impose reasonable conditions on any issued towing license. § 340-13 Rotation schedule. 9 A. The Chief of Police shall create a rotation schedule for all Licensees, such that each Licensee is on-call for an equal number of days. Only one Licensee shall be on-call on any given day, and said Licensee shall be the only towing company that is utilized by the Police Department on that day for services within the scope of § 340-11, subject to Paragraph C. B. Holding a towing license, and being placed on the rotation schedule of Licensees, does not guarantee that towing work will be needed by the Police Department on any particular day that a Licensee is on-call. C. In the event that the on-call Licensee is unresponsive, unavailable, or otherwise unable to provide prompt and complete service for a particular accident, incident, occurrence or situation, then the other Licensees shall be contacted one at a time in the order of the rotation schedule that follows the on-call Licensee, until a particular Licensee confirms that such service will be provided. § 340-14 Suspension and revocation. A. Failure of a Licensee to abide by the terms, conditions and restrictions of a towing license, of this Article IV or of any regulations promulgated pursuant to § 340-15, shall subject said license to suspension or revocation by the Chief of Police in their sole determination; provided, that any such suspension or revocation may occur only after a hearing for which the Licensee is given at least seven days prior written notice. B. Any revocation of a towing license shall preclude the Licensee from submitting a new application for a towing license for a period of three years. § 340-15 Regulations. The Chief of Police shall have the authority to promulgate regulations to effectuate the purposes of, and enforce and interpret, this Article IV. By way of example only, these regulations may provide for the following: A. The application process and requirements for a towing license; B. The standards and limitations for the issuance of a towing license, including, without limitation, with respect to insurance, residency, posting of a bond, and specifications for in-house or subcontracted equipment and personnel; C. Standards and limitations for the business operations of a Licensee in order to maintain a towing license; D. The hearing and decision-making process for suspension and revocation of a towing license; E. The nature of the rotation schedule; F. Supplemental criteria for determining the situations for which the on-call Licensee shall be utilized; and G. Additional standard license conditions beyond what are provided in § 340-16. § 340-16 Standard license conditions. 10 In addition to any conditions that the Chief of Police imposes pursuant to § 340-12D or otherwise promulgates by regulation, the following standard conditions shall apply to all towing licenses: A. By accepting a towing license, the Licensee agrees that the Town, and each of its departments, boards, commissions, committees, officers, officials and employees shall not be liable for any damages arising from, or caused by, the utilization of the Licensee by the Police Department for the towing, recovery or storage of vehicles, or for any secondary services related thereto; and further agrees to indemnify and hold harmless the Town, and each of its departments, boards, commissions, committees, officers, officials and employees from and against any claims, loss, damage or other liability arising from, or caused by, the action or inaction of the Licensee or its employees, officers, agents or contractors, and whether such action or inaction is negligent, intentional or otherwise. Or take any other action relative thereto Sponsor: Select Board ARTICLE 12: WATER DEPARTMENT RULES & REGULATIONS To see if the Town will vote, pursuant to Massachusetts General Laws, Chapter 41, Section 69B, to instruct the Board of Public Works to promulgate rules, regulations and policies, and any future amendments to the same, for the operation of the Town’s public water system, without requiring subsequent approval or adoption of the same by Town Meeting; and that, upon such promulgation, any prior iteration of such rules, regulations or policies that previously had been approved or adopted by Town Meeting shall be superseded. Or take any other action relative thereto. The purpose of this letter report is to provide comments on the proposed project as it currently relates to regulatory compliance with the applicable sections of the Zoning Bylaws of the Town of Dighton Massachusetts (June 9, 2025) and the Massachusetts Stormwater Handbook as promulgated under 310 CMR 10.00. We conducted our first review of this application and provided comments in a letter dated August 14, 2026. This second review has been conducted based on additional materials provided to us on September 14, 2026, including a response letter, a revised NOI & revised Site Plans. The review is based on information submitted to the Town including documents prepared by MBL Land Development & Permitting, Corp. on behalf of Cedar Street, LLC. the “Applicant.” Project Overview • • • • • • • Total Lot Area: 351,978 Sq.ft. Site Area: 76,013 Sq.ft. Proposed Development: Gravel storage area with associated site access & stormwater management system (expansion of the existing gravel storage area). Current Use: Gravel Storage Area As part of our initial review conducted on August 14th, 2026, Weston & Sampson reviewed the following documents submitted by the Applicant: • • • • • • A document titled “Development Impact Statement” prepared by MBL Land Development & Permitting, Corp. dated June 17, 2026 (2 sheets). The Applicant requests to waive the requirement for a Board of Health variance for an aboveground basin. Section 4324 – Basins shall be no more than three (3') feet deep based on the average bottom depth. One (1) foot of freeboard should be provided from the highest designed water level. After a permit is issued in accordance 26 with this section, continuing compliance is required. 3420. Standards. No use shall be allowed if it will cause sound, noise, vibration, odor or flashing (except for warning devices, temporary construction, or maintenance work, parades, recreational or agricultural activities, or other special circumstances) perceptible without instruments more than 200′ from the boundaries of the originating premises if in a nonresidential district, or more than 40′ from the boundaries of the originating premises if in a Residential District, unless otherwise specified herein. However, the Board of Appeals may grant a special permit for an exception for activities not meeting these standards, in cases where the Board determines that no objectionable conditions are thereby created for the use of other affected properties. westonandsampson.com Page 5 WSE COMMENT: It is unclear what equipment, if any, may be operated at the site and how frequently such equipment may be operated. We recommend that the Applicant provide additional information regarding potential impacts and proposed mitigation measures, including dust-control measures, to demonstrate compliance with this standard. WSE COMMENT: The Engineer confirmed that the proposed project will not generate cinders, dust, fumes, or other emissions that could adversely affect adjacent properties. Additionally, construction pollution prevention notes have been included on Sheet C-5.0 of the revised plans to ensure that any potential waste materials generated during construction are properly managed and disposed of. This comment has been addressed. 3422. All activities involving, and all storage of, inflammable and explosive materials shall be provided with adequate safety devices against hazards from fire and explosion, and with adequate fire fighting and fire suppression equipment standard in this industry. Burning of waste materials in the open contrary to state law is prohibited. WSE COMMENT: No storage or use of flammable or explosive materials is proposed as part of the project. This standard is not applicable. WSE COMMENT: This standard is not applicable. 3423. All materials, which may be edible by or attractive to rodents or insects, shall, when stored in or outdoors, be stored in tightly closed containers. WSE COMMENT: No materials that may be edible by or attractive to rodents or insects are proposed to be stored on-site. Therefore, this standard is not applicable. WSE COMMENT: Therefore, this standard is not applicable. 3430. Erosion Control. Site design, materials, and construction processes shall be designed to avoid erosion damage, sedimentation, or uncontrolled surface water runoff by conformance with the following: 3431. Grading or construction which will result in final slopes of 15% or greater on 50% or more of lot area, or on 30,000 square feet or more on a single lot, even if less than half the lot area, shall be allowed only under special permit from the Planning Board, which shall be granted only upon demonstration that adequate provisions have been made to protect against erosion, soil instability, uncontrolled surface water runoff, or other environmental degradation. Applications and plans for such special permits shall be referred to the Conservation Commission for its advisory review. westonandsampson.com Page 6 WSE COMMENT: The Engineer has provided the necessary erosion control measures to meet the requirements of this standard. The proposed erosion control measures are shown on Sheets 5 and 6 of 6. Regarding grading, the proposed work will result in slopes greater than 15% over an area that is less than 50% of the total lot area and less than 30,000 square feet. Therefore, a special permit is not required. This standard has been met. WSE COMMENT: This standard has been met. 3432. All such slopes exceeding 15% which result from site grading or construction activities shall either be covered with topsoil to a depth of 4″ and planted with vegetative cover sufficient to prevent erosion or be retained by a wall constructed of masonry, reinforced concrete or treated pile or timber. WSE COMMENT: Details for slope treatment in areas exceeding 15% grade were not found on the plans. We recommend that the Engineer address this. WSE COMMENT: The Engineer stated that the revised plans include details for the treatment of slopes exceeding 15% grades on Sheets C-2.0 and C-5.0. However, this information could not be identified on the referenced sheets of the revised plan set. We recommend that the Engineer clarify where the proposed slope treatment is depicted on Sheets C-2.0 and C-5.0 or revise the plans as necessary. 3433. No area or areas totaling 2 acres or more on any parcel or contiguous parcels in the same ownership shall have existing vegetation clear-stripped or be filled 6″ or more so as to destroy existing vegetation unless in conjunction with agricultural activity, or unless necessarily incidental to construction on the premises under a currently valid building permit, or unless within streets which are either public or designated on an approved subdivision plan, or unless a special permit is approved by the Planning Board on condition that runoff will be controlled, erosion avoided, and either a constructed surface or cover vegetation will be provided not later than the first full spring season immediately following completion of the stripping operation. No stripped area or areas which are allowed by special permit shall remain through the winter without a temporary cover of winter rye or similar plant material being provided for soil control, except in the case of agricultural activity where such temporary cover would be infeasible. WSE COMMENT: The Engineer confirmed that the total area of vegetation proposed to be removed is approximately 33,845 square feet (0.78 acres), which is less than the 2-acre threshold. Section numbers correspond to agenda packets and are not an indication of the order of the agenda Page 1 of 1 Town of Erving Select Board Public Meeting Participation Guidance The Select Board welcomes residents to communicate questions, comments or concerns. Participants at Select Board meetings are notified that the meetings are both video and audio recorded, and comments provided will become part of the record. While offering public input, it is important that the Select Board is also allowed enough time to conduct their other business. The following guidelines have been established to make the best use of time at Select Board meetings. 1. To request time on the Select Board agenda, persons must contact the Town Administrator at (413) 422-2800, Ext.1102 or at SBRequests@erving-ma.gov by noon on the Tuesday before the meeting. a. Requests will be submitted to the Chairperson for consideration and scheduling. b. Supporting documentation related to the request must be provided to the Administrator’s office by noon on the Thursday prior to the meeting. The Chairperson may remove requested agenda topics that are made without supporting documentation. 2. The Select Board encourages public participation as follows: a. Town residents can bring comments before the Select Board that require discussion and are on the agenda, only after being recognized by the Chair. If your issue is not on the agenda, you may bring it up under “Future agenda items”. b. “Topics not anticipated” should be brought to the Chair for possible consideration prior to the meeting. c. Please try to keep your comments short and to the point. d. If it appears that the topic(s) being discussed will consume longer than the time allocated then, at the discretion of the Chair, the matter will be placed on an upcoming Select Board meeting agenda. e. If you believe that your topic will require more time or desire to make a more formal presentation than is allowed under these guidelines, please contact the Town Administrator to ask to be put on a future agenda so that we can properly allocate enough time. f. You are free to ask questions or to make your point for all to consider. However, engaging in active debate with Select Board or audience members will not be allowed. g. All comments and questions must be directed to the Chair of the Select Board per MGL Chapter 30A, Section 20(g). h. Participants are expected to speak from the presenter/guest table. 3. Employees and Board members who have business with the Select Board should be placed on the agenda beforehand (see Item # 1.). 4. Anyone wishing to contact the Select Board in writing may do so at: Town of Erving, Attn: Select Board, 12 East Main Street, Erving, Massachusetts 01344 Alternatively, members of the public can complete a Select Board submission form at the meeting sign in table and office staff member will follow up. The Select Board appreciates your cooperation in honoring these guidelines. From Massachusetts Attorney General Official Website What public participation in meetings must be allowed? Under the Open Meeting Law, the public is permitted to attend meetings of public bodies but is excluded from an executive session that is called for a valid purpose listed in the law. Any member of the public also has a right to make an audio or video recording of an open session of a public meeting. A member of the public who wishes to record a meeting must first notify the Chair and must comply with reasonable requirements regarding audio or video equipment established by the chair so as not to interfere with the meeting. The Chair is required to inform other attendees of such recording at the beginning of the meeting. While the public is permitted to attend an open meeting, an individual may not address the public body without permission of the Chair. An individual is not permitted to disrupt a meeting of a public body, and at the request of the Chair, all members of the public shall be silent. If after clear warning, a person continues to be disruptive, the Chair may order the person to leave the meeting, and if the person does not leave, the Chair may authorize a constable or other officer to remove the person. title: City Council Meeting Agenda, October 6, 2026
text: FITCHBURG CITY CLERK Oct 01 2026 3:16 pm WELCOME TO THE FITCHBURG CITY COUNCIL October 6, 2026 Fitchburg Legislative Building 700 Main Street Fitchburg MA 01420 7:00 PM This meeting can also be viewed live on FATV. Go to www.fatv.org/watch-fatv for more information on accessing this meeting. This is intended to help you understand the meeting format and assist you with the rules of the Council as they pertain to your participation. All meetings of the Fitchburg City council are open to the public. This does not mean that the public participates in all aspects of the meeting. It simply means that the meeting itself, including all discussions and votes, is open for public view. Executive Session The only time a Council meeting can be closed to the public is when the Council votes for Executive Session in order to discuss sensitive matters in private, such as pending litigation. Any votes taken however, must be taken in open session. OPPORTUNITIES FOR THE PUBLIC TO SPEAK DURING A COUNCIL MEETING: Public Forum The Public Forum occurs immediately following the Pledge of Allegiance. The President will ask if anyone in the audience wishes to speak on any matter appearing on the Agenda. If you wish to address the Council, you must stand and be recognized and follow these rules before speaking: 1. 2. 3. 4. State your name and city of residence. Approach the center table and either stand or sit. This allows you to be seen and heard clearly by everyone in attendance. You may speak only on items appearing on the agenda for no more than (2) minutes. Copies of the agenda are available on the center table prior to the meeting. Please state the petition, order, ordinance, or resolution number to which you refer. Public Hearings Public hearings are held on various issues such as Special Permits and Zoning changes. The same rules apply with the following exceptions: 1. You must stand and be recognized either “in favor” or “in opposition” when asked by the Council President. 2. You need not refer to the petition number. If you have any questions or comments either before or after the meeting, any Councilor would be happy to assist you. Thank you for your interest! I. PUBLIC FORUM This meeting will be open to the public. Persons who wish to participate remotely in the Public Forum portion of the meeting may request a remote attendance link by contacting the City Clerk at cityclerk@fitchburgma.gov by 12:00 PM (noon) on the day of meeting. Page 3 of 3 PAGE 3 City of Gardner City Council - Informal Meeting of September 21, 2026 Minutes of the Informal Meeting Monday, September 21, 2026 – 6:00 P.M. City Council Chamber Roll Call Members Present: ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● President George Tyros Councillor Calvin Brooks Councillor Craig Cormier Councillor Alek Dernalowicz Councillor Dana Heath Councillor Brad Heglin Councillor Elizabeth Kazinskas Councillor David Thibault-Muñoz Members Absent: ● ● ● Councillor Karen Hardern Councillor Judy Mack* Councillor Paul Tassone *Councillor Judy Mack did not participate in this meeting due to being an observer in the negotiations. President Tyros entertained a motion to enter Executive Session pursuant to the Massachusetts Open Meeting Law as per the meeting notice. He stated that the Executive Session was being convened to discuss Union Negotiations Between the Teamsters (Department Heads) and the City. The noted exemptions were: Exemption #2 To conduct strategy sessions in preparation for negotiations with nonunion personnel or to conduct collective bargaining sessions or contract negotiations with nonunion personnel; and Exemption #3 To discuss strategy with respect to collective bargaining or litigation if an open meeting may have a detrimental effect on the bargaining or litigating position of the public body and the chair so declares (MGL c.30A, §21(3)); PAGE 4 City of Gardner City Council - Informal Meeting of September 21, 2026 As required by Chapter 30A of the General Laws, President Tyros declared that discussing these matters in open session would not be appropriate and detrimental to the negotiation proceedings. It was noted that the Council will not reconvene in open session at the conclusion of this executive session and that following the completion of business within the executive session, the Council will adjourn directly from that session. A Motion was made by Councillor Kazinskas and seconded by Councillor Dernalowicz to enter executive session. No Discussion. The motion to enter Executive Session was approved by roll-call vote, 8–0. Adjournment The Council recessed to Executive Session. In accordance with the posted notice, the Council did not reconvene in open session and adjourned upon completion of Executive Session. PAGE 5 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 21, 2026 Minutes of the Regular Meeting Monday, September 21, 2026 – 7:30 P.M. City Council Chamber Roll Call Members Present: ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● President George Tyros Councillor Calvin Brooks Councillor Craig Cormier Councillor Alek Dernalowicz Councillor Dana Heath Councillor Brad Heglin Councillor Elizabeth Kazinskas Councillor Judy Mack Councillor Paul Tassone Councillor David Thibault-Muñoz Members Absent: ● Councillor Karen Hardern A quorum was declared present. The Council rose for the opening prayer and pledge of allegiance. Open Meeting Law Announcement President Tyros announced that any person wishing to make an audio or video recording of the meeting, or transmit the meeting through any medium, was required to notify the Chair pursuant to Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 30A, §20. Reading of Minutes of Prior Meetings September 8, 2026 Regular Meeting Minutes Councillor Heglin moved to dispense with the reading of the minutes and accept them as presented. Councillor Heath seconded the motion. Page 1 of 10 PAGE 6 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 21, 2026 Vote: 10–0. Motion passed. Item 11935 – Response to Section 25 Information Request Regarding FY2026 Tax Title Proceedings and Properties Councillor Mack moved to place the communication on file. The motion was seconded by Councillor Dernalowicz. Councillor Mack thanked the Mayor for providing the requested information and expressed support for the City's efforts to pursue properties significantly delinquent on taxes, noting that 22 properties were currently in Land Court proceedings. Vote: 10–0. Motion passed. Item 11933 – A Measure Relative to the November 3, 2026 State Election Councillor Heglin moved that the measure be adopted. Councillor Kazinskas seconded the motion. There being no discussion, a roll call vote was taken. The motion passed 10–0. Page 2 of 10 PAGE 7 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 21, 2026 Vote: 10–0. Motion passed. Item 11841B – An Ordinance to Amend Attachment F of Chapter 8 of the Code of the City of Gardner, thereof entitled “Primary Non-Union Compensation Schedule,” to add the position of Golf Administrative Assistant Councillor Mack reported that the position was not currently covered by ordinance. Following review of the salary submitted by the Chair of the Golf Commission and discussions with the Director of Human Resources, Mayor, and City Solicitor regarding expenditures from the Golf Course Enterprise Fund, it was determined that an ordinance was necessary to establish the position. Councillor Mack moved that the ordinance be sent to its first printing. Councillor Heglin seconded the motion. Councillor Mack further discussed the municipal oversight applicable to salaries paid through enterprise funds and stated that establishing an enterprise fund does not create an autonomous entity for purposes of personnel compensation. She stated that the ordinance would establish the stipend position paid through the Golf Course Enterprise Account. On a roll call vote, the motion passed 9–0–1, with Councillor Dernalowicz abstaining. Vote: 9–0–1. Motion passed. Item 11870 – An Ordinance to Increase Financial Transparency, Financial Governance, and Budget Preparedness Page 3 of 10 PAGE 8 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 21, 2026 Councillor Heglin moved that the ordinance be sent to its first printing. Councillor Dernalowicz seconded the motion. Councillor Heglin reported that the Finance Committee had considered the ordinance during several meetings over the summer and had recommended it favorably. He stated that the ordinance was intended to improve financial planning and the City's budget process and to establish continuing requirements that would provide the City Council with information necessary to perform its financial oversight responsibilities. Councillor Heglin then proposed an amendment based upon feedback from Councillor Brooks to require expenditure reports monthly rather than quarterly. He moved to strike §XX-2(A) in its entirety and replace it with the following: “The City Auditor shall submit to the Finance Committee of the City Council, or in another manner as determined by the City Council, monthly reports on current expenditures.” Councillor Dernalowicz seconded the amendment. The Council briefly recessed to allow members to review the proposed amendment. Upon reconvening, the amendment was placed before the Council. On a roll call vote, the amendment passed 10–0. Vote: 10–0. Amendment accepted. Discussion then returned to the ordinance as amended. Councillor Brooks expressed support for the amendment and discussed the proposed five-year financial forecast. He stated that preparing such a forecast could be difficult but was worthwhile to attempt, and noted that the ordinance placed responsibility for the forecast on the Mayor. He also commented that the proposed revenue projections were comparatively straightforward and would provide an early indication of anticipated revenues before submission of the annual budget. On a roll call vote, the motion to send the ordinance, as amended, to its first printing passed 10–0. Page 4 of 10 PAGE 9 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 21, 2026 Vote: 10–0. Motion passed. Item 11889 – An Order Transferring Funds from the DPW New Salt Shed Account into the City’s Stabilization Account Councillor Dernalowicz reported that the Finance Committee had reviewed the item. He explained that funds for the salt shed project had originally been transferred from the Stabilization Account into a separate project account and that, with the project completed, the order would return the remaining balance to stabilization. Councillor Dernalowicz moved the order. Councillor Mack seconded the motion. On a roll call vote, the motion passed 10–0. Vote: 10–0. Motion passed. Item 11891 – An Ordinance to Amend the Code of the City of Gardner to Create a Regular Review Schedule for Various Rates and Fees to Ensure Financial Viability and Responsibility Councillor Heglin moved that the ordinance be sent to its first printing. Councillor Dernalowicz seconded the motion. Page 5 of 10 PAGE 10 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 21, 2026 Councillor Heglin reported that the Finance Committee had considered the ordinance several times and that the proposal followed the Council's previous discussions regarding water and sewer rates. He explained that the ordinance would establish a regular schedule for reviewing water and sewer rates, as well as requirements concerning solid waste fees, hauling contracts, notification to the Council regarding proposals and cost trends, and a five-year forecast of Solid Waste Enterprise Account expenses. He reported that the Finance Committee had unanimously recommended the ordinance. Councillor Brooks questioned how the schedule would apply to water rates given the Council's previous decision to adopt a one-year rate adjustment rather than a five-year schedule. Discussion indicated that water rates were expected to be reviewed again the following year notwithstanding the longer-term review schedule established by the ordinance. On a roll call vote, the motion to send the ordinance to its first printing passed 10–0. Vote: 10–0. Motion passed. Item 11913 – Application of Lollygag and Co. for a License to Deal in Second-Hand Articles at 13 Pleasant Street There being no objection, Council Rule 22 was suspended for consideration of the item. Councillor Cormier reported that the Public Safety Committee had met with the applicant and the Chief of Police and that neither the Police Department nor City Clerk had raised concerns regarding issuance of the license. He reported that the Committee had unanimously recommended approval. Councillor Cormier moved to approve the application. Councillor Thibault-Muñoz seconded the motion. On a roll call vote, the motion passed 10–0. Page 6 of 10 PAGE 11 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 21, 2026 Vote: 10–0. Motion passed. Item 11930 – An Ordinance to Amend Section 23 of Chapter 600 of the Code of the City of Gardner, thereof entitled “Parking Ban” There being no objection, Council Rule 22 was suspended for consideration of the item. Councillor Cormier reported that the Public Safety Committee had considered the proposed ordinance and that the issue had previously been discussed with the Traffic Commission. He stated that the Committee had voted to advance the ordinance to the full Council for discussion because of the approaching winter season. Councillor Cormier moved the ordinance. Councillor Mack seconded the motion. Councillor Cormier stated that, although the Committee had advanced the ordinance for discussion, he did not believe there was sufficient time to properly implement the proposed change for the upcoming winter. He favored further consideration for 2027, including additional opportunity for public input. Councillor Mack stated that she had initially supported returning to a date-based winter parking restriction but had reconsidered because of concerns regarding residents without adequate off-street parking, particularly residents of multifamily housing. She also expressed concern about the lack of public input and suggested further consideration of parking violation fees and other alternatives. Councillor Thibault-Muñoz stated that snow removal was an essential municipal function but expressed concern that a two-month citywide overnight parking prohibition would disproportionately affect renters, lower-income households, larger households, elderly residents, disabled residents, and families without convenient off-street parking. He suggested considering alternatives that would allow the City to adequately clear streets during snow events without imposing a continuous prohibition. Councillor Kazinskas stated that she could not support the ordinance as written. She acknowledged the public safety and operational concerns underlying the proposal but believed additional research and public input were necessary before the Council acted. She noted that Page 7 of 10 PAGE 12 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of September 21, 2026 she had received several communications from residents after the item appeared on the Council agenda and suggested that greater public outreach could improve consideration of the issue. Councillor Brooks discussed the increase in the number of vehicles and corresponding pressures on available parking. He stated that a broader, long-term discussion regarding parking was necessary and emphasized that residents who park on public streets must remove their vehicles when snow restrictions are imposed so that the City can properly clear the roads. Councillor Heglin stated that additional efforts should be made to improve implementation of the existing snow-parking system, including ensuring that the CodeRED notification system was functioning properly, encouraging residents to sign up for alerts, and potentially sending an annual citywide mailing explaining the parking rules. He also expressed appreciation for the efforts of the Police and Public Works Departments while noting that officers should not be expected to make extraordinary efforts to contact individual vehicle owners before enforcement. Councillor Mack emphasized the importance of beginning public education before the winter season, including using electronic message boards to encourage residents to enroll in CodeRED and ensuring that municipal parking lots were clearly posted with applicable parking rules. Councillor Tassone stated that he appreciated the feedback received regarding the proposal and noted that a number of issues had been discussed by the Traffic Commission. He reported receiving approximately 15 emails from residents expressing concerns and stated that he would not support the ordinance. Councillor Heath similarly noted the increased number of vehicles in households and thanked residents who had contacted him regarding the proposal. The National Volunteer Fire Council’s (NVFC) National Junior Firefighter Program supports fire and emergency service departments in fostering relationships and engaging youth in learning about, and ultimately becoming, members of the emergency services. The contents of this guide and other resources from the National Junior Firefighter Program are intended to help departments support youth involvement in the fire and emergency services. The NVFC does not advocate youth participating in operational/emergency response activities but recognizes that it is ultimately up to the individual department to determine the activities their youth can participate in and the associated liability that comes with these activities. Departments should consider consulting with a legal advisor or state fire association regarding specific participation or liability regulations within their state or locality. Visit www.nvfc.org/juniors for more information. For additional assistance, contact the NVFC at 1-888-ASK-NVFC (275-6832) or www.nvfc.org/contact. This guide was made possible through support from California Casualty, which provides auto and home insurance to educators, firefighters, law enforcement, and nurses across the country. Learn more at www.calcas.com. 3 INTRODUCTION A well-run junior program achieves two critical goals for a fire department. Firstly, and in the short term, it provides the department with needed personnel for non-operational tasks. In the long term, it provides a permanent pipeline for recruitment. Youth also benefit from junior firefighter programs as they build skills that will help them in the fire service and throughout life, such as teamwork, leadership, responsibility, and community service. build a solid foundation for your program. It provides step-by-step guidance to bring you from the initial conversation regarding junior firefighter programming in your department to welcoming new recruits through your bay doors. Throughout this guide, you will also find information on additional resources you can utilize to jumpstart the involvement of youth in your organization, find funding, train your junior firefighters, and maintain your program throughout the years. So where do you begin? Not only does it bring in new volunteers, an injection of youth and the energy they bring can invigorate your department for years to come. Traditionally, youth have joined on the heels of their family members, but with changing demographics and increased demands on peoples’ time, a program dedicated to ‘growing your own membership’ will prove a valuable asset. Whether you are a chief officer trying to determine what resources and personnel you need to start a program or a department member seeking approval to start a program, one thing is certain: support from your organization’s leaders and members is crucial. Without solid program leadership and interest from department members, the program cannot be successful. Ensure you have full buyin from your chief, administrative leaders, and members before formally launching your program. To obtain this buy-in, you will need to make the case as to why it is important for your department to encourage youth involvement and the positive impact they will have on both your department and the community. Some key points to make include the following: z z These young volunteers can help the department with non-operational tasks such as fundraising, events, and fire prevention education while bringing a new perspective and fresh ideas to the table. z Establishing a youth program will help your department form stronger bonds within your community as you grow a membership that is reflective of the neighborhoods you serve. In return, junior members learn critical skills such as leadership, teamwork, and responsibility. z Junior programs provide youth with invaluable experience and education in the fire and emergency services, and members of these programs often become lifelong supporters of their local department. z Consider showing the monetary value of the nonoperational support your junior firefighters will provide or the value of the time saved for your operational personnel. The NVFC’s Cost Savings Calculator helps demonstrate this value. You may have to alleviate concerns within your department about having youth present at your facility and events. A successful program has solid leadership that promotes safety first and ensures that there is no negative impact on the overall operation of your organization/department or its primary mission to protect and serve the community. A junior program is a great tool for recruiting potential future members and leaders of your organization. This applies to both the junior firefighters and the friends and family that they will introduce to the fire service that may then have interest in joining. It is in your best interest to consult with your insurance provider as well as with legal counsel before you start a program or change any existing requirements. Departments should check with their current insurance provider regarding requirements for youth who are present on their organization’s property and/or participants in organization activities or events, regardless of how they are involved. The advisors can make or break the program – from their character to how much effort they put towards the program, how much support they rally around it, how good they are as a mentor, and more. Hepburn ● Property Location: 982 Main Road, Granville, MA 01034 (Map 13, Parcel 41-0; Registry of Deeds Book 25200, Page 227) ● Requested Relief: Special Permit and/or Variance pursuant to M.G.L. c. 40A, §§ 6, 9, and 10, and the applicable provisions of the Granville Zoning By-Laws. ● Project Description: The applicant requests authorization for the continued use of an existing detached/integrated suite above a three-bay garage and main residence for commercial building activities, an Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU), a two-unit dwelling, and/or short-term and long-term rentals (Airbnb-type use). Review proposal from Gwendolyn Van Sant of BRIDGE for a Resolution Supporting Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitian Residents and Families G. Van Sant presented the resolution supporting the Haitian community. The resolution is included in the meeting packet materials. E. Gabriel moved to approve the Resolution Supporting Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitian Residents and Families as presented in the packet; G. Reed seconded. S. Bannon asked for any discussion – Erica Mielke (360 Park St.) and Lina Paulo spoke in support of the resolution and the Haitian Community in Great Barrington. The motion passed 5-0. e. Update on People’s Pantry location and operations Silke Aisenbrey, VP of Operations was present and described the need to relocate the Pantry from St. James. The Pantry is growing and is now serving 10 times the number of people than when it first moved into St. James. The Pantry is looking to increase services and programs and hopes to move by the end of 2026. S. Aisenbrey spoke about the need for increased pedestrian safety and communications with the Selectboard. The Selectboard expressed their thanks to the Pantry and agreed that increased pedestrian safety is a priority. There was furher discussion. f. Update on South Main Street Pedestrian Improvements L. Hartsgrove presented on the improvements to the pedestrian crossings at South Main and Reed Streets. The project engineer is Tighe & Bond. Proposed improvements include narrowing the road at the crosswalk, installing a raised crosswalk, curb bump-outs, flashing lights, and enhanced markings. L. Hartsgrove also recommends rumble strips prior to and after the crosswalk. L. Hartsgrove discussed the project costs and funding mechanisms, including $471,000 approved in FY27 Capital Funding. The recommendation is to put out a Request for Procurment that includes all five project locations along South Main Street. The Board provided feedback on the project. E. Gabriel moved to approve initial endorsement of the project; G. Reed seconded. S. Bannon asked for any discussion – there was none. The motion passed 5-0. g. Update on Brownfields sites: i. 426 Park Street aka “Cook’s Garage” L. Hartsgrove provided a historic review of the conditions of the Cooks Garage site, which was acquired through foreclosure. There was a partial collaps on August 20, 2026 of the structure, with portions falling into the Housatonic River. L. Hartsgrove discussed the immediate Town response and a planned path forward with departments including Public Works, Public Safety, and Conservation. MassDEP issued an emergency certification related to the emergency response activities associated with the collapse and debris in the Housatonic. Due to contaminants in the debris - asbestos and lead - staff cannot simply remove the materials; a qualified hazardous material removal team is required. 4a 9/14/26 minutes Page 4 of 5 The Action Plan includes addressing the fallen debris and protecting the river, controling the remaining structure to prevent further collapes, and develop a plan for disposal and redevelopment. Funding will be requsted at the October 19 Special Town Meeting for the removal of fallen debris. James Bailey asked about a previously awarded $200,000 Smart Growth Grant. P. Orenstein asked about the Town’s insurance coverage and L. Hartsgrove indicated that the building is not insured. She noted that all funding opportunities will be explored. 2026-191 2026-192 2026-133 Michelle Loubert, 70 Division Street, expressed concern over the building being uninsured. Tina Fisher, Cottage Street, asked about properties with “owner unknown” and any potential liability for the Town. C. Rembold noted, with regard to the insurance for the property, that the building itself was probably not insurable and that the Town does carry liability insurance. ii. 218 Main Street aka “Reid Cleaners,” and C. Rembold discussed the property and that the Town is using the most recent ECP assessment for Brownfield properties. He discussed previously awarded EPA grants that were utilized to address other Brownfields properties. He identified potential future uses of the property after cleanup. The building and site could be reused after cleanup. iii. 347 Main Street C. Rembold noted that the Town does not have a current title to this property yet. EPA Brownfield funds may be used at this property. h. Review FY28 Budget Action Calendar L. Hartsgrove shared the FY28 Budget Action Calendar, which has been reviewed by the Finance Committee, Chair Bannon, and other stakeholders. This will remain in draft form to ensure flexibility for any changes as needed. i. Review and approve Strategic Priorities S. Bannon reviewed the Strategic Priorities. E. Gabriel asked that hotel zoning become a priority as well as tax taking. He also asked for increased outreach and discussions with local businesses. E. Gabriel moved to approve the amended Strategic Priority Plan; G. Reed seconded. S. Bannon asked for any discussion – there was none. The motion passed 5-0. 7. PREVIOUS BUSINESS a. Continued discussion of the 79 Bridge Street hotel project Michael D’Ortenzio, Town Counsel, was present. He noted that this discussion could not be taken up under Executive Session under the provisions of MGL. E. Gabriel moved to release the information to the public; G. Reed seconded. S. Bannon asked for any discussion – there was none. The motion passed 5-0. M. D’Ortenzio discussed the special permit, which was granted with conditions in 2016, for the project at 79 Bridge Street. The permit was initially approved for an 88-room upscale boutique hotelHe noted that the developer owns the property outright and has no obligation to do anything with the lot beyond paying the 4a 9/14/26 minutes Page 5 of 5 taxes. In 2019 the Board modified the special permit and has the option to offer another amendment if it desires, or could revoke the permit. P. Orenstein remarked that the lack of progress on the project has had a meaningful impact to the Town. P. Orenstein moved to that the Selectboard rescind the special permit relating to the Searle School Hotel project effective December 31st 2026. However prior to the end of the year, this decision can be reversed by a vote of the Selectboard provided that the developer provides additional information indicating that meaningful progress has been made and a financing package is in place allowing construction work to begin along with an estimated timetable for completion.; G. Reed seconded. S. Bannon asked for any discussion – E. Gabriel confirmed with Counsel that the developer could argue that the permit is vested and the Board discussed possible arguments from both sides. The motion passed 5-0. 8. CITIZEN SPEAK AND MEDIA TIME Donna Jacobs, 260 Park Street, was present on behalf of the Great Barrington Library Board of Trustees. She discussed the Board of Trustee’s ability to raise funds and asked the Selectboard for clarification. Debra Herman, 373 North Plain Road, discussed the Old Maids Park and concern that the name was highly offensive. She asked for the park to be renamed. Michelle Revere, 72 Division Street, noted that she is not offended by the name Old Maids park. She also thanked the Board for fixing a dangerous pot hole and provided comments and thanks on items discussed in the meeting. J. Bailey asked for a response to a letter he sent to the Town. An unidentified speaker asked about use of the Gazebo on Monday, September 21 from 9:00 to 9:07 am for International Peace Day to hold a moment of silence. James Garzon, 84 North Plane Road, echoed J. Bailey’s sentiments. He thanked the Board for rescinding the permit for 72 Bridge Street. Narrative: Special Permit for Fence Construction Greenberg Residence, 267 Long Pond Road, Great Barrington Parcel 34-18-A, Zone R2, WQPOD Surface Water Zone B The property at 267 Lond Pond Road includes approximately 820 feet of frontage. About 40% of this frontage is open to the property around and north of the home, with barn, small orchard, and fields. The other ~60% is bordered by an existing 8-foot-tall stockade fence that connects to the garage. The property historically straddled Long Pond Road, with a 2.15-acre portion on the easterly side of the road. That smaller portion is now considered a separate parcel (parcel 3419-A). The home, built in about 1946, sits approximately 33 feet from the property line and 71.5 feet from the road. A corner of the garage sits within 1 foot of the property line (39 feet from the road). The existing structures are therefore nonconforming with the current 50’ front setback. In recent years, my client Melanie Greenberg has removed a portion of the 8-foot-tall fence connecting to the garage and installed a driveway/parking area (permitted in May 2023) relating more closely to the garage, mudroom and front entry. A 31-inch-tall stone wall and a wooden arbor sit at the end of the parking as a visual stop for cars and a welcome to the home and property. These elements relate in geometry to the home and garage and are thus not in line with the road or property line. The face of the wall sits about 24 inches behind the face of the garage, ranging from 15 feet to 21.5 feet from the property line (36 feet to 42 feet from the road). We wish to install an open lattice fence about 27.5 feet long atop the stone wall to help with a visual buffer between the road and the home, which has windows facing the road. As mentioned before, the home is extremely close to the road, which is unusual for Long Pond Road. The road is also higher than grade at the home, putting it in a superior viewing position, which contributes to the feeling of exposure from the main living floor and need for a tall fence. The lattice addition would bring the total height to 6 feet, for which a Special Permit is needed. The face of the garage sits proud of the face of the wall and proposed fence, already setting a visual precedent for structure and height within the setback. The lattice openings will be 4-5 inches square, with lattice slats only about 1 inch thick – much more than 50% transparency for the lattice portion. There are new plantings between the home and the wall, which are meant to be visible through and climb up the proposed lattice fence. There are also new plantings between the garage and the road, some of which are in front of the wall (see plant list following this narrative). These plantings were installed in 2026. The resulting 6-foot-tall fence/wall combination is meant to help with a visual buffer from the road, adding some privacy for this home that is uncommonly close to the road for the area. However, it will not be a solid fenced barrier. The 8-foot stockade fence it replaces walled off both the home and the road. This fence, however, adds beauty to both the home view and the road view. The large openings allow plantings to be seen through the fence, and the fence structure supports flowering vines, including the native Coral Honeysuckle. The height of the fence connects to an arbor at the end, a welcoming entrance to the property. It is our view and desire that this feature becomes a net positive for the home and the neighborhood. Walkers-by often look at the improvements to the entrance. What was un-viewable due to the 8foot-tall fence barrier is now more open and made lush with new plantings and stonework. We believe the lattice fencing will only add to its beauty. Please reference the included drawings and illustrations, and thank you for considering a permit for this construction. Respectfully submitted, Kirsten Baringer Walter Cudnohufsky Associates, Inc. for Melanie Greenberg 267 Long Pond Road, Great Barrington Greenberg Residence: Special Permit Fence Walter Cudnohufsky Associates, Inc. 8/17/2026 Page 2 The Project’s Relation to the Great Barrington Master Plan, dated Oct 10, 2013 The proposed project does not have significant relation to the Great Barrington Master Plan. However, by pulling cars and car parking closer to the street, it is helping to protect the Resource of Long Pond. Likewise, a decorative fence in this location makes best use of the existing infrastructure, keeping future owners from desiring to build closer to the Pond, Surface Water Zone A, and land listed in the Master Plan as a Priority Conservation Area (Figure 18, Master Plan Appendices Vol II, pg. 35). The project overall adds to and benefits the neighborhood, Long Pond, and the homeowner. title: Select Board
text: Posted 10.01.2026 at 2:00pm by MMS SELECT BOARD AGENDA Tuesday, October 6, 2026 7:00pm SusanMary Redinger, Ahmet Corapcioglu, Kara McGuire Minar, Eve Wittenberg, Eric Ward The meeting of the Select Board will be held virtually in accordance with Chapter 2 of the Acts of 2025, An Act extending certain COVID-19 measures adopted during the state of emergency and signed into law on March 28, 2025. To attend and have the ability to participate in meeting, use the Zoom link below. Display full name when entering Zoom. Join Zoom Meeting: https://us02web.zoom.us/j/89888842490?pwd=23fjI6PmU6QC4yUVTtximrwRsLoYal.1 Meeting ID: 898 8884 2490 / Passcode: 648017 One Tap Mobile: +16469313860,,89888842490# US // +19294362866,,89888842490# US (New York) AGENDA ITEMS 1) 2) 3) 4) 5) 6) 7) 8) Call Meeting to Order – SusanMary Redinger, Chair (7:00) Public Communication (7:00) Approve Prior Meeting Minutes of 9/10/2026 and 9/22/2026 (7:05) Vicksburg Square Presentation – Michael Sweeney, MassDevelopment (7:10) Super Town Meeting Scheduling – Michael Sweeney, MassDevelopment (7:35) Special Town Meeting Preparation & Implemented Changes (7:40) All Boards Meeting Scheduling (7:45) Consider and Vote to Amend One-Day License for Loyal Foe Brewing Due to Inclement Weather: From 9/27/2026 to 10/25/2026* (7:50) 9) Review and Vote to Approve Revised MVP Action Grant (NextGen) Submission* (7:55) 10) Town Administrator’s Report (8:05) 11) Select Board Reports (8:15) 12) Public Communication (8:25) 13) Adjournment (8:30) Next Regular Select Board Meeting Tuesday, November 10, 2026 *Denotes Select Board Vote Select Board Minutes Thursday, September 10, 2026, 9:00am Town Hall Meeting Room, 13 Ayer Road Select Board participants: SusanMary Redinger, Ahmet Corapcioglu, Eric Ward, Eve Wittenberg, Kara McGuire Minar Town Department participants: Town Administrator Dawn Dunbar and Assistant Town Administrator Julie Doucet DPW / Transfer Station Proposals and Strategy The Board discussed preparation for public information sessions on DPW and Transfer Station siting ahead of the Special Town Meeting. Eric and Eve will present, with a focus on educating residents about Comm97 and alternative capping options. Soil and CSA capping information will be offered separately, with DEP potentially participating. Site options C and D remain viable, while E appears cost-prohibitive. Two public sessions will be held one on October 5th @ 1:00pm via Zoom and the other will be held on Thursday, October 8th @ 7:00pm at the Council on Aging. They will outline pros and cons of each option and gather input before decisions later in the fall. Solar Project Discussions (Solect Energy and NextGen) The Board reviewed solar opportunities with Solect and NextGen. Solect’s Community Purchase Agreement requires ATM approval but is seen as lower risk, with siting work ongoing at several parcels. NextGen’s project raised significant concerns due to increased grant scope, unclear liabilities, and a model not yet used in Massachusetts. Members agreed confidence in NextGen is low, and Dawn will seek guidance from the state on withdrawal impacts and possible redirection of grant funds. Devens Update and Super Town Meeting Planning The members reviewed the Devens disposition process, noting a likely Spring ATM vote. Concerns were raised about the timing and preparedness needed for a potential Super Town Meeting for rezoning. Board members emphasized that extensive public education and consultant support are required, suggesting a shift to a fall timeline. Alignment among committees is evolving, and updated coordination with regional partners will be needed. FY28 Budget Process Overview Eric presented a revised FY28 budget framework structured around phases rather than fixed dates to improve clarity and collaboration. The memo clarifies the roles of the Select Board and Finance Committee under the Charter. The Board discussed potential guidance for departments, including limits on new hires and the use of percentage-based targets. The memo is considered ready, though detailed guidance will be refined further. Compensation and Classification Study The Board considered adding a compensation and classification study to the Special Town Meeting warrant. The Collins Center proposal would update job descriptions and verify market alignment, with the last study completed in 2016. Costs are moderate, and no major salary increases are expected. The Personnel Board supports the effort, and members agreed it is a worthwhile project to fund with free cash. Review of Goals The Board briefly reviewed ongoing goals. While no additional detail was provided in discussion, the topic remains part of the Board’s continuing workplan for the year. The meeting was adjourned at 12:15pm. Select Board Minutes prepared by Julie Doucet 1 September 10, 2026 Select Board Minutes Tuesday, September 22, 2026 2:00pm A special meeting of the Select Board (the “Board”) was held in-person on Tuesday, September 22, 2026 at the Harvard Town Hall located at 13 Ayer Rd, Harvard, Massachusetts 01451. Select Board Participants: SusanMary Redinger, Chair; Ahmet Corapcioglu, Vice-Chair; Eric Ward, Eve Wittenberg; Kara McGuire Minar. Town Department Participants: Dawn Dunbar, Town Administrator; Julie Doucet, Assistant Town Administrator; Jared Mullane, Finance Director; Michelle Stockman, Executive Assistant to the Town Administrator. A quorum was declared and the meeting was called to order by Chair SusanMary Redinger at 2:00pm. Michelle Stockman kept the minutes of the meeting. Fiscal Year 2028 Budget Guidance The Board discussed its strategic guidance to town department heads, boards, committees, and commissions for Fiscal Year (“FY”) 2028 budget development. A previous Board memorandum (“memo”) regarding the FY 2027 budget request submission process was referenced (Attachment A), and a document outlining the Board’s FY 2028 budget development philosophy was reviewed (Attachment B). The Board determined that town departments, boards, committees, and commissions would be advised to build FY 2028 budgets on a base increase of 3.25%, exclusive of debt, benefits, sewer subsidy, and raise and appropriation. Each would be invited to submit a separate, prioritized list of additional items with associated costs and justifications. The rationale for the 3.25% figure would be clearly articulated as aligning with the average projected inflation rate, thereby challenging the town to consider creative, cost-cutting solutions and limit the override. It was clarified that while the guidance would be shared with the schools, there was no requirement that they follow it. Developed budgets would be due to the Finance Committee in early 2027 for their review and recommendations. The Board concluded that the guidance memo would be drafted and presented at the next Board meeting for approval. Use of Rantoul Fund to Cover Cost of Compensation and Class Study Select Board Meeting Minutes – September 22, 2026 1 A motion was made by Mr. Ward and seconded by Mr. Corapcioglu to use the Rantoul Fund to cover $18,500 of the compensation and class study cost. With all in favor, the motion carried unanimously, 50. Prior to adjourning, the Board previewed scheduling and future agenda items. The Board approved the closing of the Harvard Town Hall on September 30 from 1:00-2:30pm so that town employees may attend Custodian Edward Stoffel’s retirement party. The meeting adjourned at 3:08pm. convened in 2025 to consider ways to encourage new housing development, including rezoning ITC • HWG unanimously recommended residential uses be permitted in ITC and building conditions reports for Vicksburg Square be updated to inform rezoning efforts (among other studies) • An Executive Office of Housing & Livable Communities (EOHLC) grant provided most of the funding for these updated assessments 11 Study Overview CONSULTANT TEAM WHAT WAS ASSESSED DELIVERABLES • Structural systems and stability • Building narrative • Exterior envelope (roof, walls, windows) • Hazmat report • ~1,300 hazardous material samples • Abatement cost opinions • Cost estimates: abate, stabilize, demolish • Cost Estimates ASSUMPTIONS & EXCLUSIONS Costs include: direct trade costs, 15% design contingency, general conditions (10%), insurance (1.5%), bonds (1%), fee (3%), escalation (9.33% to Summer 2027). Costs exclude: design fees, soft costs, owner's administration, MEP systems, interior renovation, furnishings. NOTES ON COST ESTIMATES • Source: Miyakoda Consulting, May 13, 2026; Fuss & O'Neill abatement opinions, February 2026. • Estimated costs do not full renovation or adaptive-reuse costs. Abatement is required for either stabilization (for adaptive-reuse) or demolition. 12 Summary of Key Findings • Total estimated abatement and stabilization cost: ±$44.0M • Hazardous materials abatement alone: ±$9.5M (buildings contain confirmed asbestos and presumed PCBs) • Allen Hall accounts for nearly 40% of total cost • Allen Hall is in imminent danger of further deterioration that will dramatically increase the costs to address the building condition • Revere & Knox Halls are in similar conditions with advanced levels of deterioration 13 Summary of Key Findings • Hale Hall is the most structurally sound of the four primary Vicksburg Square buildings • BOQs and Washington Hall are stable and require minimal, though meaningful, investment • Stabilization does not include any costs toward adaptive reuse/renovation Image: Unbraced chimney, Washington Hall. (ICON Architecture, 2026.) 15 Sherman Avenue Conditions Images (clockwise from top left): Wooden trusses in good condition (BOQs); typical view of pipe trench (BOQs); Washington Hall roof (well past useful life); example of damaged exterior wall system (Washington Hall). ABATEMENT) STABILIZATION (INCL. ABATEMENT) 17 Deteriorations Over Time 2017 Conditions 2026 Conditions • • • • • Roofing was already beyond its useful life, with brittle or missing shingles and localized roof-deck damage. Most visible roof framing and the majority of structural members were described as generally sound, in good condition, or in fair condition. Concrete porch spalling and delamination were present, but the recommended work generally involved localized repairs or temporary structural support. Allen Hall’s structure was characterized as mostly fair, while Knox Hall had a localized roof opening of approximately 2 feet by 3 feet. • • • Sloped roofs are now failing across all four buildings, and flat porch roofs have failed, allowing continued water infiltration. The assessment documents wet and rotted roof decking, mold growth, sill-plate rot, and failed porch-roof framing. Allen, Knox, and Revere now have significant concrete spalling and deterioration of reinforcing steel. Allen Hall is in the worst condition, with failed porch enclosures, standing water, mold, vegetation, and advanced deterioration. Knox and Revere have similar but less advanced damage; Hale remains the most structurally stable.
