The purpose of Article XV, Site Plan Approval, is to ensure the impacts of proposed development, whether allowed as a matter of right or by special permit, are in accord with the purposes of the Norton Zoning Bylaw; that proposed development preserves and protects the natural environment; that proposed development adequately provides in its design and layout for the transportation, water supply, drainage, sewerage, open space, recreation and amenity needs of the occupants; that proposed development minimizes, to the maximum extent feasible, any adverse off-site impacts to public facilities and services; including consideration of the developmental impacts on municipal revenues, services, and infrastructure; and that proposed development is in harmony with the existing neighborhood character and protects against adverse impacts to adjoining landowners. § 175-15.6 Objectives to be met. In evaluating and rendering a decision on a proposed development plan which requires site plan approval and/or a special permit, the Planning Board shall consider the degree to which the proposed development achieves the following objectives and may require conditions or modification to the proposed site plan to ensure the objectives are fulfilled: E. Developmental impact Evaluate the projected developmental impacts of the proposed development on municipal revenues, services, and infrastructure, including, but not limited to: (1) The estimated municipal revenues generated by the proposed development. (2) The projected impacts on municipal services and facilities, including public safety public works, and other municipal services, (3) The projected capital and operating costs to the Town associated with the proposed development. (4) The net developmental impact of the proposed development, considering both projected revenues and costs. § 175-15.7 Submission requirements. (14) Developmental impact analysis. The Planning Board may require the applicant to submit a developmental impact analysis prepared by a qualified professional acceptable to the Planning Board. Such analysis shall evaluate the projected impacts of the development on municipal revenues, services, and infrastructure, including but not limited to property tax revenues, public safety services, public works, and other municipal service demands. The developmental impact analysis shall be prepared at the applicant’s expense and ina form and level of detail acceptable to the Planning Board and may be subject to peer review in accordance with applicable law. or take any other action relative thereto. (PLANNING BOARD) FINANCE COMMITTEE: Recommended. Property is located at 390/390B Circuit St. in residential District A, as shown on the Assessor’s Map 59, Block 37, Lot 40, and recorded at the Plymouth County Registry of Deeds Book 59268 Page 0347. The applicant is a non-profit dedicated to supporting individuals and families impacted by Duchenne muscular dystrophy, seeking Site Plan Approval for a new educational retreat campus on the 9.176-acre property. The project envisions fully accessible retreat center providing 24-hour, year-round programming for guests ages 6 and older. Phase 1 includes construction of a 10,845 sq. ft. twostory Retreat Center (with program space, guest accommodations, and staff areas), a new paved driveway, and a 30-space paved parking lot (26 regular + 4 HC spaces). Future phases include four 800 sq. ft. cabins for overnight guests, a new animal therapy barn, an aquatic therapy indoor pool, and a staff/workspace facility. The existing property includes a main house, two working barns, guest cottage and a detached 2 car garage. Phase 1 demolition includes the 1.5 wood stable and one-story wood cottage. 7:35 P.M. – 21 Norwell Ave. - For a Special Permit under § 201-3.3, § 201-4.1 & 201-9.3 D (building circle) of the Norwell Zoning Bylaw. The applicant is seeking approval to raze the existing single-family dwelling at the pre-existing non-conforming premises as it relates to building circle and build a new 3,821 sq ft dwelling which will not be more non-conforming than the existing. title: Conservation Commission
text: Conservation Commission Meeting Agenda Date: Tuesday, October 6, 2026 Time: 6:00 PM *** NOTE EARLIER START TIME Location: Virtual Only Please join our meeting from your computer, tablet or smartphone. https://meet.goto.com/mtgtownpepperellmaus/conservationcommission You can also dial in using your phone. +1 (571) 317-3122 Access Code: 331-415-893 1. Public Hearings, Public Meetings & Appointments - PUBLIC WELCOME A. 6:05 PM - Continuation Of Public Hearing - Burkes Pond Dam Removal, Ongoing Restoration And Re-Naturalization, And Monitoring - MassDEP 259-0854 The Commission will consider a Notice of Intent filed by the Applicant, the Town of Pepperell Department of Public Works, and the Owner, Brian McPhail regarding the Burke’s Pond Emergency Dam Removal Project at 2 Blood Street in Pepperell, Massachusetts. Project design was underway to remove the dam for the purposes of ecological restoration. However, accelerated rates of deterioration warranted the emergency action taken to remove it, for which an Emergency Certificate was issued by the Pepperell Conservation Commission on December 16, 2025. Burke’s Pond Dam was located on Sucker Brook, approximately 2 miles upstream of the confluence of Sucker Brook with the federally designated Wild and Scenic ecological restoration. However, accelerated rates of deterioration warranted the emergency action taken to remove it, for which an Emergency Certificate was issued by the Pepperell Conservation Commission on December 16, 2025. Burke’s Pond Dam was located on Sucker Brook, approximately 2 miles upstream of the confluence of Sucker Brook with the federally designated Wild and Scenic Nissitissit River. Following the 2021 removal of the Keyes-Parker Conservation Area Dam, the Burke’s Pond Dam was the only remaining dam along Sucker Brook. Approximately 1.1 miles of the stream upstream of the dam were disconnected from the downstream reaches, limiting habitat access for target species such as the eastern brook trout. The majority of the Project area is within Riverfront area (7,050 sf), including 2,900 sf of overlapping Bordering Land Subject to Flooding. The Project has restored approximately 950 sf of Land Under Waterbodies and Waterways (LUWW). Additionally, approximately 60 lf of Bank were restored following removal of the obsolete structure. Supplemental materials to support the NOI were recently submitted to the Conservation Commission and MassDEP, including a Planting Plan and PostConstruction Monitoring Plan. B. 6:15 PM - Appointment - Al Patenaude, Planning Board Chairman - Planning Board Request To Discuss Proposed Zoning Articles For Fall Town Meeting And Town Meeting Support C. 6:20 PM - Continuation Of Public Hearing Re: The Commission Will Consider A Notice Of Intent Filed By Gabriel Gomes For Demolition Of The Existing Structure And Construction Of A New 4-Story Mixed Use Building With Associated Grading, Retaining Walls, Fencing, Surface Parking, Utilities, Stormwater Management Infrastructure. Work Is Proposed Within The 100-Ff Buffer Zone To Bordering Vegetated Wetlands And The 200-Ft Outer Riparian Area To A Perennial Stream At 81 Main Street, MassDEP 2590852 2. Review Of Draft Minutes A. Review Of Draft Minutes Of September 15, 2026 3. For Signature: Schedule Of Bills Payable 4. Conservation Administrator's Report A. Merrimack River Revive (MRR) - Work With NMCOG And Other Regional Municipalities B. Deer Hunting Season Extended Beyond December 31, 2026 In Zone 9 (Pepperell) 5. Matters That May Be Raised That The Chairman Didn't Reasonably Anticipate Upcoming Conservation Commission Meetings, 6 PM, Virtual Only. The deadline for applications to be heard at the October 20, 2026 meeting is October 1, 2026. The deadline for applications to be heard at the November 10, 2026 meeting is October 22, 2026.

Marchetti, Mayor of Pittsfield PITTSFIELD CITY COUNCIL REGULAR MEETING CITY COUNCIL CHAMBERS September 22, 2026 at 6:00 p.m. President Persip called the meeting to Order in regular session at 6:00 p.m. Present: Absent Councilors Amuso, Conant, Cunningham, Kavey, Lampiasi, Moody, Persip, Warren, White and Wrinn Councilor Costa In accordance with MGL Chapter 30A, Section 20, President Persip notified those present that the proceedings were being audio and video recorded. She also thanked the Pittsfield Fire Department and recognized Officers William Prendergast. Matthew Kiernan and for saving four lives by installing smoke detectors. Public Comment is in-person only. If you support the mission you need to support funding the mission. Kamaar Taliaferro, Pittsfield, spoke in reference to petitions from two councilors on surveillance. He insists on civilian oversight stating the councilors are the only oversight we have. We don't have Approval of the September 8, 2026, meeting minutes. Councilor White made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. APPOINTMENTS A communication from Mayor Marchetti appointing Jenny Bell to the Human Services Advisory Council. Councilor White made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti appointing Soumalia Bance to the Affordable Housing Trust. Councilor White made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti reappointing Floriana Fitzgerald to the Community Development Board. Councilor White made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. COMMUNICATIONS FROM HIS HONOR THE MAYOR A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order transferring and appropriating the amount of $200,000.00 from Overlay Surplus to fund the ongoing rehabilitation work at Springside House. Councilor White made a motion to approve. Councilor Warren asked what the previous $35,000.00 is intended for. Director Kerwood stated at this time they do not have plans for it. Councilor Warren stated there is a lot of work to be done at the Springside House. He asked the mayor about the recent vandalism issue and if the funds will be used to replace windows. The mayor said they will not be using these funds for that as they are seeking restitution from the individuals who caused the destruction. Mr. Kerwood stated there is a hearing scheduled for Monday to address this issue. Councilor Cunningham asked Mr. Kerwood what the timeline and estimated cost for this project is. Mr. Kerwood said they are good questions as the exterior has been addressed and they are currently working with an architect to complete the full build out and expect to have a plan and cost estimate to complete. They intend to use it for city offices, and they must add an elevator to the building to get out of lease space. The motion to approve carried by a unanimous of the ten members present. A communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Order authorizing the City of Pittsfield to enter into a Memorandum of Understanding with Berkshire Medical Center for the project at the North Street Roundabout. Councilor White made a motion to approve carried by a unanimous of the ten members present. PUBLIC HEARING Reports from the Ordinances and Rules Committee A public hearing on a report from the Ordinances and Rules Committee on a petition for the proposed "Battery Energy Storage Systems" Zoning Amendment, recommending to approve as amended 5/0. City Planner Kevin Rayner spoke on behalf of the petitioner. This amendment will replace the current ordinance that ls extremely restrictive and make it less restrictive. The state released regulations on how municipalities can regulate these uses, what is reasonable and what is unreasonable. This ordinance is close to what the state's model regulations are. The Community Development Board has created some intent and description as to why they deviated from the state law. The public hearing was open to the public to speak for or against for the first time, a second time, and a third time. No one appeared to speak at the public hearing. Councilor White made a motion to accept the report carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. Councilor White made a motion to Ordain. Councilor Cunningham inquired about the range for small, medium and large BESS. He questioned what kilowatt hour we want to say is safe. He said there should be a lower bound to what a small BESS is and change the definition to not include a generator or portable generator use cases. Planner Rayner stated that they already address this, it is in the ordinance and portables batteries are exempt from the provisions in the small battery storage and there is a clause within the medium scale where the building inspector can approve temporary medium scale batteries up to ten megawatt hours through the temporary used section 4.3. Anything over 100 megawatt hours is the sole jurisdiction of the state for permitting. Councilor Cunningham asked if there is a control for the lower bound. Planner Rayner said the medium is under C-15 with provisions found in Section 4.316 of the zoning ordinance and the small are by right under MGL. He is open to amending and adding a section for small. Councilor Cunningham made a motion to add a section to cover this. The city planner will add this under Section V, C17. Councilor Cunningham made the motion to amend stating all small-scale portable BESS units shall be exempt from the provisions of this section. Councilor Moody asked if the two-kilowatt hour section is being removed. Councilor Cunningham said we won't include that. Councilor Moody said it is important that it is not included. The motion carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. Councilor Cunningham asked Planner Rayner if small systems are allowed. Mr. Rayner said you will need a building permit to comply with the requirements of small BESS but not zoning approval. Medium and large scall requires a special permit by the Zoning Board of Appeals and site plan review by the Community Development Board. Councilor Cunningham proposed the question of whether the council should be involved with the approval process. No other members spoke in support of adding the council to the approval process. The motion to Ordain carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. A report from the Ordinances and Rules Committee on a proposal to reclassify a parcel of land located at 1 Federico Drive, recommending to approve 5/0. Jim Scalise from SK Design spoke on behalf of Federico Realty Corp and the Berkshire Mountain Collision Center. He stated this is the former FedEx facility that has a fully developed 14,850 sf building with access roadways, two curb cuts with water and sewer on a light industrial property. The proposal is to extend the neighboring light industrial zone. There is also general industrial and limited industrial that surround this parcel. They are requesting to extend the IL zoning from the abutting property to include 1 Federico. The reason for this is to allow operation of a collision center or an auto body shop at this location. This use will be entirely in the building. The proposal is to create a workflow inside the building with stations for automobile repairs. There is vehicle storage outside, but this site actually has a low portion to the rear, and they are proposing privacy fencing to shield and screen that area. This lot is surrounded by current industrial uses, and he believes that the building as it sits can be adaptively reused for this purpose. They have gone through a full site plan review and approval with the Community Development Board. They addressed traffic, sewer, water, stormwater, and all of those things are less impactful. They had unanimous support when it went to Ordinances and Rules. The zone changes go with the land so the approval is not only this particular use, but the land could be used for light industrial use rather limited in the long term. This is an expensive undertaking and a long-term investment from a local operator who wants to use this facility. This would be a low intensity use. The description in the zoning ordinance for light industrial uses that have light traffic and low noise impacts rather than general industrial. They believe it is in keeping with the neighborhood and request the council's consent to move this forward. The public hearing was open to the public to speak for or against for the first time, a second time, and a third time. No one appeared to speak at the public hearing. Councilor White made a motion to accept the report carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. Councilor White made a motion to Ordain. Councilor Wrinn stated he is a neighbor in this area, and he is in full support and said that we need more body shops in this community. We are on the right track with this adding more jobs and businesses. Councilor Amuso asked how many new jobs will this bring in. Mr. Scalise stated his filing shows 10-12 jobs. The motion to Ordain carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. REPORTS FROM COMMITTEES A report from the Ordinances and Rules Committee on a communication from Mayor Marchetti on an Ordinance amending City Code, Chapter 2, to rename the Office of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion, recommending to approve as amended 5/0. Councilor White made a motion to accept the report carried by a unanimous vote of the ten members present. Councilor White made a motion to Ordain as amended. Councilor Cunningham is concerned by the versions in the packet. He asked the mayor what problem this is intended to solve. The mayor said it is intended to solve two problems. If you want him to go on record to say that it takes us out of the federal guidance of DEi, you got it. He doesn't want the city to be jeopardized for funding and does not want to change what we have already done. He believes that poverty is the root of all our evils in the city and needs to be addressed. This revised office will allow us that opportunity. It is there to do what it has always done and the ability to work on poverty issues, to improve the quality of life for the people of Pittsfield. Councilor Cunningham asked if he had data to support that hiring practices and atmosphere is an issue. The mayor stated that we have an affirmative action plan that is used occasionally. It was used more often when we had an active affirmative action committee with the city of Pittsfield that lasted a few years. The creation of the DEi office was supposed to carry it further, but no appointments were made to the committees. Currently the city, the council and mayor are in violation of the affirmative action policy because there has not been a report provided . to the City Council since 2020. It was supposed to come from both personnel of both the school department and the city. Councilor Cunningham did not think the council would be in violation. The mayor is changing this to merge the Human Rights Commission and the Affirmative Action Committee together. He did not appoint because he directed the DEi office to create a joint committee that is currently being worked on. Councilor Cunningham asked if there has been progress. The mayor stated it is before the council tonight as a new, improved office, a new improved ordinance and a direction to create one committee to include both. The mayor said we all took the same oath, if we are missing something as a city, whether it be his responsibility or the council, we're all guilty because we all took an oath to uphold the Constitution of the United States and the rules and ordinances of the city of Pittsfield. It's nice that you can point fingers, but when something doesn't happen, it is on all of us. When the auditor wasn't appointed in a timely fashion he and Councilor Warren joked that it was his job to remind them to do their job. Councilor Cunningham is not going to take the blame for that because he was not on the council. Councilor Cunningham asked to speak to someone who is on this joint committee. The mayor stated the ordinance needs to be approved before he can put the joint committee forward which is part of this ordinance. Councilor Cunningham asked who put this ordinance together. The mayor stated it was him, Mr. Obasohan, Attorney Grierson, Attorney Pagnotta and Attorney Grandchamp and they met just prior to submitting the ordinance that had been in discussion for two years. Councilor Cunningham stated that he held off during the budget and is now going to hold people accountable. Councilor Cunningham asked Mr. Obasohan when the committee met. Mr. Obasohan said the committee had not met and when he came on board, he was set to combine the Affirmative Action Committee and the Human Rights Commission. This has taken an extended time as the ordinance has seen many iterations. Councilor Cunningham asked when he was hired. Mr. Obasohan stated that he was hired in 2022. Councilor Cunningham questioned why it took so long to fix and asked about amendment 2-154.4 (1) and what the DEi department did in the last four years. Mr. Obasohan said the mission was to develop the Office of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion. There was no department when he came in, he hired a coordinator, developed systems within the department, developing a budget, crafting a curriculum for workshops and trainings for all departments and getting to know all staff, crafting the ambassador program, recruiting and training along with getting involved with the community letting them know the department exists. They developed small community gatherings which took time. Along with supporting the schools and both superintendents assisting families that were experiencing racism and discrimination because there was no place to go within the schools. An assessment of what is happening in the department around language, our language access plan, and digital equity. Putting a name to the work that is happening will suit the department. Councilor Cunningham restated what took place over the past four years. He asked what existing problem do we have in the city. NOTES: ACTION TAKEN: Moved: Seconded: Condition(s): VOTED: Yea ___ Nay ___ Abstain ___ TOWN OF PLYMOUTH ACCOUNTING & FINANCE DEPARTMENT 26 COURT STREET, PLYMOUTH, MA 02360 PHONE: (508) 747-1620, EXTENSION 10247 WWW.PLYMOUTH-MA.GOV MEMORANDUM TO : SELECT BOARD FROM: TIFFANY PARK, GRANT WRITER, FINANCE DEPARTMENT SUBJECT: AUTHORIZATION FOR GRANT APPLICATIONS, AWARDS, AND/OR DONATIONS DATE: OCTOBER 2, 2026 To comply with Section 53A of M.G.L. Chapter 44 (Grants and Gifts; Acceptance and Expenditure), I recommend that the Select Board vote to authorize the application for, and (if awarded) acceptance and expenditure of, the following grants and/or gifts. USDOJ Edward Byrne Justice Assistance Grant – Tactical Equipment (Application) The Police Department will again partner with Plymouth County on an application to the FFY26 Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant (JAG) – Local Solicitation. Offered each year by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), the local solicitation component of the Byrne JAG program provides public safety and crime prevention support to cities and towns that qualify through the grant program’s statutory grant formula. Funds awarded to a town under the FFY26 solicitation may be used to provide additional personnel, equipment, supplies, contractual support, training, technical assistance, and information systems for criminal justice. Plymouth is one of three communities within Plymouth County identified as qualifying applicants for this year’s grant cycle—with Brockton and Middleborough being the other two. As in years past, the County Administrator’s Office will apply for, and administer, the grant on behalf of Plymouth, Brockton, and Middleborough. Plymouth’s formula allocation, calculated through the federal FFY26 grant cycle, is $20,999.00. The Police Department will utilize Plymouth’s allocation of the Byrne JAG grant for the purchase of tactical breaching equipment (door rams and Halligan tools) for all of its marked cruisers. The provision of this equipment within each cruiser will eliminate the need for responding officers to wait for specialized personnel, during incidents when rapid entry to a building may be required to protect officers, victims, or members of the public. Page 1 of 2 MEGA Insurance Loss Control Grant – Purchase of Replacement AEDs (Application) The Town’s Safety Compliance Officer will apply for $5,000.00 through an insurance grant opportunity, to purchase automated external defibrillators (AEDs) for Town facilities. The Town’s new Workers’ Compensation insurance carrier, Massachusetts Education & Government Association (MEGA), offers an annual Loss Control & Safety grant program. Offering a maximum award of $5,000.00, MEGA ‘s program aims to fund loss control and safety equipment and/or initiatives, to provide a safe and healthy environment for employees. Presently, the Town furnishes at least one AED in each of its municipal facilities where employees are regularly assigned/stationed. Several of Plymouth’s AED units, however, have reached the end of their useful life cycle and require replacement. The Town’s Safety Compliance Officer, therefore, is working towards the systematic replacement of outdated AED units, beginning with the municipal locations that house the most employees and receive the most visitors from the public: ▪ ▪ ▪ ▪ Town Hall Center for Active Living Library (Main Branch) Airport If awarded with MEGA grant funding, the Town will immediately procure the AED equipment and deploy it to the currently established locations within the identified facilities. It is anticipated that the selected new AED units will have a useful lifespan of approximately ten years. Contributions Made to Plymouth’s Mobile Wildlife Education Center (Donations) The Department of Energy and Environment (DEE) respectfully requests Select Board authorization to accept and expend the following generous contributions made for DEE’s Mobile Wildlife Education Center. ▪ ▪ Sustainable Plymouth, Inc: $550.00 Thomas & Kathryn Gloster: $50.00 Both donations will be used towards the cost of funding new taxidermy and educational displays within the trailer, which is used at various events, such as the annual Plymouth Herring Run Festival, DCR events, and local Boy Scout programs. Contribution Made to the Fire Department (Donation) The Manomet Community Garden Association, Inc. has made a generous, unrestricted donation of $200.00 to the Plymouth Fire Department, to be used for general fire safety purposes. RILEY CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-133 ORDERED: October 05, 2026 ORDINANCE ESTABLISHING A ROLLING FIVE-YEAR CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT PLAN WHEREAS, sound long-term capital planning enables the City to identify, evaluate, and coordinate needed investments in its buildings, infrastructure, facilities, equipment, and other capital assets; WHEREAS, a multi-year Capital Improvement Plan provides the City Council, the Mayor, City departments, and the public with a forward-looking view of the City’s planned capital investments, anticipated costs, timing, and funding sources; WHEREAS, capital projects may be funded through municipal bonds or other borrowing, grants, City funds, revolving funds, and other resources, and comprehensive capital planning should consider such projects regardless of funding source; and WHEREAS, an annually updated five-year Capital Improvement Plan promotes responsible fiscal planning, helps coordinate capital needs with available resources, and supports informed decision-making regarding the City’s long-term development and financial commitments; NOW THEREFOR BE IT ORDAINED that the City Council of the City of Quincy, as follows: Section 1. Rolling Five-Year Capital Improvement Plan. The Mayor shall submit to the City Council a rolling five-year Capital Improvement Plan (“Plan”) no later than February 1 of each year. The first Plan shall be submitted no later than February 1, 2027, and shall cover Fiscal Years 2028 through 2032. The Plan shall identify the capital projects and capital improvements the City anticipates undertaking during the five-year period, regardless of funding source, and shall include, for each project, the anticipated cost, timing, and funding source or sources, including municipal bonds or other borrowing, grants, City funds, revolving funds, and other resources. ORDER NO. 2026 – 133 Page 2 of 2 The Plan shall be revised and extended annually to update the status of projects and add one additional fiscal year to the five-year planning horizon. The Plan shall be submitted to the City Council and made available to the public. Section 2. Effective Date. This ordinance shall take effect upon passage and publication as required by law. INTRODUCED BY: WARD TWO COUNCILLOR – RICHARD C. ASH WARD FIVE COUNCILLOR – MAGGIE MCKEE WARD SIX COUNCILLOR – DEBORAH A. RILEY CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-134 ORDERED: October 05, 2026 Order Regarding the City of Quincy’s Noise Control Advisory Board WHEREAS, Chapter 215 (entitled “Noise”) of the City of Quincy Code was amended and/or restated in 2010; WHEREAS, at this time, the City adopted and/or instituted a Noise Control Advisory Board (the “Board”); WHEREAS, said Board has been signed into law to “advise the Mayor, Director of Inspectional Services, City Council, and Planning Board on noise control issues, including administration and enforcement of this chapter;” WHEREAS, the Board consists of seven members including one Chairperson and one Vice Chairperson, appointed by the Mayor and confirmed by the City Council; WHEREAS, the Board must meet at the call of the Chairperson as required to perform its duties, but not less than once each quarter, and a majority of the members of the Board constitutes a quorum for transacting business; WHEREAS, no later than March 1 each year, the Chairperson of the Board must report to the Director of Inspectional Services, the Mayor, the City Council, and the Planning Board on activities and actions the Noise Control Advisory Board took during the previous calendar year; WHEREAS, over the last ten (10) plus years, the City of Quincy has experienced one of the most transformative construction booms in its history, resulting in a significant increase in residents and the overall population; WHEREAS, in recent years, there has been a noticeable uptick in excessive speeding, drag racing, and loud vehicle noise; ORDER NO. 2026 – 134 Page 2 of 2 WHEREAS, excessive speeding, drag racing, and loud vehicle noise lead to a Summer 2026 “pilot program” that closed Wampatuck Road and Chickatabot Roads within the Blue Hills Reservation in Quincy on the weekends; WHEREAS, nearby municipalities have recently amended their respective laws and/or legislative authority to enhance precautions related to and/or to prohibit high noise outputs near residences; WHEREAS, nearby municipalities have recently amended their respective laws and/or legislative authority to include restrictions on vehicles with modified exhaust systems and/or muffler cutouts or bypasses; and WHEREAS, nearby municipalities have recently approved appropriations for “noise cameras” and/or increased police presence in problem areas. NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the Administration, including but not limited to the Noise Control Advisory Board, the Quincy Police Department, and the Inspectional Services Department review and present recent considerations, issues, complaints and suggested remedies; NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that the Administration, including but not limited to the Noise Control Advisory Board, the Quincy Police Department, and the Inspectional Services Department review and consider benefits of adopting or changing current measures to address the adverse effects these issues have on our residents’ quality of life; THEREFORE, BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that this review should include financial and environmental concerns for all residents, any or all contractors and also the City’s first responders. INTRODUCED BY: WARD THREE COUNCILLOR – WALTER HUBLEY CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-135 ORDERED: October 05, 2026 RESOLUTION ORDERING A REVIEW OF CITY WEBSITE USAGE AND NAVIGATION REQUIREMENTS FOR POPULAR ONLINE MUNICIPAL SERVICES WHEREAS, the City of Quincy is committed to providing efficient, accessible, equitable, and responsive municipal services to all residents; and WHEREAS, the City Council previously requested a review of resident interactions with City Hall and opportunities to expand accessible online municipal services, and the Administration provided a responsive report dated September 16, 2026, concerning Council Order No. 2026-36; and WHEREAS, that report indicated that most of the most frequently requested constituent services can already be completed online through the City website, departmental portals, and related digital platforms; and WHEREAS, during subsequent discussion of that report, it was observed that the City website does not currently provide reporting tools sufficient to quantify how many constituents request or complete a given online service; and WHEREAS, it was further observed that the City does not currently report the number of clicks or selections required for a resident to locate and access the most popular online services from the City website; and WHEREAS, accurate measurement of website usage for popular constituent requests would allow the City to identify high-demand services, evaluate resident demand over time, and support data-driven operational and budgetary decisions; and WHEREAS, measuring the number of clicks or selections required to reach popular services would help identify opportunities to simplify website navigation, reduce friction, and make frequently used services easier to find; and WHEREAS, website analytics and navigation-path measurement are established tools for improving digital service delivery, provided that any such tools are implemented consistent with applicable privacy, cybersecurity, and accessibility standards; and ORDER NO. 2026 – 135 Page 2 of 2 WHEREAS, improving the findability of popular online services can complement the City's existing investments in information technology, website accessibility, and online municipal services; and WHEREAS, a focused review of website usage data and click-path requirements will assist the Council and the Administration in considering optimizations that make popular services easier to locate while preserving in-person and assisted options for residents who need them; NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Quincy City Council hereby requests that the Administration, through the appropriate departments, explore options for providing actual usage data for the City website and related online platforms with respect to popular constituent requests and services; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that such review identify, to the extent practicable, the most frequently used online municipal services and report available or obtainable measures of usage, including page views, form starts and completions, or comparable metrics; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the report include an accounting of the number of clicks or selections required for a resident to locate and access the most popular online services from the City website homepage or other primary entry points; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the report outline options and considerations for implementing or expanding website usage reporting, including but not limited to available tools, estimated costs, staffing implications, cybersecurity, data privacy, and integration with existing City systems and digital platforms; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the report identify opportunities to optimize website navigation so that the most popular services are easier to find, while maintaining compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and applicable accessibility and language-access standards; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the report be submitted to the City Council within a reasonable timeframe to assist the Council in evaluating future policy, operational, and budgetary decisions related to digital municipal services. INTRODUCED BY: COUNCILLOR AT LARGE – ANNE M. MAHONEY WARD FIVE COUNCILLOR – MAGGIE MCKEE WARD SIX COUNCILLOR – DEBORAH A. RILEY CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-136 ORDERED: October 05, 2026 Quincy Center Station and Long-Term Redevelopment WHEREAS, Quincy Center Station is one of the City’s most important transportation hubs, connecting the Red Line, commuter rail, bus service, pedestrians, businesses, residents, and the surrounding downtown; and WHEREAS, the former Quincy Center parking garage was closed in July 2012 because of significant structural deterioration, and more than fourteen years later the station property remains without the comprehensive redevelopment long envisioned for this critical downtown site; and WHEREAS, over that period, various proposals have contemplated replacement parking, improved bus and rail connections, pedestrian and accessibility improvements, transitoriented development, and mixed-use redevelopment; and WHEREAS, despite prior planning efforts, development proposals, and subsequent demolition of the deteriorated garage, comprehensive redevelopment of Quincy Center Station has not moved forward; and WHEREAS, during the same period, the City has made substantial public investments in roads, utilities, parking, public spaces, and other downtown infrastructure, while significant private development has transformed much of Quincy Center; and WHEREAS, significant transit infrastructure and station modernization projects have also advanced in other communities throughout the MBTA system, while Quincy Center remains a visibly unfinished component of the City’s downtown revitalization; and WHEREAS, the Mayor of Quincy holds significant leadership roles within the MBTA governance structure, giving the City an important voice in regional transportation policy and capital planning; and WHEREAS, the MBTA’s FY2027-FY2031 Capital Investment Plan now includes approximately $96 million in authorized funding associated with Project P1165, involving work at Quincy Center including garage-related infrastructure and relocation of the adjacent traction power substation; and ORDER NO. 2026 – 136 Page 2 of 2 WHEREAS, after more than fourteen years, the City Council and the public should have a clear understanding of what has delayed comprehensive redevelopment, what efforts have been undertaken to advance it, what the current investment will accomplish, and what the long-term plan is for Quincy Center Station. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that the Quincy City Council requests a comprehensive written and public update regarding the history, current status, and future of Quincy Center Station and the surrounding MBTA property. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that this matter be referred to the appropriate committee of the Quincy City Council for Oversight, and that representatives of the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority, MassDOT, the MBTA Advisory Board, and the Mayor’s Administration be invited to participate. As part of that review, the Council requests a chronological report beginning with the closure of the Quincy Center parking garage in 2012 and continuing through the present, identifying: 1. Each major plan, proposal, study, development concept, agreement, approval, funding commitment, and significant decision involving Quincy Center Station; 2. The City, MBTA, MassDOT, Commonwealth, private developer, or other parties involved in each initiative; 3. The follow-up or next steps contemplated after each major proposal or decision, whether those steps occurred, and, where they did not, the reasons the initiative did not advance; 4. The actions taken by the City and the Mayor’s Administration to advocate for, fund, or advance the redevelopment and modernization of Quincy Center Station; 5. The improvements and infrastructure work actually completed since 2012 and the funding committed, expended, or programmed during that period; 6. The current scope, funding, design status, and anticipated schedule for MBTA Project P1165, including what the approximately $96 million investment will accomplish at Quincy Center; 7. The current long-term vision for the station and surrounding MBTA property, including transportation improvements, passenger amenities, accessibility, parking, bus and rail connections, pedestrian circulation, and potential transit-oriented or mixed-use development; and 8. The specific next steps required to advance the project, including responsible parties, funding needs, major milestones, and an anticipated timetable. The report should clearly distinguish between what was proposed, what was approved, what was funded, what was completed, what remains outstanding, and what is planned next. The purpose of this Oversight review is to provide the City Council and the public with a clear record of what has occurred at Quincy Center since 2012, what progress has been made, what barriers have delayed further redevelopment, and what specific plan now exists to move the station forward. INTRODUCED BY: WARD ONE COUNCILLOR – DAVID A. JACOBS WARD FIVE COUNCILLOR – MAGGIE MCKEE WARD SIX COUNCILLOR – DEBORAH A. RILEY CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-137 ORDERED: October 05, 2026 RESTITUTION ON THE THOMAS CLASBY CASE WHEREAS, former Elder Services Director Thomas Clasby Jr. pleaded guilty to stealing more than $136,000 from the City of Quincy, including money collected through programs and café sales at the Kennedy Center; and WHEREAS, the court ordered Clasby to pay approximately $136,000 in restitution to the City; and WHEREAS, the Council on Aging and the seniors it serves were most directly affected by his actions; and WHEREAS, restitution for these thefts should be used for the benefit of Quincy’s seniors. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that it is the wish of the Quincy City Council that the full amount of restitution received from Thomas Clasby Jr. be placed in the Council on Aging Department budget and used solely by that department for programs, services, and other needs that benefit Quincy’s seniors, rather than being used for unrelated purposes through the City’s General Fund; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the City Council requests that the Mayor and the City’s financial officials take the steps necessary, consistent with applicable law and the City’s appropriation process, to make the full amount of restitution available to the Council on Aging Department; and BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the City Council requests to be notified when restitution payments are received and to be shown where those funds have been added to the Council on Aging Department budget. INTRODUCED BY: MAYOR THOMAS P. 4) Administrative ➢ Request to transfer local filing fee funds for MACC training The next Conservation Commission virtual meeting is scheduled for Wednesday, November 4, 2026 ---PUBLIC HEARING GUIDELINES The meeting will be conducted with decorum. This means that the members of the Commission and the public are required to respect each other at all times. We may not always agree with one-another but we can work to resolve differences with patience and understanding. As a member of the public, your questions will be answered in an orderly manner IF you follow these procedures: (1) Raise your hand to be recognized. All those who wish to be heard will be heard. (2) Direct all questions to the Commission through the Chair. (3) Limit your questions and statements to five (5) minutes. After everyone has had a turn to speak, you may be given a second chance to speak, time permitting. (4) Limit your statements/questions to the applicant’s project. (5) Talk ONLY about issues that are under the jurisdiction of the Conservation Commission. These include issues dealing with wetlands, the ocean, streams, quarries, and vernal pools, among many others. The commission DOES NOT have authority over building heights, zoning issues, rights of way, property ownership, or historic structures, to mention but a few. The order of discussion is as follows: (1) The applicant will make his/her presentation. (2) The Conservation Commission will question the applicant. (3) The public will then be given time to ask questions about the project. The commission will then either: (a) conclude that they have sufficient information and close the hearing: No new information will be accepted except under extra ordinary conditions, or (b) the hearing will be continued to a date certain where all will be permitted to participate. The date and time of this continuance will be announced ONLY at the first and subsequent meetings. You have the right to record any session of this meeting if you inform the chairman prior to the session. If you have any questions about procedures, please feel free to contact our agent, John Lopez at 978-546-5005 during regular office hours, which are Monday through Wednesday 9:30 AM – 12:00 PM and Thursday 12:00-3:00 PM. The volunteer members of the Rockport Conservation Commission work for the people of Rockport. Please help us serve you better by keeping us and yourselves informed. Mel Higgins Chair

Notwithstanding section 14 of chapter 64G of the General Laws or any other general or special law to the contrary, the City of Salem is hereby authorized to impose an annual excise on the privilege of operating a short-term rental, as defined in the City’s short-term rental ordinance, in the City of Salem. The excise shall be payable by the operator of the short-term rental in the amount of $1,000 per unit per year for a short-term rental of a residential unit that is not the operator’s primary residence, as those terms are defined in said ordinance, and $500 per unit per year for all other short-term rentals. The City Council may, by ordinance, adjust said amounts annually by not more than the 6 CITY OF SALEM October 8, 2026 REGULAR MEETING percentage change in the Consumer Price Index for the preceding year. The excise shall not apply to a short-term rental of a room or rooms within a residential unit that is the primary residence of its owner while the owner is present, or to a short-term rental located in a lodging house or bed and breakfast licensed or permitted as such by the City. The excise shall be in addition to any short-term rental registration fee, room occupancy excise, or community impact fee imposed under any other general or special law. SECTION 2. The excise authorized by this act shall be adopted by ordinance of the City Council of the City of Salem, with the approval of the Mayor, which ordinance shall establish the effective date of the excise and provisions for its collection, enforcement, and abatement. SECTION 3. Notwithstanding section 53 of chapter 44 of the General Laws or any other general or special law to the contrary, the City of Salem is hereby authorized to establish a Housing Stability Fund, into which all revenue collected from the excise authorized by this act shall be deposited. The Fund may also receive appropriations, gifts, grants, and investment earnings. Any balance in the Fund at the close of a fiscal year shall not revert to the general fund. Monies in the Fund may be expended, subject to appropriation, only for emergency shelter, transitional housing, and homelessness-prevention services, and reasonable costs of administering such programs. SECTION 4. This act shall take effect upon its passage. Section 10.0 Definitions is hereby amended by inserting the following definition after the definition for “COOP”: Data Center: A facility, or portion thereof, primarily designed or used to house computer servers and related information technology infrastructure for the storage, processing, management, or transmission of electronic data. A Data Center may include, but is not limited to, server racks, data storage systems, cooling systems, power conditioning equipment, substations, uninterruptible power supplies, backup generators, telecommunications equipment, security systems, and associated mechanical and electrical infrastructure. For purposes of this ordinance, a Data Center shall not be considered an Office, Warehouse, Manufacturing, or Research use. A Data Center shall not include such computer servers and related information technology infrastructure that is accessory, incidental and subordinate to a lawful principal use at the same facility, or portion thereof. However, this exception does not cover a separate business providing data storage, server hosting, distributed processing, or similar technology to third parties. Sampson, S. Hoctor, P. Ellis, C. Holden, D. Sullivan G. Dunham, Town Manager; H. Harper, Assistant Town Manager Mr. Sampson opened the meeting at 6:00 PM. PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE PUBLIC COMMENT None. REVIEW AND APPROVAL OF MINUTES Mr. Holden moved to approve the minutes of September 10, 2026 as presented. Seconded by Mr. Ellis. Approved unanimously (4-0). • TOWN MANAGER REPORT The next Board meeting is in two weeks - October 8, 2026. • The DOR will be holding an auction for the year round all alcohol license seized from Carluccio's. It will take place on Tuesday at noon at Carluccios. The State has set a beginning bid of $25,000 plus 10% with increases of $5,000. • Mr. Dunham thanks the DPW for all the paving that has been done throughout Town. • Storm preparation - the Emergency Management team met and County Management as well. Updates are being received by email. • The Cape Cod Metropolitan Planning Organization that deals with transportation issues needs a representative from Upper Cape. There is one designee from the Upper Cape, which is a 3-year appointment for a Select Board member. If interested contact Steve Tucker. Mr. Ellis has agreed to do it. • Ms. Harper reported that there is a community event scheduled for Substance Abuse Prevention month. It will be on October 16th at 7:30 PM at the CAL. There will be a keynote speaker on helping parents understand the effects of substances on the brain and how to have meaningful talks with their children about it. The event is supported by the Opiate Settlement funds. Sandwich Fest will be next weekend, and the Town table will be located in the area of the Hoxie House; several departments will be represented. • The Base has been going through a master planning process overseen by Mass Development. They have been holding sessions on different topics and yesterday's topic was water and wastewater. The meeting had to be moved, from the Base and the CAL offered to hold it, so it was held there. We were well represented in comparison to other towns. We emphasized the regional approach to dealing with wastewater at the Base. We are still having trouble getting information from the State -for over ten years. Mr. Dunham thanked the staff at the CAL for having the meeting there; it looks like several more may need to meet there as well. CORRESPONDENCE/STATEMENTS/ANNOUNCEMENTS/FUTURE ITEMS/FOLLOW-UP Mr. Holden reported that the School Safety Committee met and talked about technology and facility updates and potential expansion. October is National Pedestrian Safety month. The Town of Sandwich will be undertaking public outreach; this will include cooperation from the Sandwich Police Department at Truck or Treat. The Mass Trails grant for Service Road/Canal path included discussion with the Commission on Disabilities. There has been progress on the Cape Cod Commission bike rack program. The School Committee met and student reps were introduced. Curriculum and professional development priorities for 26-27 school year were presented by Dr. Quinn and K-6 curriculum director Jen Kirk. School improvement and action plans for the three schools were presented and approved unanimously. The Sandwich Emergency Management services are prepared for the storm, and the CERT has been alerted for support. Mr. Sampson encouraged anyone who needs support during the storm to contact the CAL for help. There was an open house at Sandwich Media that was well attended. STAFF MEETING 6:05 Public Hearing- Seasonal On-Premises All Alcoholic Beverages Liquor License to Fork Selah Boss, 331 Cotuit Road - Kemroy Jarrett, Proposed Manager. Mr. Sampson read the hearing notice. Mr. Hoctor moved to open the public hearing. Seconded by Mr. Holden. Approved unanimously (5-0). Mr. Jarrett is present. His plan is to bring seasonal wines and special cocktails to the restaurant. He and his family have many years' experience as cooks and in the restaurant business. The restaurant will serve Jamaican/American food. It will be a family-oriented restaurant that will have a dining room and bar. It is currently undergoing renovations, and the estimated opening is in late February or early March. They want to be involved in the community. All checks have been completed. No input from the public. Mr. Hoctor moved to close the public hearing. Seconded by Mr. Holden. Approved unanimously. Mr. Hector moved to approve the Seasonal On-Premises All Alcoholic Beverages Liquor License to Fork Selah Boss, 331 Cotuit Road - Kemroy Jarrett, Proposed Manager as presented. Seconded by Mr. Holden. Approved unanimously. OLD BUSINESS Town Hall Restoration Project Update Ms. Harper reported that progress has been awesome. The scope of work is 99% complete. They need to refinish the floors and the stage. The Arts Alliance will be holding an events concert on October 9th • Mr. Hoctor asked if there would be an open house for the public -yes. Other Matters Not Reasonably Anticipated for Old Business None. NEW BUSINESS Approval of Election Warrant A copy of the State election warrant articles is in the agenda packet. Mr. Hoctor moved to approve the election warrant as presented. Seconded by Mr. Holden. Approved unanimously. Recommended Conservation Commission Alternate Appointment-Jack Vaccaro Mr. Hoctor moved to approve the appointment of Jack Vaccaro as a Conservation Commission Alternate. Seconded by Mr. Holden. Approved unanimously. Other Matters Not Reasonably Anticipated for New Business None. PUBLIC COMMENT None. CLOSING REMARKS Mr. Holden says to continue to pray for peace, restraint among leaders, and protection of innocent life with justice guided by wisdom. Mr. Sampson reminded the public about the upcoming Sandwich Fest and encouraged people to prepare for the storm. Mr. Sampson said that the Board will be moving to Executive Session according to M.G.L. c.30A, §21 (a)- The Chair declares that having an open session may have a detrimental effect upon the Town's bargaining, litigating, or negotiating position, as applicable: Purpose: to comply with the Open Meeting Law G.L. c.30A, §22(f)- Review, potential approval and potential release of Executive Session meeting minutes -9/10/2026 Purpose #6- Disposition of Real Property- Town Hall Lease, 130 Main Street. Mr. Hoctor moved that the Board go into executive session, not to reconvene in public session. Seconded by Mr. Holden. Approved unanimously by roll call vote. SECTION 30911 PURPOSE To develop, implement and maintain laws and regulations that will enhance and preserve the ecological health, pristine waters and the natural beauty of waters within the limits of the town of Scituate for future generations, to preserve the public peace, good order and welfare, to protect the coastal waters within the limits of the town of Scituate and all beaches, flats, tidelands and submerged lands lying seaward of the line of the mean high water, to prevent encroachments therein, to promote, preserve and protect the exercise and enjoyment of the public rights of fishing, fowling and navigation; to promote, preserve and protect the exercise of marine and aquacultural uses and pursuits while sustaining harmony among all users of waters within the limits of the town of Scituate. SECTION 30912 FAIR ACCESS TO FISH, FOWL AND NAVIGATE A. Notwithstanding any provisions of these by-laws to the contrary, fair access to waters within the limits to fish, fowl and navigate is hereby recognized to exist within the waters of the town of Scituate. The abovedescribed activities may, subject to certain rules and regulations occur on holidays, weekdays, and weekends by night or day and shall include the attendant incidental impacts associated with normally accepted fishing, fowling and navigation practices. It is hereby determined that whatever impact may be caused to others through the normal practice of accepted fishing, fowling and navigation practices is more than offset by the benefits of each of these activities to the community and society in general and fair and 7 equitable access to the waters within the town of Scituate for such activities. The benefits and protections of this by-law are intended to apply exclusively to those recreational and commercial accepted fishing, fowling and navigation operations and activities conducted in accordance with generally accepted fishing, fowling and navigation practices. Moreover, nothing in this by-law shall be deemed as acquiring any interest in land, or as imposing any land use regulation, which is properly the subject of state statute, regulation, or local zoning law. B. The right to commercially and recreational fish and conduct aquaculture activities is hereby recognized to exist within the Town of Scituate, it's waterways and extend out to three nautical miles. This Bylaw should not impact, change or restrict access to: commercial wharfs, piers, floats, docks; moorings, parking, loading/un-loading areas, both publicly and privately owned that are used for local catch sales, exports of commercial catch both domestic and international. Activities may occur on holidays, weekends and weekdays on both private and town owned property. There may be instances when incidental noise from commercial equipment and or odors of catch and bait are unavoidable. The town shall be cognizant of parcels of land; both residential and commercial that store commercial equipment and that commercial fishing is a year-round process of building/repairing gear for specific targeted species of seafood. The referenced commercial activities shall be recognized by the town as part of the Town's historical heritage to avoid potential conflicts and nuisance claims. In part, Commercial fishermen shall be stewards of our working waterfront and promote economic opportunities consistent with the goals of the Town as expressed through its various boards, committees and actions. Moreover, nothing in this Bylaw shall be deemed to authorize acquisitions of land, and or to impose regulations, which actions are subject to state law, local zoning, Town By-laws and the vote of town meeting. Sullivan, S. Smith, M. Bingham, S. Escaler, P. Dunn, J. Perry, S. Smith, B. Hoch, and John Aubin (Town Planner) Absent with cause: Chair D. Sullivan opened the meeting at 7:05 PM Regular Business: 1. Site Plan Application of Jose DeSousa for a dual-use solar field, on the property located at 0 County/ 0 Miller, being AP 5, Lots 16 and 9 within an R-4 Zoning District. Continued from August 11th, 2026 D. Sullivan introduced the continued application. J. Aubin stated the applicant submitted a revised plan and also a buffer plan. It was confirmed that all the equipment is located outside the 25-foot vegetative buffer area. The applicant is also subject to a 10-foot height limit at the property line for that buffer, as established by the Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA). The access has also been revised, but confirmation from the Fire Department has not been made. Implementation of the site plan has not been discussed yet. He asked if the applicants wanted to come explain the changes they made. B. Hoch disclosed that he is a direct abutter to this application and said he wanted to excuse himself from the discussion at 7:06 pm. Jessie Alderman, the applicant's outside counsel from Foley and Hoag, was present to speak on the buffer zone. He stated there is more than 25 feet of a buffer zone around the solar field at all points. He explained the green area shown on the plan is shaded to show active farming areas. He stated this is a dual-use property with solar and agricultural. He stated they had revised the access road so now it stretches 12 feet and will have a 51-foot turnaround area for an F350 truck. In terms of the 10-foot height requirement from the ZBA, additional screening beyond the buffer around the property. They had originally proposed arborvitaes that would grow to that intended height. They have not reached a final resolution with the abutter due to the elevation discrepancy between hers and the subject property. D. Sullivan asked if this 10-foot buffer is in addition to the other buffer requirements. J. Aubin answered it would only be an additional 4 feet; 10 feet in total height. D. Sullivan asked if we were able to obtain a zoning determination letter from the Zoning Enforcement Officer that states the use for this parcel. J. Aubin stated that the Building Department is still in the process of obtaining a new Zoning Enforcement Officer. D. Sullivan asked about the decommissioning surety bond since it was not discussed at the last meeting. Andrew Hamel from Weston and Sampson Engineering said a decommissioning estimate was submitted in the original application, but he does not remember the exact amount. Page 2 of 6 Planning Board Minutes September 8, 2026 D. Sullivan asked J. Aubin to make sure that the amount provided is sufficient. J. Aubin said the operation and maintenance plan should also be provided but that the applicant could loop it in with the Fire Department's plan submittal package. Jessie Alderman asked if the Board will approve with an additional condition for a 10-foot buffer height. D. Sullivan said the Planning Board is more so reinforcing the Zoning Board’s condition. Outside counsel asked for more clarification on which property line this condition is placed on. J. Aubin said the Planning Board seems to be agreeable to letting the applicant work out with the abutter which area to put this buffer but would like to see the final plan before anything is signed to ensure the issue has been addressed. J. Alderman asked for more clarification as to which borders. J. Aubin suggested anywhere the height does not already reach 10 feet. J. Aubin physically showed where he was describing on the plan. D. Sullivan asked for specific language so that if anything changes, the borders still apply. J. Aubin suggested along the southwest property line of lot 13 and lot 80 A. Hammel asked if the Board needed anything else besides the decommissioning cost estimate. D. Sullivan said that was all. Rebecca Henderson, 961 County St, an abutter to the subject property, was present. She said she reached out to BlueWave after the last meeting and they told her that her questions could be continued tonight. J. Aubin said the Planning Board cannot force them to put anything on her own property but that the buffer should be on their property. R. Henderson said she thinks it was kind to offer to install any screening on her own property. She said she is in a unique situation but also appreciates all the collaboration that has taken place. It was confirmed that if a tree falls or any unexpected view opens up, it is the responsibility of the applicant to correct that. S. Escaler asked if the Fire Department has given a final approval. J. Aubin said they have not given any final approvals, which is why J. Aubin invited them to the next Technical Review Committee (TRC) meeting. J. Perry made a motion to approve the proposed site plan with stipulations such as a 25-foot buffer, the 10-foot height zoning condition, review of the decommissioning surety bond, and the confirmation of the Fire Department access and review, and all conditions stated in the Town Planner’s memo. Seconded by S. Smith. VOTE: 5-0-1 (B. Hoch recused due to being an abutter) 2. ANR Application of Tony Albuquerque to create three non-buildable parcels, one of which will be added to 84 Massasoit to correct an occupation issue and two for future use for the property located at 0 Olney Street being AP 7, Lot 1 within an R-3 Zoning District. J Aubin said this is a large parcel behind Mohawk Drive and Cole Street. There is an encroachment onto the property from another property on Massasoit Drive. This ANR plan will resolve that encroachment issue as well as create two smaller parcels not for development. Mark Mariano from Oakhill Engineering was present to represent the applicant. M. Mariano stated the applicant intends to downsize and eventually sell his house. The two smaller parcels will not be buildable due to the lack of frontage. J. Perry made a motion to endorse the ANR of Tony Albuquerque to create three non-buildable parcels as presented for the property located at 0 Olney Street. Seconded by B. Hoch. VOTE: 6-0-0 3. Category 17A Earth Removal and 17B Earth Import review- Lynch Corp. for the property located at 0 Taunton Avenue, being AP 12, Lots 422, 423, and 424 located in an Industrial Zoning District Page 3 of 6 Planning Board Minutes September 8, 2026 D. Sullivan introduced the application into the record. J. Aubin said this is an annual application for earth import and export but we are still waiting for a formal application to be filed. He suggested continuing this application until we receive that application. S. Smith made a motion to continue this application for Category 17A and Category 17B for Lynch Corp. at 0 Taunton Avenue to the next meeting. Seconded by M. Bingham. VOTE: 6-0-0 4. Discussion of amendments to the Zoning By-laws of the Town of Seekonk for submission to the Select Board and Town Meeting for formal consideration. J. Aubin directed the Board to the documents from Town Council. J. Aubin then went over each individual amendment. The first Amendment deals with extensions to a non-conforming use. Right now, in a residential district, to extend a non-conforming use, you need a special permit. This amendment would allow that change by right. Amendment number two is regarding abandonment of uses. Previously, abandonment would occur after a use was abandoned for two years or more with some other indication of abandonment. The amendment changes this from two to four years. Amendment three changes the trigger for protection from subsequent zoning amendments from the issuance of a permit or special permit to just the application for such permit or relief. These changes are due to the Massachusetts budget act amendment that came with zoning changes. The proposed zoning amendments will bring Seekonk back into conformance with the State Laws. J. Aubin stated the next amendment extends the time for which a special permit must be acted upon. This change goes from six months to two years. The next amendment removed the requirement regarding frontage and depth for a single- and two-family residential use. J. Aubin expounded on this for the Board. J. Aubin stated the next amendment changes the definition of a variance. M. Bingham asked who decides the difference between a substantial hardship and a practical difficulty. J. Aubin answered the Zoning Board of Appeals. The next amendment removed language in the definition of variances. The next amendment allows for residential use variances where they were not allowed at all before. Next, this adds data centers to the list of prohibited uses. J. Aubin said a definition of a data center should be added. He then went over what the Town of Mansfield has done. A conversation about data centers was had. J. Aubin does not think that Seekonk has the infrastructure to support data centers but still believes the Board should have regulations in place regardless. D. Sullivan thinks the Board should send out a memo to other boards such as Conservation, Board of Health, Zoning Board, and the Select Board to get their input on how to write the language. D. Sullivan thinks this should also be its own warrant article. J. Perry made a motion for the submission and transmittal of the Zoning Amendments. Seconded by M. Bingham. VOTE: 6-0-0 5. Update and discussion of recommendations to the Zoning Board of Appeals regarding the 40B application located at 95 Sagamore Road. J. Aubin said that the applicant is saying the Subdivision Rules and Regulations should not apply, as their application does not qualify as a subdivision. The applicant is also saying that the multifamily requirements should be waived as well. The applicant is also asking for their roadway width requirements to be waived, as well as sidewalk requirements. Further discussion ensued about how the board should reply. D. Sullivan said that he believes the multifamily development requirements should be applied. He also stated that for the record, he does not agree that this development does not qualify as a subdivision and believes the rules and regulations should still apply. J. Aubin suggested the Board be as specific as possible. Page 4 of 6 Planning Board Minutes September 8, 2026 D. Sullivan stated that the Planning Board issue a statement that says this development qualifies as a multifamily development and therefore those construction standards should apply. He also believes that the 5.6 environmental impact statement should not be waived. S. Smith said he could understand a waiver for the sidewalks because that has been done before; however, the street width requirement should not be waived. D. Sullivan said he agreed but also feels sidewalks would be important here from a safety perspective as there will be families and a lot of traffic going in and out. D. Sullivan reiterated the list of items the board believes should not be waived. It was stated that the roads will stay private. Further conversation about eliminating access on Miller Street and safety was had. M. title: NOTICE OF SITE VISIT Zoning Board of Appeals
text: TOWN OF SOMERSET ZONING BOARD OF APPEALS NOTICE OF SITE VISIT Date & Time: Thursday, October 1, 2026 — 5:15 P.M. Location: Stevens Street, near and around the property site located between County St. & Riverside Ave., Somerset, MA 02726 Please be advised that the Somerset Zoning Board of Appeals will conduct a site visit on Thursday, October 1, 2026, at 5:15 p.m. at Stevens Street, near the tanks located between County Street and Riverside Avenue. The purpose of the site visit is to allow members of the Zoning Board of Appeals to observe and visualize the proposed height of the sound wall associated with the pending Salt Cod Energy B.E.S.S. Planned Development application. This site visit is for observation purposes only. No deliberation or decision-making will take place at the site. Amy L. Messier Town Planner

title: Planning Board Public Hearing - Sign Bylaw Amendments
text: DIANE SUPCZAK-MULVANEY, Chair BOB SZKLARZ, Vice Chair BRAD HUTCHISON, Clerk LINDA GOUIN, Member VACANT, Member JOHN MULLIN, Associate Member Anne Capra, Director of Planning & Conservation acapra@southhadleyma.gov TOWN OF SOUTH HADLEY PLANNING BOARD NOTICE OF HYBRID PUBLIC HEARING Amendments to the Zoning Bylaw Regarding Signs The Planning Board will hold a hybrid public hearing on October 5, 2026 at 6:30 PM to consider comments from the Office of the Massachusetts Attorney General regarding their review and denial of certain provisions of Section 255-85 Signs as amended by Annual Town Meeting on May 13, 2026, specifically 255-85 (G) (2) fine provision and Section 255-85 (G) (3) enforcement mechanism because this text conflicts with state law. Such provisions were disapproved by the Attorney General. The Planning Board will consider amendments to the above referenced sections of the bylaw for submission to the November 9, 2026 Special Town Meeting for adoption. The public hearing will be held through hybrid format with in-person attendance to be located in the multipurpose room of the South Hadley Senior Center, 45 Dayton Street South Hadley MA 01075. Virtual attendance will be hosted through the log-in information below: URL to join: https://us02web.zoom.us/j/86811043641?pwd=gutF0ZiarRQLVbl4EDXwdYBhwnwhVt.1 Or join by phone: +1 (646) 558 8656 Webinar ID: 868 1104 3641 Passcode: 751020 Materials are available on file in the Planning & Conservation Department Office (Room U6) in Town Hall and is posted at www.southhadley.org on the Planning Department page under ‘Proposed/Draft Bylaws’ or can be viewed at: https://www.southhadley.org/1318/ProposedDraft-Bylaws. Any person interested in, or wishing to be heard, should appear/join the hearing at the time and in the manner designated. Publication: Friday, September 18, 2026 Friday, September 25, 2026 Brad Hutchison, Clerk South Hadley Planning Board
