text: COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS WILLIAM FRANCIS GALVIN SECRETARY OF THE COMMONWEALTH ~ WARRANT FOR 2026 STATE ELECTION Ss. To the Constables of the City/Town of SUTTON GREETINGS: In the name of the Commonwealth, you are hereby required to notify and warn the inhabitants of said city or town who are qualified to vote in Primaries to vote at: Precinct One at the Middle/High School, 383 Boston Rd. Precinct Two at the Fire Station, 345 Manchaug Rd. Precinct Three at the Middle/High School, 383 Boston Rd. On TUESDAY, THE THIRD DAY OF NOVEMBER, 2026, from 7:00 A.M. to 8:00 P.M. for the following purpose: To cast their votes in the State Election for the candidates for the following offices and questions: SENATOR IN CONGRESS For this Commonwealth GOVERNOR and LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR For this Commonwealth ATTORNEY GENERAL For this Commonwealth SECRETARY OF STATE For this Commonwealth TREASURER For this Commonwealth AUDITOR For this Commonwealth REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS Second District COUNCILLOR Seventh District SENATOR IN GENERAL COURT Worcester & Hampden District REPRESENTATIVE IN GENERAL COURT Eighteenth Worcester District DISTRICT ATTORNEY Middle District REGISTER OF PROBATE Worcester County REGIONAL SCHOOL COMMITTEE Blackstone Valley District QUESTION 1: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. This proposed law would exempt documents related to the development of public policy and communications between legislators and their constituents, if those communications are reasonably related to a constituent’s request for assistance in obtaining government-provided benefits or services or interacting with a government agency. A YES VOTE would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. ; A NO VOTE would make no change to the Massachusetts Public Records Law. QUESTION 2: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would specify that employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services (“CPCS”) are permitted to engage in collective bargaining with their employer. It would also require CPCS, after executing a collective bargaining agreement, to request the appropriation necessary to fund such agreement from the Governor. A YES VOTE would specify that Committee for Public Counsel Services employees may form a union to collectively bargain with their employer. ANO VOTE would make no change to the law governing labor relations for Committee for Public Counsel Service employees. QUESTION 3: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would eliminate political party primaries for state elections and instead establish a system where there would be a single, all-party primary in which all candidates, regardless of their party affiliation, would be listed on one ballot, and voters could vote for any candidate on the ballot. The two candidates receiving the most votes in the primary would advance to the general election ballot. This proposed law would require candidates for governor and lieutenant governor to run and be listed jointly on the ballot in the primary. ; This proposed law would provide political party status to any group whose candidates for any statewide office received at least 3% of the ballots cast in the state primary. A YES VOTE would eliminate separate patty primaries for state elections and require a single primary in which all candidates appear on one ballot, voters could vote for any candidate, and the top two candidates would advance to the general election. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing primary elections. QUESTION 4; LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would permit eligible individuals to register to vote or update their voter registration address on Election Day. : An individual who is eligible to vote could register to vote on Election Day by going to the polling place in the “precinct where they live during voting hours and presenting proof of residency and signing a written oath. Proof of residency could be a valid photo identification, or documentation showing the individual’s name and the address where the individual resides, such as a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, residential lease, wireless telephone statement, paycheck, current student fee statement or other document from a post-secondary school, or another government document or correspondence. The written oath would require the individual to certify that they are a citizen of the United States, are at least 18 years old, are not legally prohibited from voting, and have not and will not vote in the same election at another location. The oath would require the individual to acknowledge that providing false information is a felony punishable by not more than 5 years imprisonment or a fine of not more than $10,000, or both. If an individual did not present proof of residency, they would be allowed to cast a provisional ballot, which would be counted only if the individual returned to provide the required information before the close of polls for a municipal election; within two days after a state primary; or within six days after a state election. Individuals who register to vote on Election Day would be registered to vote in future elections as well as in the election taking place that day. Individuals who are already registered to vote would not be able to change their political party affiliation on Election Day. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028. A YES VOTE would permit eligible citizens to register to vote or to update their voter registration address at their polling place on Election Day. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing voter registration. QUESTION 5: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would change the limit on how much revenue the state can collect in a given year. The proposal would limit state revenue in a given year to the net amount of state revenue from the year before, increased by a rate equal to the average growth of wages and salaries in Massachusetts over the most recent three years. If revenue collected by the state in a given year exceeds the limit, the excess amount would be refunded to taxpayers the following year. The proposed law would include all revenue from the surtax on incomes over $1 million when calculating the revenue limit and when determining whether state revenue exceeds the limit. The provisions of the proposed law would all be effective as of July 1, 2027. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect. A YES VOTE would change the limit on state revenue collection, tying it to prior year collections plus average wage and salary growth, and provide for a rebate of revenue exceeding that limit. ANO VOTE would make no change in the law relative to state revenue collection. QUESTION 6: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would establish a Nature for All Fund that, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, would receive 50% of state taxes collected from the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses for the first year of its operation. After July 1, 2028, the Nature for All Fund would begin receiving, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, 100% of state taxes collected on the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses. The sales tax revenue received by the Nature for All Fund would exclude sales tax revenue transferred to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority State and Local Contribution Fund and the School Modernization and Reconstruction Trust Fund. The proposed law would allow the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to spend the money in the Nature for Afl Fund for natural resource conservation. The proposed !aw would allow public and private donations to the Nature for All Fund. The proposed law would prevent the state comptrolier from transferring surplus funds in the Nature for All Fund at the end of the fiscal year. It would also allow state agencies, municipalities, public charities involved in natural resource conservation, tribal governments, and other regional public entities to receive money from the Nature for All Fund. Natural resource conservation would include the conservation or restoration of land to protect drinking water, streams, rivers, lakes, coasts, farms, forests, connectivity between open spaces, and lands and natural resources of indigenous cultural significance. Natural resource conservation would also include the creation, improvement, and management of parks, trails, greenspaces or outdoor recreation access. The proposed law would establish a 15-member Nature for All Board that consists of five state officials and ten members of the public appointed by the Governor. The proposed law would require the ten members of the public to include representatives of underserved communities and indigenous peoples and at least one person with expertise or experience in natural resource conservation. The proposed law would allow the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to spend money from the Nature for All Fund to hire staff to manage the fund. The proposed law would also require the Nature for All Board to establish rules about how the money in the Nature for All Fund should be spent, including rules regarding alignment with environmental justice principles, access to and restoration of lands and natural resources of indigenous cultural significance, promotion of affordable housing development, and other matters regarding spending and bond issuance. The proposed law would require the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to submit an annual report to various state committees regarding the funds spent to buy or improve land in cities and towns containing environmental justice populations. ; The proposed law would take effect on July |, 2027. AYES VOTE would create a fund that could be utilized for natural resource conservation that would receive some state taxes collected on the sale and use of sporting goods and recreational vehicles, and the use of golf courses. ANO VOTE would not create this natural resource conservation fund or change how sales and use taxes are spent. QUESTION 7: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would allow single-family homes to be built in a residentially zoned area as long as the land on which it is to be constructed is at least 5,000 square feet, has at least 50 feet of land bordering the street, road, or public way that it faces, and has access to public sewer and water services. The proposed law would allow cities and towns to reasonably regulate certain aspects of those single-family homes, including their height, distance from neighboring buildings, open space, parking requirements, and whether they can be rented out on a short-term basis. The proposed law would also allow the Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities to issue guidance or regulations to administer the proposed law. AYES VOTE would allow single-family homes to be built on lots of 5,000 square feet or more in residential areas, subject to reasonable local regulation of certain aspects of those homes. ANO VOTE would make no change to the law relative to building single-family homes. QUESTION 8: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY The proposed law would change the type and amount of marijuana that may legally be possessed in Massachusetts by repealing the laws that legalize, regulate, and tax the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana in Massachusetts. The proposed law would also permit persons 21 years of age and older to possess 1 ounce or less of marijuana including no more than 5 grams in the form of concentrate, and to gift or transfer to another person 21 years of age and older 1 ounce or less of marijuana including no more than 5 grams in the form of concentrate. The proposed law would also impose a civil penalty of $100 and forfeiture of the marijuana for the possession of marijuana between the weight of 1 and 2 ounces. For persons 21 years of age and younger, the proposed law would make the possession of 2 ounces or less of marijuana a civil infraction subject to a $100 fine, forfeiture of the marijuana, completion of a drug awareness program and community service, and notification to their parents or legal guardian of the offense and penalties. The proposed law would allow currently licensed adult recreational marijuana businesses to apply on an expedited basis to become a licensed medical marijuana dispensary and to sell their remaining inventory of adult recreational marijuana to medical marijuana dispensaries. The proposed law would retain the Cannabis Control Commission but modify its authority so it would regulate only the medical marijuana market. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028. A YES VOTE would prohibit the legalization, regulation, and taxation of the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana, and change the penalties for possession of marijuana. A NO VOTE would make no change to the law relative to marijuana. QUESTION 9: REFERENDUM ON AN EXISTING LAW Do you approve of a law summarized below, which was approved by the House of Representatives on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 124 to 33, and approved by the Senate on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 35 to 5? SUMMARY This law makes a number of changes to Massachusetts laws governing firearms. The law adds school administrators and licensed healthcare providers as parties permitted to ask a court to issue an Extreme Risk Protection Order — requiring an individual to surrender or relinquish their firearm licenses, permits, and firearms - if an individual is a present danger to self or others. The law also provides that, when issuing an Harassment Prevention Order, a court may also order the surrender of firearms licenses, permits, and firearms. The law imposes penalties for possessing, creating, and transferring untraceable “ghost gun” firearms and requires all firearms except antiques and relics, including unfinished frames and receivers that can be readily made into a finished product, to have serial numbers. The law includes privately-made guns like 3D-printed guns within the provisions governing untraceable “ghost gun” firearms. The law changes firearms licensing requirements to: (1) allow local licensing authorities to request prior license and permit information from the state, as well as access petitions for involuntary mental health commitments denied by a court in addition to prior involuntary commitments, as a part of their review of applications for licenses to carry firearms, firearm ID cards, and licenses to sell firearms; (2) require an individual to be 21 years of age to own semiautomatic rifles or shotguns; (3) add the possibility of incarceration of up to six months for a second offense of failing to report a firearm loss or theft; and (4) enable 12-15 year olds to apply for a self-defense spray permit with parental permission, and 15 to 18 year olds to apply independently. The law allows local firearm licensing authorities to transfer the responsibility to inspect firearm dealers to the State Police. The law requires local licensing authorities to attend statewide training regarding those inspections. It requires dealers to confiscate expired or suspended licenses and report them to the state and to local licensing authorities. The law changes the definition of “machine gun” to include bump stocks, trigger cranks, Glock switches and auto sears among the devices whose possession and use are subject to penalties. It expands the definition of “silencer” to include the parts used to construct a silencer. The law clarifies how to determine whether a firearm is an assault-style weapon and the circumstances under which a person may continue to possess assault-style weapons and large capacity feeding devices they already own. The law requires the state Firearm Control Advisory Board and the state Secretary of Public Safety and Security to review and update the rosters of prohibited assault-style firearms, approved firearms, and approved firearms sold for target shooting. The law clarifies requirements relating to the carry and transport of firearms in motor vehicles and ATVs. It prohibits the carrying of firearms in government buildings, polling locations, and schools, with certain exceptions. The law expands data compilation and reporting requirements to and from the state, and creates a publicly-accessible dashboard of anonymized aggregate firearm data, along with a commission to study that data. The law requires the State Police to provide training and a test for new applicants for licenses to carry or Firearm ID cards, The law establishes two special legislative commissions — one to examine funding for violence prevention services, and one to study emerging firearms technology. The law criminalizes discharging a firearm and striking a building in use. A YES VOTE would keep in place the law, which increases the regulation of firearms, including ghost guns, machine guns, and assault-style weapons. ANO VOTE would repeal this law. Dello Russo, Jr. 15 Summer Street - Taunton MA 02780 CHIEF FINANCIAL OFFICER (508) 821-1000 MAYOR SHAUNNA O’CONNELL Gill E. Enos BUDGET DIRECTOR October 1, 2026 Council President Barry Sanders Members of the Taunton Municipal Council 15 Summer Street Taunton, MA 02780 Dear Council President Sanders and Members of the Municipal Council, I am writing to express concern about the pattern of interaction between some members of the City Council and our City employees. The concern is how questions are asked and how employees are treated in the process. At times, discussions have become dismissive or unnecessarily adversarial, conclusions appear to be reached before all the facts are heard, and statements have been made about City operations or finances that do not fully reflect the facts. Oversight is most effective when focused on the facts and issues at hand. Tone matters just as much as words. How we speak to people, how we treat them, and whether we are genuinely willing to listen all matter. Several basic principles should guide our discussions: e Treat our employees with respect. Councilors have every right to ask difficult questions and disagree with the answers. Those questions and disagreements can be expressed while still treating employees with courtesy and respect. e Listen to the facts. Effective oversight requires hearing the full picture before reaching conclusions. Employees should have the opportunity to explain the facts and provide context, and that information should be genuinely considered, even when it may challenge an initial assumption or opinion. e Keep oversight focused on the issues. Oversight is most productive when it remains focused on the facts and issues rather than becoming adversarial or making statements for rhetorical effect. e Financial Accuracy and Context. Taunton, like municipalities across Massachusetts, faces inflation, rising costs, and stagnant state aid; yet continues to provide exceptional services and maintain strong financial management. Statements about City spending and finances should be grounded in fact. The Finance team consistently provides information to the Council, and the Council approves all appropriations. Statements not supported by facts risk spreading misinformation. e Preserve order and decorum. Everyone participating in or attending Council meetings should be expected to conduct themselves respectfully and appropriately. Maintaining a productive and orderly environment benefits Councilors, City employees, and members of the public. City Councilors are leaders in our community and should set the standard for professionalism, decorum and teamwork. The Council has an important role in providing oversight, but oversight does not have to lead to conflict. Like the Councilors, our entire City team is committed to protecting taxpayers, serving residents, and doing what is best for Taunton. I look forward to moving ahead together with a renewed commitment to facts, fairness, professionalism, and respect. Respectfully, eras Mayor Shaunna O’Connell City of Taunton Ligia M. Madeira, Esq. text: Notice of Posting Time: Bi AG £m ** ADDENDUM ** ple. MUNICIPAL COUNCIL AGENDA Yt CHESTER R. MARTIN MUNICIPAL COUNCIL CHAMBERS 15 SUMMER STREET, TAUNTON, MA 02780 OCTOBER 6, 2026 AT 7:00 PM COMMUNICATION FROM CITY OFFICERS Pg. 1 Com. from Executive Director, Office of Economic and Community Development — Regarding Weir Street Tunnel Easement (Separate Packet: Description of Uniqueness) Respectfully submitted, isibe A kige— City Clerk CITY OF TAUNTON OFFICE OF ECONOMIC AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT 15 Summer Street, Suite 302 Taunton, MA 02780 . Jay Pateakos Phone: 508-821-1030 Jim Howland Executive Director Assistant Director October 5, 2026 Councilor Barry Sanders Public Property Committee Taunton City Council Re: Weir Street Tunnel Easement Dear Councilor Sanders: On September 30, 2026, the City was notified that it has been awarded an $83,000 grant from the Executive Office of Economic Development (EOED) Massachusetts Downtown Initiative (MDI) Capital Program to renovate the blighted Weir Street Tunnel. As a condition of the grant contract received October 1, 2026, the City must secure an easement for pedestrian access through the tunnel, and our office must provide proof of that easement by October 22, 2026. Because this requirement was not reasonably anticipated and the deadline is short, this request is time-sensitive. After consulting with the Law Department, we were advised that the easement must be referred to the Public Property Committee and that the Committee must approve a description of uniqueness. The property owner, Ken Wisniewski, and the abutters, Jay Dorsey, Phil Giffee of NOAH, and the Downtown Taunton Foundation, have all agreed to work with us on this project and have no objections to the beautification plan. This grant will transform a dim, neglected space into a vibrant, safe pedestrian route connecting Weir Street to Merchants Lane. The project is designed to eliminate the safety concerns surrounding the tunnel and breathe new life into an area of downtown Taunton that is already home to a significant number of revitalization projects. We respectfully request that this matter be referred to the Public Property Committee for consideration at its October 13 meeting, so that the Committee may act on the easement and approve the attached description of uniqueness prepared by the Law Department. Thank you for your consideration. Please let me know if you have any questions. Sincerely, Jay Pateakos ; Executive Director Office of Economic and Community Development Attachment: Description of Uniqueness

Tewksbury Memorial High School Town of Tewksbury Website: http://www.tewksbury-ma.gov 2 TOWN MEETING GUIDELINES ** Voters and visitors shall have their identification ribbons conspicuously displayed. ** Visitors shall sit in the designated VISITORS SECTION unless they are assigned to a designated area. ** Standing at the doors or in the aisles inside the gymnasium or auditorium is prohibited. ** No one shall enter the gymnasium or auditorium while voting is in progress. ** Everyone shall be at a seat to allow the vote to be counted without hindrance. ** Collecting signatures upon petitions or nomination papers is prohibited in the building where the Town Meeting is being held. ** Food and beverages are not allowed in the gymnasium or auditorium as per order of the School Committee. ** Smoking is not allowed in the School Building or on School Property. ** To prevent active interference with the conduct of the Town Meeting, any person taping, videotaping or using any other means of sonic reproduction is assigned to the designated Press Table or the side aisle perimeters of the gymnasium or auditorium. Fund Programs and Purposes Departmental Receipts Fire Department Life Safety Education Course Fees Authorization to Expend Funds Select Board FY27 Spending Limit $15,000 Article 7: Amend Town General Bylaws - Article I “Town Meetings” To see if the Town will vote to amend the Town’s General Bylaws, specifically Article I “Town Meetings” by adding a new Section 9 and a new Section 10 thereto, which shall appear as printed below, or take any other action relative thereto. Section 9. A registered voter may request a reconsideration of a warrant article for which action has already been taken only if that voter was on the prevailing side of the action in question. Said reconsideration must be made within 30 minutes of the original vote. Upon making the motion and obtaining a second, the intervening voter shall present to the moderator evidence that new information is available that wasn’t available at the time and shall convince the moderator that this new evidence is material to the question at hand. The moderator shall be the sole determining authority on whether or not the new information is material to the question at hand. If the moderator determines the information is material, a 2/3rds vote of Town Meeting shall be required. If the vote to reconsider passes, the article in question shall be back on the table and shall be subject to the original vote requirement. Only one reconsideration may be made per article in each Town Meeting. Section 10. Each voter at Town Meeting shall be entitled to speak for three (3) minutes on each individual article. Additionally, each voter shall be entitled to a one (1) minute rebuttal on each article. This time limit shall not apply to the petitioner of each article. The provision of this section shall be enforced using a digital clock display 3 facing the speaker and the audience to ensure that the speaker and the audience can track remaining time. Article 8: Non-Criminal Disposition Bylaw Amendments To see if the Town will vote to amend the Town’s General Bylaws to substitute a Non-Criminal Disposition Bylaw under to G.L. c. 40, § 21D, for the existing Article V of the Bylaws, entitled “Penalty,” and to further incorporate the provisions of the new Non-Criminal Disposition Bylaw into other Articles and Sections of the Bylaws via supplemental amendments thereto, all specified below, or take any other action relative thereto. (i) Article V of the General Bylaw, entitled “Penalty,” shall be deleted in its entirety and the following substituted therefor: ARTICLE V. PENALTIES & NON-CRIMINAL DISPOSITION SECTION 1. Statutory Authority The Town hereby adopts the following bylaw providing for noncriminal disposition as authorized by Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 40, Section 21D (MGL c. 40, § 21D). SECTION 2. Scope and Authority This bylaw provides for noncriminal disposition of any violations of these By-Laws, the Town’s Zoning Bylaw, or any rule or regulation of any Town officer, board, or department, the violation of which is subject to a specific penalty. This bylaw is enacted in accordance with M.G.L. c. 40, § 21D. Any specific monetary fine or penalty that is set forth in any provision of these By-laws for the violation of same shall be considered to apply only to a non-criminal disposition of such violation and shall not be construed as a limitation upon the monetary penalty otherwise recoverable. This procedure shall not be used for the enforcement of municipal traffic rules and regulations. SECTION 3. Enforcing Person “Enforcing person” as used in this bylaw shall mean any of the following persons or officials which took cognizance of the violation of a By-Law: (1) regular police officers of the Town of Tyngsborough, (2) the Select Board, (3) the Building Commissioner, (4) Superintendent of Public Works/Town Engineer, (5) the Conservation Director and Conservation Commission, (6) the Plumbing Inspector, (7) the Electrical Inspector, (8) Health Director and Board of Health, (9) the Licensing Department and/or Authority, (10) the Animal and/or Dog Control Officer, (11) designated agents thereof, or (12) any such other official as the Select Board may from time to time designate, each with respect to violations of By-Laws, the Zoning Bylaw, or rules and regulations within their respective jurisdictions. If more than one Town department or official has 4 jurisdiction over a given matter, any such Town department or official may be an enforcing person with respect thereto. SECTION 4. Notice to be Served 4.1 Any enforcing person as an alternative to initiating criminal proceedings, may give to the offender a written notice to appear before the Clerk of the Lowell District Court at any time during office hours, not later than twenty-one (21) days after the date of such notice. Such notice shall be in triplicate and shall contain the name and address, if known, of the offender, the specific offense charged, and the time and place for his or her required appearance. Such notice shall be signed by the enforcing person and shall be signed by the offender, whenever practicable, in acknowledgment that such notice has been received. 4.2 Any person who is found to be in violation of any By-Law, the Zoning Bylaw, or rule or regulation of any Town officer, board or department, who fails to provide his or her true name, address and/or other verifiable information to a police officer so that a noncriminal violation notice may be issued for such violation, and after having been warned that such failure to provide said information may result in his or her arrest, may be arrested, in accordance with any applicable law of the Commonwealth, and brought before the Lowell District Court, upon a complaint being made for a violation of this section. 4.3 The enforcing person shall, if possible, deliver to the offender a copy of said notice at the time and place of the violation. If it is not possible to deliver a copy of said notice to the offender at the time and place of the violation, said copy shall be mailed or delivered by the enforcing person or by his or her commanding officer or the head of his or her department or by any person authorized by such commanding officer or department head to the offender's last known address, within fifteen (15) days after said violation. Such notice as so mailed shall be deemed a sufficient notice, and a certificate of the person so mailing such notice that it has been mailed in accordance with this section shall be prima facie evidence thereof. 4.4 At or before the completion of each tour of duty or at the beginning of the first subsequent tour of duty, the enforcing person shall give to his or her commanding officer or department head those copies of each notice of such a violation he or she has taken cognizance of during such tour which have not already been delivered or mailed as aforesaid. Said commanding officer or department head shall retain and safely preserve one copy and shall, at a time not later than the next court day after such delivery or mailing, deliver the other copy to the Clerk of the Lowell District Court. SECTION 5. Proceedings 5.1 Any person notified to appear before the clerk of the Lowell District Court may so appear and confess the offense charged, either personally or through a duly authorized agent or by mailing to the Town Clerk with the notice and payment for the penalty. Such payment shall, if mailed, be made only by postal note, money order or check. Upon receipt of such notice, the Town Clerk shall 5 notify the Clerk of the District Court of such payment and the receipt by the District Court Clerk of such notification shall operate as a final disposition of the case. 5.2 If any person so notified to appear wishes to contest the violation alleged in the notice to appear, he or she may, within twenty-one (21) days after the date of the notice, request a hearing in writing. 5.3 Proceedings pursuant to this bylaw and MGL c. 40, § 21D shall not be deemed to be criminal proceedings. 5.4 If any person so notified to appear before the Clerk of the Lowell District Court fails to pay the fine provided hereunder within the time specified or, having appeared, does not confess the offense before the Clerk or pay the sum of money fixed as a penalty after a hearing and finding, the Clerk shall notify the enforcing person who issued the original notice, who shall determine whether to apply for the issuance of a complaint for the violation of the appropriate By-Law, Zoning Bylaw or rule or regulation. text: Selectboard: Joshua A. Kusnierz, Kenneth R. Willette, Valerie E. Granger, John A. Desmond, Steven M. Roll Call: Ken Willette YES Valerie Granger YES John Desmond YES Steven Hawk YES All in favor 4/0/0 • SCHEDULED APPEARANCES • Healthy Quaboag Update Representatives from Healthy Quaboag were not present. Town Manager S. Beckley summarized a written update from co-facilitators Gail Gramarossa and Emily Kirby indicating that stakeholder interviews are being scheduled within the next two weeks as the first step in a regional community health planning process supported by the New England Rural Health Association and the Massachusetts Department of Public Health's State Office of Rural Health. The Board confirmed willingness to participate in the stakeholder interview process, with Vice Chair K. Willette and Clerk V. Granger volunteering to represent the Board. The Board directed Town Manager S. Beckley to 2 Open Session Minutes 08/05/2026 Approved on ___ Selectboard: Joshua A. Kusnierz, Kenneth R. Willette, Valerie E. Granger, John A. Desmond, Steven M. Hawk Town Manager: Stuart Beckley coordinate participation from town departments including the Board of Health, planning board, fire, police, DPW, schools, and senior center. Vice-Chair K. Willette expressed concern about the pace of the process and urged acceleration given the potential time sensitivity of rural health transformation funding at the state level. The Board noted that Jen Healey of Quaboag Connector, recently appointed to the state-level rural health transformation advisory committee, should also be engaged. OLD BUSINESS • Open Meeting Law Complaint filed against Selectboard by Cynthia Allen, dated July 7, 2026: Acknowledge receipt of complaint; Review and discuss response; and Authorize submission of response by Town Counsel; votes may be taken. Town Manager S. Beckley provided an update noting that Ms. Allen had disputed the town attorney's response and communicated further with the Attorney General. The Board was informed that the town intends to correct the procedural deficiencies in approximately ten sets of Open Session minutes, specifically the absence of adequate reconvening language following Executive Sessions. These corrected minutes will be brought back to the Board for reapproval at the first September meeting. The town attorney is consulting on the applicable response deadline. NEW BUSINESS • Water Department Shut Off Policy Water and Sewer Operations Manager John Stanton and Interim DPW Director Ken Calder presented a proposal to implement a structured utility disconnection program for nonpayment. Mr. Stanton outlined the relevant Massachusetts state law protections—exempting households experiencing financial hardship with documentation, serious illness, infants under 12 months, residents 65 or older, and a winter moratorium from November 15 through March 15 and noted that existing town bylaws (Section 4-6) already authorize shutoffs following 30-day nonpayment notices. The financial case was presented using data verified as of July 14, 2026: outstanding water and sewer liens total $268,303.03; outstanding utility bills not yet liened total $655,008.45; combined outstanding utility receivables total $923,311.48. Over the past eight years, more than $1.1 million in unpaid charges has been transferred to municipal liens. The current lien-only approach often delays recovery for years and fails to incentivize timely payment. Mr. Stanton noted that a comparable program in the Town of Wilbraham reduced overdue balances from $128,000 to $61,000. The Board was broadly supportive of the concept but identified several prerequisites, including the need for a detailed written policy to be reviewed by town counsel, notification protocols involving the Board of Health and Building Commissioner, and a public hearing prior to implementation. The Board directed Mr. Stanton and Mr. Calder to develop a comprehensive draft policy including a step-by-step timeline from bill issuance through shutoff for informal review by the Chair and Town Manager before returning to the full Board for final approval. No decision was made or action taken. • Water Kiosk Mr. Calder presented a proposal from Blue Drop, LLC for a filtered public water dispensing kiosk to address resident concerns about water discoloration. The unit would connect to the town water supply, pass water through a multi-stage filtration system including PFAS reduction and ultraviolet treatment, and allow residents to fill their own containers at a publicly accessible outdoor station. Blue Drop would handle all installation, maintenance, and filter changes under a five-year lease agreement at a total monthly cost of $6,180.00 ($4,630.00 for the unit and $1,550.00 for installation, permitting, and bi-weekly maintenance), totaling approximately $370,000 over the fiveyear term. Possible locations included the Senior Center and the Church Street area. An MVP climate resilience grant could contribute up to $20,000 toward the cost. 3 Open Session Minutes 08/05/2026 Approved on ___ Selectboard: Joshua A. Kusnierz, Kenneth R. Willette, Valerie E. Granger, John A. Desmond, Steven M. Hawk Town Manager: Stuart Beckley The Board raised concerns regarding potential use by non-residents, hours of operation, container sanitation liability, and the overall cost given that town water already meets all state quality standards. The Board directed Mr. Calder to obtain additional information from Blue Drop addressing these questions, consult with the town attorney regarding municipal liability, and inquire with the Town of Randolph which operates two similar kiosks about their operational experience. No decision was made or action taken. • Town Manager’s Job Description The Board considered the Town Manager Job Description (Draft Version 1, dated July 30, 2026), developed by Vice Chair K. Willette, Clerk V. Granger, and Town Manager S. Beckley. The document establishes the position summary grounded in the Ware Home Rule Charter Section 4-2, and defines essential duties across executive leadership, financial management, human resources, strategic planning, community engagement, and emergency management. MOTION by Clerk V. Granger to approve the Town Manager Job Description, Town of Ware, Massachusetts, as presented, dated July 30, 2026. Seconded by Member John Desmond. No further discussion. Roll Call: Ken Willette YES Valerie Granger YES John Desmond YES Steven Hawk YES All in favor 4/0/0 • Town Manager’s Goals Town Manager S. Beckley presented his proposed goals for Fiscal Year 2026–27, organized under four categories. Under Organization, goals include supporting the Selectboard in developing its own strategic goals, implementing a communications plan, and coordinating a school civics/community involvement program. Under Staff, goals include formalizing training, updating evaluations, publicizing departmental progress, and filling vacancies in Finance, Fire, and DPW. Under Finance, goals include updating the 10-year Capital Improvement Plan, updating the 5-year financial model, negotiating four union contracts, and drafting the FY2028 budget without reliance on Free Cash for operations. Under Projects, goals include establishing a recycling program, advancing water, wastewater, and road infrastructure projects, updating emergency management plans with MEMA, assisting with MSBA school roof applications, conducting a facility needs review, and completing the Town Hall electrical and fire upgrade. Selectboard Member J. Desmond recommended adding health insurance cost review as a priority. Vice Chair K. Willette requested the addition of economic development, specifically exploring establishment of an Economic Redevelopment Authority as recommended in the recently completed mill yard and healthcare district study, and scheduling an annual economic development forum with the business community. The Board agreed on quarterly check-ins to track progress against these goals. The Board expressed unanimous support without a formal vote. End of discussion. TOWN MANAGER REPORT Town Manager S. Beckley presented the following: • The Water Department completed its spring flushing on Monday evening. • A public forum on the Church Street sidewalk program is scheduled for Thursday, August 7 at 5:30 PM at Town Hall. o Vice Chair K. Willette requested that a Zoom link also be made available. • Contracts for demolition and hazardous materials oversight at 92–104 Main Street have been issued. The project is required to be completed by the end of September. • The Zoning Board of Appeals and Planning Board both approved their respective components of the National Grid substation expansion on Gilbertville Road. Conservation Commission hearing remains pending. • The Mary Lane site fence has been removed and grass installed, also improving sight lines at the Marjorie Street intersection. 4 Open Session Minutes 08/05/2026 Approved on ___ Selectboard: Joshua A. Kusnierz, Kenneth R. Willette, Valerie E. Granger, John A. Desmond, Steven M. Hawk Town Manager: Stuart Beckley • Recent heavy rainfall caused partial collapse of a retaining wall on Sherwin Avenue at Bellevue Street. The homeowner is working with their insurance company on permanent repairs. • A road blowout on Grenville Park Road, and a significant washout from the Monson Turnpike Road solar project affecting a neighboring property; the developer was on site the same day to begin cleanup and has been asked to redesign the stormwater detention system. • Training on the BETA road assessment digital system is scheduled within the coming week. Vice Chair K. Willette expressed concern about the recurring washout at the Monson Turnpike Road solar project and requested that any redesign of the stormwater system be subject to full Conservation Commission review including a public hearing, with mandatory coordination with DPW on culvert capacity. Town Manager Beckley confirmed this would be required under a new Notice of Intent. Member J. Desmond raised concerns about the Church Street sidewalk project timeline, coordination with future water and sewer main replacement, and traffic management, indicating these issues would be addressed at the Thursday public forum. Member S. Hawk requested an update on the status of the departmental mower, and was informed it was repaired and back in service. Vice Chair K. Willette inquired about the status of the town motto signs and S. Beckley replied the DPW needs time to install but we have them at the highway barn. Clerk V. Granger inquired about the status of the veterans’ monuments. Town Manager stated there has not been resolution yet. ADJOURNMENT MOTION to adjourn by Member John Desmond at 8:47pm. Seconded by Member Steven Hawk. All in favor 4/0/0. title: Annual Fall Town Meeting Warrant
text: COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS TOWN OF WEBSTER ANNUAL TOWN MEETING WARRANT OCTOBER 19, 2026 Worcester, ss To either of the Constables in the County aforesaid: In the name of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts you are hereby required and directed to notify and warn the inhabitants of the Town of Webster aforesaid who are qualified to vote in elections and Town affairs to meet in the Bartlett High School, 52 Lake Parkway in said Webster on Monday, October 19, 2026 at 7:00 PM then and there to act on the following Articles to wit: ARTICLE 1. REPORTS FROM THE FINANCE COMMITTEE OR BOARD OF SELECTMEN To hear and act upon the report and recommendations of the Board of Selectmen and the Finance Committee, or take any other action thereon. Sponsored by the Board of Selectmen ARTICLE 2: FIRE STATION 2 CAPITAL IMPROVEMENTS To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, borrow, or otherwise appropriate the sum of One Hundred Fifty Thousand Dollars ($150,000), or any other sum, for the purpose of funding capital improvements to Fire Station 2, located at 170 School Street, including roof replacement, gutter replacement, front door replacement, tree removal, fence replacement, and all costs incidental and related thereto; or take any action thereon. Sponsored by the Fire Chief ARTICLE 3: APPROPRIATE FUNDS TO REPLACE TOWN HALL MESSAGE SIGN To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, borrow, or otherwise appropriate the sum of Sixty Thousand Dollars ($60,000), or any other sum, for the purpose of removing and disposing of the existing electronic message sign and deteriorated support structure located at Town Hall; designing, constructing, and installing a new support structure and foundation; purchasing and installing a new double-sided electronic LED message sign; including any associated electrical, site, engineering, and related costs; or take any other action relative thereto. Sponsored by the Town Administrator and Information Technology Department ARTICLE 4: WASTEWATER TREATMENT FACILITY DISINFECTION SYSTEM UPGRADE DESIGN To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, borrow, or otherwise appropriate the sum of $300,000 for the purpose of funding study and design efforts to upgrade the Wastewater Treatment Facility disinfection system, including all costs incidental and related thereto, or take any action thereon. Sponsored by the Water/Sewer Commission ARTICLE 5. FRENCH RIVER SEWER INTERCEPTOR REHABILITATION DESIGN To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, borrow, or otherwise appropriate the sum of $150,000 for the purpose of funding design efforts to repair and rehabilitate portions of the French River Sewer Interceptor, including all costs incidental and related thereto, or take any action thereon. Sponsored by the Water/Sewer Commission ARTICLE 6. WASTEWATER TREATMENT FACILITY BIOSOLIDS DEWATERING PROJECT DESIGN To see if the Town will vote to raise and appropriate, transfer from available funds, borrow, or otherwise appropriate the sum of $150,000 for the purpose of supplemental design costs of a Biosolids Dewatering Project at the Wastewater Treatment Facility, including all costs incidental and related thereto, or take any action thereon. Sponsored by the Water/Sewer Commission And you are directed to serve this warrant by publishing attested copies thereof in a newspaper published within the Town of Webster at least seven (7) days preceding the meeting and by posting attested copies thereof with the Town Clerk and filing in the Public Library. Thereof fail not and make due return of your doings thereon to the Town Clerk at the time and place of holding said meeting. Given under our hands this Fourteenth Day of September in the year of our Lord Two Thousand and Twenty-six. TOWN OF WEBSTER BOARD OF SELECTMEN: Thomas Klebart, Chairman Mark Rogers, Vice Chairman Elaine Davies, Clerk Scott Dziedzic

The Select Board is being asked to approve a new five-year Cable Television Renewal License with Verizon New England Inc. The Select Board serves as the Town’s Issuing Authority for cable television licenses pursuant to M.G.L. Chapter 166A. Verizon’s current five-year renewal license became effective November 6, 2021, and the proposed renewal would take effect November 6, 2026 and continue through November 5, 2031. The renewal authorizes Verizon to continue providing cable television service in Wellesley and establishes the terms governing service, Public, Educational and Governmental (PEG) access, financial support to the Town, customer service, reporting, and other license obligations. Town staff, Wellesley Media Corp Executive Director James Joyce and cable counsel Bill August have negotiated the renewal with Verizon. The proposed agreement generally maintains the significant municipal and PEG benefits contained in the current license while updating several provisions to reflect changes in technology, federal requirements and the cable television market. Key Municipal Benefits and Changes PEG Operating Support – Maintained at 5% The most significant ongoing financial benefit is preserved. Verizon will continue to provide annual PEG Access/Cable-Related Support equal to 5% of Verizon’s annual gross cable revenues in Wellesley, paid quarterly. These funds may be used by the Town for cable-related purposes and to support personnel, operating and other costs associated with PEG programming. The methodology for calculating revenues from bundled cable and non-cable services is also continued under the renewal. PEG Capital Funding – $142,395 The current license provided $150,000 in PEG capital funding, paid in three $50,000 installments. The proposed renewal provides $142,395, paid in three installments of $47,465 during the first three years of the license. While this represents a $7,605 reduction from the current license, the modest reduction should be viewed in the context of a significant decline in Verizon’s Wellesley subscriber base—from approximately 3,107 subscribers when the current license began in 2021 to 2,218 at the end of 2025, a decline of nearly 30%. The negotiated amount is based on the same capital funding structure used with Comcast: an amount equivalent to 0.45% of Verizon’s current gross revenues, converted to a fixed annual dollar amount so that it will not decline if Verizon’s revenues continue to decrease, plus an additional $9,800 annually despite Verizon having fewer subscribers than Comcast. The resulting five-year commitment is $142,395, only $7,605 less than the prior agreement. Importantly, the Town also negotiated payment of the full five-year commitment during the first three years of the license, providing the Town with the benefit of receiving the capital funding earlier and reducing the risk associated with future subscriber or revenue declines. The renewal also expressly provides that the PEG capital grant is separate from the 5% operating support and license fees, and that equipment purchased with the grant will be owned by the Town and/or its designated PEG provider. PEG Channels and High-Definition Capability – Enhanced The agreement continues Verizon’s obligation to provide the Town with three standard-definition PEG channels and one high-definition PEG channel. The renewal provides additional flexibility by allowing the Town or its PEG Access Designee to request that some or all of the existing standard-definition channels be replaced with high-definition channels. Verizon must make each requested replacement HD channel available within 270 days. HD programming may be provided in either 720p or 1080i format. PEG Interconnection and Equipment – Additional Town Protection Verizon will continue its PEG interconnection with Town equipment at 485 Washington Street. The new agreement provides an additional protection for the Town by clarifying that the Town will not be responsible for Verizon-side upgrade or repair costs when the work is necessary to comply with applicable law or to correct a defect in equipment or facilities for which Verizon is responsible, including issues affecting video or audio quality. Cable Service to Public Buildings The renewal continues to identify the Town and school buildings eligible for cable service in Exhibit A, including Town Hall, Police and Fire Stations, libraries, DPW facilities and public schools. The provisions governing complimentary service have been revised to address the FCC's treatment of free or discounted municipal cable service under the federal franchise-fee cap. Existing service to designated buildings will continue until Verizon implements the applicable federal requirements following the notice process contained in the agreement. PEG Administration The renewal replaces the more limited reference to an “Access Corporation” with the broader term “PEG Access Designee.” This allows the Select Board to designate either a nonprofit/noncommercial entity or a municipal department to manage PEG channels, facilities, funding and programming, providing the Town with greater flexibility in how PEG services are administered. Comparison to Current License Provision Current License Proposed 2026 Renewal Term 5 years: 2021–2026 5 years: 2026–2031 PEG Operating Support 5% of annual gross revenues 5% maintained PEG Capital Funding $150,000 $142,395 Capital Payment Schedule $50,000 in each of first 3 years $47,465 in each of first 3 years PEG Channels 3 SD + 1 HD 3 SD + 1 HD, with ability to convert SD channels to HD HD Format 720p 720p or 1080i PEG Interconnection Continued interconnection; Town Continued, with additional protection responsible for certain Townfrom costs associated with Verizon initiated changes defects or legally required changes Broader PEG Access Designee, including ability to designate a municipal department PEG Administration Access Corporation Public Building Service Existing service initially continued; Complimentary service subject to updated provisions address FCC federal requirements franchise-fee requirements License Fee $0.50 per subscriber annually $0.50 per subscriber annually, with ability to adjust if State law changes Following the required public hearing, the Select Board may take final action on the proposed Verizon renewal license. State law requires a Select Board public hearing before final action on the renewal to provide an opportunity for public comment regarding the Town’s cable-related needs and the proposed license. Approval of the renewal will authorize Verizon to continue operating its cable television system in Wellesley under the negotiated terms for the five-year period beginning November 6, 2026. The agreement maintains the Town’s 5% PEG operating support, provides $142,395 in frontloaded PEG capital funding, preserves PEG channel capacity and other municipal benefits, and provides additional flexibility for HD programming and PEG administration. MOTION MOVE for Wellesley Verizon License Renewal Vote by Wellesley Select Board Acting in its capacity as the statutory cable television license Issuing Authority pursuant to MGL 166A; and Finding that the cable license renewal proposal of Verizon New England, reasonably meets the cable-related renewal needs and interests of the public and Town; and Finding that Verizon’s financial and technical qualifications, and Verizon’s local programming channels, facilities and services are reasonable to meet Town cable license needs; The Wellesley Select Board hereby approves and shall execute the proposed Wellesley Verizon renewal license to be effective November 6, 2026. Requests for removal from the consent agenda should be sent to the Executive Director or Chair by Monday morning. Should items not be removed from the Consent Agenda, here is a motion for acceptance: MOTION MOVE to approve the Consent Agenda. • Discuss and Vote Special Municipal Employees and Disclosure Forms The Town has several employees that work for two departments. Town Counsel has opined that two positions likely should be designated as Special Municipal Employees. Those positions are Recreation Department Night Monitor and Camp Counselor. MOTION MOVE to approve the positions of Recreational Department Night Monitor and Camp Counselor as Special Municipal Employees. 5. 6:45 Discuss and Vote Appointment of Police Officer Candidates Please find a memo detailing the recommendation of Chief Whittemore to appoint three (3)) police officer candidates. Chief Whittemore has included the resumes of the candidates for the Board’s review. MOTION MOVE to appoint John Canal, Georgia Jones, and Nicolas LeVangle, to the position of patrol officer effective October 13, 2026 contingent upon passage of the Police Academy, passage of a physical abilities, medical, and physiological exam, and a one-year probationary period. 6. 7:10 Discuss and Vote FY28 Budget Guideline Discussions The FY28 budget continues to present significant financial challenges, with pressure coming from health insurance, collective bargaining and step increases, departmental operating costs, capital requirements, and competing demands for Free Cash. While the Town-Wide Financial Plan (TWFP) provides the starting framework for FY28, several significant assumptions remain unresolved and will need to be monitored as the budget develops. Health Insurance and Fixed Costs Health insurance remains one of the largest variables in the FY28 budget. At this stage, the Town does not yet have a formal trend analysis on which to base a revised projection. The current TWFP therefore continues to carry an 8% increase for medical health insurance and 5% for all other insurance (dental, life insurance, accident, hospital indemnity, eyemed). There is reason to believe actual FY27 medical claims experience may improve. Coverage for GLP-1 medications has been significantly reduced, which is expected to reduce claims costs in FY28. However, until sufficient claims experience and trend information are available, staff is not recommending that the Town reduce the existing TWFP assumption. The health insurance projection should continue to be reviewed as additional claims information becomes available, which likely is start of December. Personnel Services and Collective Bargaining Personnel costs remain a significant component of the FY28 budget, particularly as the Town continues negotiations with its municipal and school collective bargaining units. The draft guidelines therefore identify departments with open collective bargaining agreements separately rather than assigning a fixed personnel services percentage before those negotiations are completed. FY28 also represents a 52.4-week payroll year, a circumstance that occurs approximately once every seven years. As a result, personnel budgets will experience an additional year-over-year increase simply from the additional payroll obligation. This increase occurs before accounting for COLAs, merit increases, contractual wage adjustments, staffing changes or other compensation costs and is reflected in the departmental personnel service guidelines. For non-union employees, based on the Select Board's discussion last week and the recommendation of the Human Resources Board, the CFO and Executive Director are recommending a 2% COLA for FY28. In addition, the recommendation continues the $300,000 Merit Pay Plan pool for eligible employees and includes $25,000 for other compensation adjustments. The recommended approach provides a consistent general wage adjustment while preserving the Town's performance-based compensation structure. The $25,000 adjustment allocation provides limited capacity to address individual compensation issues that may arise during the year without incorporating those costs into the general COLA or Merit Pay Plan. The departmental personnel guidelines reflect these assumptions, the 52.4-week payroll year, and known staffing or department-specific circumstances. Departments with open collective bargaining agreements—including Police, Fire, DPW, Facilities Management and the Library— remain identified as Union Negotiations pending resolution of those agreements. Operating Expense Budget Pressures The draft guidelines attempt to hold most departmental operating expense budgets level while recognizing specific costs that cannot reasonably be absorbed within a 0% guideline. Information Technology is recommended at an 8% expense guideline, together with approximately $100,000 for the Munis increase and $25,000 for applicant tracking software, reflecting continued increases in cybersecurity, licensing, telephone and enterprise software costs. Facilities Management is recommended at 5% for expenses, with an additional lease-related increase identified in the draft. Utility costs remain an additional unknown because MLP and natural gas increases have not yet been finalized. National Grid could be increased for both commodity and transmission up to 10%. Other identified pressures include a contractual Audit Committee increase, increased hybrid cruiser costs for Police, Library licensing and subscription costs, a projected $75,000–$100,000 trash contract increase for DPW, new transportation contract costs for the Schools, and a 6% Workers' Compensation increase associated with the recent valuation. Capital Financing and Cash Capital The preliminary FY28 capital model presents an additional challenge. Staff is recommending that cash capital be modeled at 6% of recurring revenues, which is below the minimum range established in the Town's existing capital financing framework. Even at 6%, based on current projections, approximately $1.3 million in capital reductions will be required. This means that the 6% recommendation should not be viewed as creating additional budget flexibility. Rather, it already assumes that projects currently contemplated in the capital program will need to be reduced, deferred or funded through another source. Staff will work through the capital program to identify options for achieving the required reduction and bring those choices back to the Board as the capital and operating budgets develop. All capital submittals are not due until November 20th for FY28. Free Cash and Additional Capital Needs Free Cash is likely to play an important role in the FY28 financial plan, but it is important to consider the FY28 discussion in the context of the significant uses of Free Cash already made or planned during FY27. Free Cash has been identified for the following FY27 purposes: • • • • Comprehensive Plan – $350,000 Library LED – $325,000 School AC Design – $1,423,400 School AC Design – Accelerated – $170,200 (SC Request) Free Cash has been identified for the following FY28 TWFP purposes: • • • • • Snow and Ice Supplemental – $1,000,000 Operating Budget Balance – $2,000,000 (Best Case Scenario) School Facilities Strategic Planning – $200,000 Fire Station Feasibility – $750,000 (2 Sites is approximately $1.6M) Pre-School Feasibility – $500,000 These uses total approximately $6.72 million. Looking ahead to FY28, additional demands on Free Cash are already emerging. In addition to projects currently contemplated in the TWFP, Facilities Management has provided preliminary estimates for: • • • $1,114,000 – Middle School Roof Interim Repairs $850,000 – Bates Parking Lot and Site Renovation (ROM estimate; engineering/design is underway) $405,000 – FMD/Land Use Lease Cost – Accommodations These preliminary FY28 needs total an additional $2.369 million. Taken together, the identified FY27 uses and these preliminary FY28 needs represent approximately $9.09 million in Free Cash demands, before considering any additional At the same time, a Citizen Petition proposes an additional expenditure of Free Cash ($7.8M). Any significant additional appropriation from Free Cash must therefore be considered in the context of both the Town's available Free Cash balance and the uses of Free Cash that may otherwise be necessary to support the FY28 budget and capital program. This is particularly important because Free Cash is a finite, non-recurring resource that must also be replenished each year. Using Free Cash for one purpose necessarily reduces the amount available for other one-time capital needs, budget balancing, reserves, or other financial priorities. The Board will need to consider these competing uses collectively rather than evaluating individual Free Cash requests in isolation. Preliminary Departmental Guidelines The attached draft reflects department-specific recommendations based on the requests presented through the All-Board process and the cost drivers currently known. Most departmental expense budgets are being held at 0%, while targeted increases are recommended where contractual, utility, technology or other identifiable costs make a level-funded budget unrealistic. Personnel guidelines have similarly been adjusted based on known circumstances. Departments with open collective bargaining agreements are identified separately because assigning a percentage guideline before negotiations are completed could create an inaccurate budget assumption. The Schools' preliminary FY28 personnel guideline is 3.4%, reflecting the impact of the 52.4week payroll schedule on the TWFP percentage. Schools continue to be in negotiations as well. The Schools have also identified additional potential cost pressures, including new transportation contracts and the proposed statewide MassCore graduation requirements. While the Healey administration has recommended implementation on MassCore beginning with incoming ninthgrade students in the 2027–2028 school year, legislation establishing the statewide requirement has not been enacted. The potential financial implications for Wellesley remain uncertain and will need to be evaluated as the State's implementation requirements and timelines become clearer. Guideline Framing Given the combined pressures on the FY28 budget, the recommended guidelines are intended to establish a disciplined starting point rather than predetermine the final budget. Departments should continue to prioritize existing core services and contractual obligations, identify opportunities for efficiencies, and distinguish unavoidable cost increases from program enhancements. New programs, positions or service expansions should be considered in the context of the Town's overall financial capacity and should not be assumed simply because they are included within a departmental request. The more significant FY28 challenge will be balancing the operating budget, capital program and Free Cash strategy together. The current plan already assumes a capital level that will require approximately $1.3 million in reductions, while additional Facilities needs and other potential Free Cash appropriations could further constrain the Town's ability to use Free Cash as originally contemplated in the TWFP. The draft guidelines are therefore presented as a starting point for Select Board consideration. They will continue to be refined as collective bargaining, health insurance experience, capital planning and other major cost drivers become clearer. Please find attached. title: Site Inspection and Public Hearing Wellesley St Sidewalks
text: TOWN OF WESTON P.O. BOX 378 WESTON, MA 02493 PLANNING BOARD TEL: 781-786-5065 FAX: 781-786-5069 PUBLIC HEARING NOTICE WESTON PLANNING BOARD Pursuant to Article XIII of the Town of Weston Bylaws, the Planning Board will hold a Public Hearing remotely via Zoom on 10/7/2026 at a meeting to start at 7:00 p.m. on an application for Scenic Road ROW Work for WELLESLEY ST, where the applicant is proposing to remove 13 trees and remove and rebuild a stonewall as part of intersection improvements at Wellesley St/ Route 20/ Boston Post Road. The Zoom instructions can be found below and will be provided on the 10/7/2026 agenda when it is posted to the town website. A site walk will be held on Wednesday, 10/2/2026 at 10:00 am. If there are any questions or concerns before the Public Hearing you may contact the Town Planner Imaikalani Aiu, aiu.i@westonma.gov. The applicant and owner is the Weston DPW and Traffic and Sidewalk Committee. Copies of the plans are available for public inspection at the Weston DPW Monday to Friday from 8:30am to 3:00 pm https://www.westonma.gov/DocumentCenter/Index/6091. Pursuant to Chapter 22 of the Acts of 2022, which includes an extension of Governor Baker’s March 12, 2020 Order Suspending Certain provisions of the Open Meeting Law, G.L. c. 30A, §18, this meeting will be held via an online meeting platform. No in-person attendance of members of the public is available but every effort will be made to ensure that the public can adequately access the proceedings in real time including a dial-in option. By: Alex Selvig, Chair Weston Planning Board Weston Observer 9/18/2026 9/25/2026

Adequate, alternative access includes the opportunity to attend a hybrid or fully remote meeting, and a link to join the meeting is included in this Open Meeting Law posting. However, if there are interruptions, the meeting will be temporarily shut down and restarted as a “webinar”, which format Town Counsel has confirmed is compliant with law . title: Public Hearing
text: Town of Winchester By Town of Winchester at 3:19 pm, Sep 24, 2026 PLANNING BOARD 71 Mount Vernon Street Winchester, MA 01890 planningboard@winchester.us (781) 721-7162 WINCHESTER PLANNING BOARD NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING In accordance with M.G.L. c. 40A, § 5, the Winchester Planning Board will hold a public hearing on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, at 7:00 PM in the Select Board Room, Winchester Town Hall, 71 Mt. Vernon Street, Winchester, MA 01890. The hearing will consider the following proposed amendments to the Winchester Zoning Bylaw and Zoning Map, and a related article, to be acted on at the Town Meeting beginning November 5, 2026. ARTICLE 4 (PLANNING BOARD): To amend Section 3.5.5 of the Zoning Bylaw to add insufficient lot width to the circumstances under which a reconstruction, extension, alteration, or change to a conforming structure on a nonconforming lot may be permitted; and to amend Table 4.1.1, Table of Dimensional Requirements, to reduce the minimum lot width in the RDA District from 120 feet to 100 feet. ARTICLE 5 (PLANNING BOARD): To amend Section 7.3.15.2 of the Zoning Bylaw to eliminate the Center Business District Review Subcommittee and provide instead for concurrent design review by the Design Review Committee and historical review by the Historical Commission, each submitting its own report to the Special Permit Granting Authority; and to amend Section 7.3.17.5 to remove the reference to the CBD Review Subcommittee. ARTICLE 6 (PLANNING BOARD): To amend Sections 9.4.3, 9.5.4, and 9.5.5 of the Zoning Bylaw to remove the required number of paper copies for special permit and site plan review applications, deferring submission requirements to the rules and regulations of the Special Permit Granting Authority; to amend Section 9.5.5 to assign transmittal of site plan applications to the Special Permit Granting Authority and extend the transmittal period from three to five days; and to amend Section 9.5.6 to provide that where a use requires both site plan review and a special permit, the site plan shall be reviewed as part of the special permit application with a single hearing and decision. ARTICLE 37 (CITIZEN PETITION): To amend the Winchester Zoning Map by changing the zoning district of the property at 114 Church Street (Assessors' Map 17, Block 198, Lot 0) from the ConservancyInstitutional District (SCI) to the Apartment House Residential District B (RB-20). ARTICLE 38 (CITIZEN PETITION): To amend the Winchester Zoning Map by changing the zoning district of the property at 18 Raymond Place (Assessors' Map 11, Block 75, Lot 0) from the ConservancyInstitutional District (SCI) to the General Resident District (RB-6.5). ARTICLE 40 (CITIZEN PETITION): To amend the Winchester Zoning Map by changing the zoning district of a portion of the property known as The Ledges Condominium, located at 7 Wainwright Road, from the Planned Residential District (PRD) to the Residential District A (RDA-20). TOWN OF WINCHESTER | PLANNING BOARD Page 1 of 2 The Planning Board will also hear the following related article, which concerns property that is also the subject of Article 40: ARTICLE 39 (CITIZEN PETITION): To release a portion of the unimproved common area open space of The Ledges Condominium, 7 Wainwright Road, as required under Zoning Board of Appeals Decision No. 2699 dated November 18, 1985, which requires a majority vote of Town Meeting to release any unimproved common area open space shown on the approved plans before it may be developed. The full text of the proposed amendments, including maps and legal descriptions of the affected properties, may be inspected upon request at the Office of the Town Clerk, Winchester Town Hall, during regular business hours, and online at www.winchester.us. All interested persons will be given an opportunity to be heard. WINCHESTER PLANNING BOARD Publish: Winchester Daily Times Chronicle on October 6 and October 13, 2026. GRANT OF PERMANENT DRAINAGE EASEMENT This Grant of Permanent Drainage Easement (“Grant”) is made as of July , 2026 by THE PLEASANT PARK YACHT CLUB, a corporation duly organized under the laws of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts (“Grantor”), whose address is 562 Pleasant Street, Winthrop, County of Suffolk, Massachusetts, in favor of THE TOWN OF WINTHROP, a Massachusetts municipal corporation (“Grantee”), whose address is Town Hall, 1 Metcalf Square, Winthrop, County of Suffolk, Massachusetts. 1, Recitals Grantor is the owner of certain real property located at 562 Pleasant Street, Winthrop, Massachusetts, described as follows (the “Property”): A certain parcel of land situated in Winthrop, Suffolk County, Massachusetts , on the westerly side of Pleasant Street, being Lot B-1on a “Plan of Land in Winthrop, Mass.,” dated June 9, 1950, by Whitman and Howard, C.E.’s and more specifically described in a Deed dated July 13, 1950, recorded with Suffolk Registry of Deeds in Book 6644, Page 382. 2. Grant of Permanent Drainage Easement For good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which are acknowledged, Grantor hereby grants and conveys to Grantee and its successors and assigns a non-exclusive perpetual easement (“Easement”) over, under, and across the Property, for the purpose of constructing, installing, operating, maintaining, repairing, replacing, and removing a municipal drainage pipe. 3. Easement Location The Easement area is particularly set forth in the description and map/plan ad Exhibit “A” which contains the Easement Description/Map, Surveyor-prepared metes and bounds description, and a Depiction of the Easement Area. : 4. Rights Granted Grantee shall have the right to: a. access the Easement Area for any utility-related purpose; b. place, install, and maintain utility pipes, conduits, meters, valves, vaults, and appurtenances; c. use all reasonable means of construction and maintenance, including excavation; and, d. take all actions necessary to operate and maintain the municipal stormwater pipe and facilities. 5. Consideration Grantor grants this Easement for good One ($1.00) Dollar and other valuable considerations given and received. 6. Conditions / Restoration Following excavation and other work in the Easement Area, Grantee will restore the surface to substantially the same condition as reasonably practicable, excluding below ground utility facilities and reasonable utility-related grading differences. 7. No Warranty Grantee is not obligated to install any utilities except as Grantee determines necessary. Grantor makes no warranties regarding underground conditions except as expressly stated elsewhere. 8. Indemnification Grantee agrees to be responsible for damages to the Property caused by Grantee’s construction, maintenance, repair, replacement, or removal activities, except to the extent caused by Grantor’s negligence or willful misconduct. 9. Access: Grantor agrees to provide full access to the stormwater drainage facility and shall clear boats, vehicles, and other obstructions from the Easement Area in the event that the Grantee shall require access to the pipe or other elements of the stormwater drainage facility. This Grant is intended to allow the Town to ensure drainage function. Nothing in this Grant limits the Grantee’s ability to take actions necessary for public health, safety, or emergency drainage needs, including emergency access and temporary measures. 10. Grantor’s Reserved Rights (Subject to Easement) Grantor retains the right to use the Property in any manner that does not unreasonably interfere with the Easement’s exercise. Grantor shall not construct, place, or install improvements within the Easement Area that would unreasonably interfere with the drainage facilities; or take actions that would unreasonably restrict, reroute without approval, or impair drainage within the Easement Area. If interference occurs, Grantee may require modifications to restore functionality at the Grantor’s expense, to the extent allowed by law. Il. Term This Easement is perpetual and shall run with the land. 12. Binding Effect; This Grant binds Grantor and Grantor’s heirs, successors, and assigns and inures to the benefit of Grantee and its successors and assigns. ‘ 13. Governing Law This Grant is governed by the laws of the Commonwealth or Massachusetts.. 14. Recording: Grantee shall record this Grant in the property records of the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds. 15. Entire Agreement: This document constitutes the entire agreement between the parties concerning the Easement. 16. Authority: The signatories below represent that they, and each of them, are authorized to execute this document in the name of and on behalf of the respective parties. 17. text: Town of Yarmouth Per M.G.L.: All town and school boards, committees, commissions, and authorities shall post a notice of every meeting at least 48 hours prior to such meeting, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays. Notice shall contain a listing of topics/agenda that the chair reasonably anticipates will be discussed at the meeting. Notice of Meeting Name: Conservation Commission Date: Thursday, October 1, 2026 Time: 5:00 PM Yarmouth Town Hall Hearing Room 1146 Route 28, Yarmouth, MA OR Place: Zoom Link: https://us02web.zoom.us/j/88471726922 Webinar ID: 884 7172 6922 Or by phone: +1 301 715 8592 or +1 346 248 7799 *Remote attendance is provided for public access.
