Finley, Jr:, Senior Associate, Fire and EMS Community Risk Assessment Standards of Cover Community Risk Assessment (CRA) and Standards of Cover (SOC) are analysis tools used by fire departments to evaluate and formulate planning initiatives to mitigate risks within a community. Together, they align resources, strategies, and performance objectives with the unique risks and needs of a community. Community Risk Assessment Standards of Cover • Identification of and assessing community risk. • Analysis of demographic, geographic, and socioeconomic factors that impact risk levels. • Guide community risk reduction strategies. • Ensure that the distribution and capabilities of emergency response units align with identified risks. • Provide a framework for delivering the right level of service to reduce harm and improve outcomes in emergencies. • Define specific, measurable goals for response times, resource deployment, and operational efficiency and effectiveness. CPSM Report Key Findings • CPSM found the Yarmouth Fire Department to be a professional and a professionally managed Fire and EMS department. • The Town of Yarmouth has achieved a Class 03 ISO-PPC rating, a very good rating, which is an achievement the community should be proud of. • The community risk and service demands in Yarmouth are numerous and include EMS, fire, technical rescue, hazardous materials, diverse building stock, increasing density challenges, transportation emergencies, environmental factors, and socio-needs population. CPSM Report Key Findings CPSM Report Key Findings • The YFD has developed a comprehensive Emergency Medical Services (EMS) program that reflects the community's needs and strives for excellence in all aspects of service delivery. CPSM Report Key Findings • The Fire Marshal’s Office estimates there are about 935 inspectable properties in the Town and the number is increasing with redevelopment. Fire Inspection Type 2023 2024 2025 Fire Prevention Inspections Conducted 1,750 1,675 1,815 Plans Reviews 45 459 423 Fire Protection System Inspections Conducted 14 12 11 • Recent push to begin inspecting all Air BNB type occupancies of which the YFD are estimates to total nearly 2,000 in Town. CPSM Report Key Findings • YFD meets all mandatory Fire and EMS training to include state certification standards. • In the latest ISO Fire Suppression Rating Schedule evaluation the YFD received 7.08/9.00 credits for the training segment. ✓ Biggest deficiency was in the company training category. YFD received 12.5/25 credits in this category. • YFD training programs and training program management are well organized and delivered to high standards. • YFD recently hired a Deputy Fire Chief whose main job is managing the training program. CPSM Report Key Findings • Town and YFD are currently working collaboratively with Provincetown, Barnstable County, the Cape and Islands Fire Chiefs Association, and the Massachusetts Department of Fire Services to build a regional environmentally friendly training facility at Station 3. CPSM Report Key Findings Fire and EMS Workload YFD Historical Calls and Runs Three Year Period Overall, Calls increased 5.5% during the three-year period. EMS calls increased by 5.4%. 10,166 7,879 10,349 9,920 8,312 7,768 Fire calls increased by 10.6%. Total runs increased 1.8% during the threeyear period. 6/1/2022 - 5/31/2023 6/1/2023 - 5/31/2024 Calls Runs 6/1/2024 - 5/31/2025 CPSM Report Key Findings Fire and EMS Demand CPSM Report Key Findings Fire and EMS Demand CPSM Report Key Findings Response Times Response Time Category NFPA 1710 Benchmark 90th Percentile ≤ 64 seconds 90% of the time Call Processing ≤ 90 seconds 90% of the time (Special Call Types) Turnout ≤ 80 seconds for fire and special operations 90% of the time ≤ 60 seconds for EMS responses 90% of the time Travel YFD 2024 Data 132 seconds (All Call Types) 162 Seconds 96 Seconds ≤ 240 seconds for the first arriving engine company to a fire suppression incident 90% of the time 474Seconds ≤ 240 seconds for the first arriving unit equipped with an automated external defibrillator (AED) or higher-level capability to an EMS incident 90% of the time. 414Seconds ≤ 360 seconds for the second company 90% of the time By GIS: 32.9% of Town meets standard. ≤ 480 seconds to assemble the initial first alarm assignment on scene 90% of the time for low/medium hazards, and By GIS: Each district 610 seconds for high-rise fire incidents 90% of the time. has moderate gaps. CPSM Report Key Findings Response Times Utilizing current road network, 32.9% of the Town meets the NFPA 240 second travel time benchmark. ■ As a note, this is a 90th percentile standard. ■ The YFD travel time by Station District for Fire and EMS incidents is 7.2 minutes at the 90th percentile. 90th Percentile Response Time First Due Area Dispatch Turnout Travel Total South Yarmouth 2.2 3.0 6.8 10.3 West Yarmouth 2.2 2.9 6.6 10.3 Yarmouth Port 2.0 3.0 9.5 12.6 Total 2.2 3.0 7.2 10.8 The 90th percentile travel time for EMS is 6.9 minutes (414 seconds). The 90th percentile travel time for Structure Fires is 9.8 minutes (588 seconds). CPSM Report Key Findings • Based on current daily staffing levels and response configurations, the YFD does not meet the effective response force benchmarks outlined in National Fire Protection Association NFPA 1710 for single-family residential fires, openair commercial occupancies, and multi-family apartment structures without the assistance of mutual aid. • The mutual aid system the YFD is signatory to is robust in that it includes contiguous and regional assets. • Automatic aid is a greater benefit—the YFD has automatic aid with several surrounding towns. CPSM Report Key Findings • The YFD’s ability to absorb multiple calls and restore response capabilities to a state of normalcy can be challenging at certain times such as during working structural fires and other multi-company responses (runs). 57.2% of all calls in Yarmouth are overlapped with at least one other call. 6.4% of all calls in are overlapped with three or more calls leaving Yarmouth with no available resources. CPSM Report Key Recommendations • To remain at the forefront, CPSM recommends the YFD sustain a compliance-driven EMS operational footprint and continue to implement a learning and adaptive EMS system. • Fire apparatus staffed with ALS-qualified personnel should be equipped with a full complement of ALS equipment to allow providers to operate at the highest level of care when they are first on scene. • The chief should contact ISO and request an up-to-date evaluation in the coming months. CPSM believes, with potential enhancements to telecommunicators, staffing, deployment, and hydrant inspection and testing by the town, earning an ISO Class 2 rating is very achievable for Yarmouth. CPSM Report Key Recommendations • The YFD continue to deliver a Fire and EMS training program that includes initial, incumbent, and specialty training certification and non-certification courses/hours. • The YFD continue to develop an officer development program by, to the extent possible, requiring officers to obtain additional training and certifications. CPSM Report Key Recommendations • The YFD develop a comprehensive fire prevention code enforcement inspection plan that aligns with NFPA 1730 - Standard on Organization and Deployment of Fire Prevention Inspection and Code Enforcement, Plan Review, Investigation, and Public Education Operations, 2019 Edition, and ensures that town bylaws are followed that relate to fire prevention and fire code enforcement. • The YFD review, update, and implement procedures that ensures all commercial, industrial, institutional, and other similar type buildings and targeted hazards are identified and have a pre-fire plan inspection conducted by fire operational companies annually, which will ensure preparedness and effective response to incidents in these buildings. CPSM Report Key Recommendations • The YFD should adopt a performance benchmark for dispatch time or call processing time that includes the adoption of call processing performance standards of 64-seconds at the 90th percentile for fire and fire-related calls, and a realistic performance benchmark for EMS calls that does not exceed 120 seconds. • The YFD should adopt a performance benchmark for turnout time of ≤ 80 seconds for fire and special operations and ≤ 60 seconds for EMS responses at the 90th percentile. This is one part of total response time the YFD has the most direct control over. CPSM Report Key Recommendations • The YFD adopt a performance benchmark requiring the first-arriving fire suppression unit for fire responses and the first arriving unit (Fire or EMS) for EMS incidents to reach the scene within 240 seconds in the central core areas of each station district (generally within a ± 2-mile travel distance). For low- and medium-hazard incidents occurring in the more distant portions of each district the target first unit on scene time should be 360 seconds. CPSM Report Key Recommendations 32.9% Coverage 71.4% Coverage CPSM Report Key Recommendations • The YFD continue to prioritize regional planning efforts that expand mutual aid into automatic aid with contiguous jurisdictions. Strengthening these relationships will bolster first-alarm structure fire responses, increase resiliency, and improve the YFD’s ability to consistently assemble an Effective Response Force for building fires particularly beyond single-family residential structures. • The YFD adopt a performance benchmark for assembling an Effective Response Force (ERF) within 600 seconds (≤ 10 minutes) throughout the Town. This benchmark should represent assembling the initial first-alarm assignment on scene 90 percent of the time for low- and medium-hazard incidents, using a combination of YFD and automatic-aid resources as appropriate based on incident type and location. CPSM Report Key Recommendations • The Town of Yarmouth and YFD begin the planning process for constructing a new state-of-the-art Fire Station 4 and Fire Headquarters facility. • Due to its age, location, and limitations to any type of expansion/addition it is our opinion that it would not be economically feasible to attempt to renovate and/or upgrade the existing Station 1 facility. • A long-range Town of Yarmouth planning document notes the need to consider the relocation of Station 1 out of the hurricane SLOSH (National Weather Service Sea, Lake, and Overland Surges from Hurricanes model) zone. CPSM Report Key Recommendations 32.9% Coverage 43.0% Coverage CPSM Report Key Recommendations 74.4% Coverage CPSM Report Key Recommendations • The Town of Yarmouth and YFD begin a long-range feasibility and planning process to replace both Stations 1 and 2 as substation facilities. • CPSM further recommends in the interim: • The more serious life safety and fire code issues at Fire Station 2 should be addressed as soon as possible. • A second approved means of egress from the second-floor crew quarters of Fire Stations 1 and 2 should be installed/ constructed (such as a code-compliant exterior fire escape) in order to provide protection for second floor occupants. CPSM Report Key Recommendations • The single unenclosed/partially enclosed stairway at Fire Station 2 should be upgraded and fully enclosed, as soon as possible, with an appropriate fire rating for a means of egress in order to provide protection for the second-floor occupants. • Should the Town of Yarmouth decide to keep the existing Fire Station 2 (and also Fire Station 1) in service long term, it should be equipped with a complete, automatic fire sprinkler system for the protection of the occupants, building, and equipment. CPSM Report Key Recommendations • Consideration be given to staffing on the tower be increased from three personnel to four. • Allows the crew to be split into two, two person crews that can simultaneously perform critical tasking operations such as forcible entry/laddering/ventilation and occupant search and rescue. • The Town of Yarmouth and YFD should consider upgrading four firefighter positions to the rank of lieutenant to provide appropriate supervision on the Tower. • The engine at Station 1 should also be supervised by a Lieutenant (or acting Lieutenant) at all times. CPSM Report Key Recommendations • Overall, this plan recommends gradually transitioning one ambulance from a cross-staffed model to a fully dedicated, noncross-staffed unit. • Ensures continuous EMS coverage without removing fire suppression resources from service. • This adjustment will improve reliability in both EMS and fire response, reducing system strain and enhancing overall readiness. • In parallel, the department should pursue the construction of a new Station 4 in a strategically identified area of Town as is being considered currently. CPSM Report Key Recommendations • A proposed gradual staffing increase from 13 to 18 and eventually 21 personnel will allow YFD to assemble an Effective Response Force (ERF) more consistently, particularly for single-family dwelling fires, which remain the most common building risk in the town. • Achieving ERF benchmarks ensures that critical fireground tasks, such as fire attack, search and rescue, ventilation, and rapid intervention can be performed simultaneously and safely. • Enhanced staffing will also strengthen initial operations at moderate- and high-risk structures, where early coordination and sufficient personnel are essential to limiting fire spread and improving life safety outcomes. CPSM Report Key Recommendations • Strengthen the Effective Response Force (ERF) deployment will: Enhance operational effectiveness, efficiency, and safety for both firefighters and the public. • Allow faster compliance with the two-in/two-out standard and support more timely assembly of an ERF to perform critical fireground tasks. • Improve overall system resiliency. • Ensure that at least one fire suppression unit is always maintained available to provide for immediate response to fire related incidents. Dear Kathy: We want to extend our thanks to you and the Selectboard for the time and attention you have given to our neighborhood request to revisit the STR Bylaws. We were viewing the last meeting on Zoom. You listened and showed an understanding of our concerns. We appreciate that very much. We also acknowledge the amount of time you devoted to gathering all the town departments together to work on a solution. We wish to always create and sustain neighborhoods where people interact and know one another, watch over the property of our neighbors during storms, like this recent event, pick up packages, help with challenging tasks , and just reach out to each other. Four years ago we knew all the owners on Tanglewood Drive and much of adjacent Webster Rd. Now, on one portion of Tanglewood alone, we have 10 rental properties and 6 of them in a row, generating rows of cars on our very narrow street. Last January's storm, there was only 1 other neighbor of the 17 houses on our side (1/2) of the loop of Tanglewood living in their home besides us. We received phone calls from some of the owners that know us requesting us to check their properties and being neighborly, we did so. We no longer have a neighborhood - we have a rental community. We hope, as we move forward, that everyone will be clear about their responsibilities as homeowners and renters. We are grateful that resources will be available to us should we need to notify the town of concerns. You clarified that although my 49,51,53 south shore drive cottages are in a HMOD2 zone, STRs remain permitted under the zoning bylaw because they were not developed under the HMOD. I also expressed concerns/suggestions in our conversation, that you asked me to send in writing, as follows 110-6 6(c) last sentence “An adverse effect may occur…production of noise, light, glare, trash” I believe is extremely vague and should be stricken. I believe the intent is to prohibit nuisances, and common law nuisance is activity that is a substantial and unreasonable interference with a reasonable person’s use and enjoyment of their property, which protects the neighborhood. I’m not sure of the intent in setting forth as a zoning bylaw what all property owners must do, i.e., meet all local and state regulations. adhere to building,pet, fire, heath codes etc—in the zoning regulation-and, if the effect is making any violation of any regulation or law a zoning violation, would be legal or enforceable. For penalties and enforcement, you mentioned you added verbiage to clarify that the 3 incidents are 3 separate STR stays. I also suggested including that three or more “material and willful” violations so that minute innocent technical violations aren’t so harshly penalized. I also suggest that the maximum legal occupancy set by the health department under 110-6 (4) state that it be established “in accordance with state and local law” . Thank you and have a great weekend! Dawn Karol, Esq. KAROL & KAROL Counsellors at Law 424 Adams Street Milton, MA 02186 Tel (617) 696-1000 Fax (617)696-0420 ARTICLE #5: General Bylaw Chapter 110 – Short-Term Rentals (1): To see if the Town will vote to add to the Town of Yarmouth General Bylaws Chapter 110 – Short Term Rentals, or take any other action relative thereto, as follows: Chapter 110 SHORT-TERM RENTALS § 110-1. Purpose. To provide for the orderly operation of short-term rentals for residential properties that balance private, neighborhood and public interests, and will: 1. Protect and maintain the residential character of existing neighborhoods. 2. Protect public health and safety. 3. Protect and preserve year-round housing stock. 4. Inhibit the commercialization of housing for use as Short Term Rentals. 5. Enable residents to better afford to live in Yarmouth, maintain their properties and contribute to the community. 6. Ensure the continued revenues to the Town from the short-term rental excise tax. § 110-2. Definitions. OWNER – Any person, corporation, LLC, trust or other entity that, alone, or severally with others, directly or indirectly, has legal or equitable title or beneficial interest in any dwelling unit. OPERATOR – A person or entity who is designated by an Owner to be responsible for the dayto-day operations of the Short-Term Rental and who serves as the local 24-hour emergency contact person with the Town of Yarmouth. An Owner may also be an Operator provided they are available 24 hours a day during the rental period to address operational issues at the Short-Term Rental. SHORT-TERM RENTALS (STR) - defined as owner-occupied, tenant-occupied or non-owner occupied residential property including, but not limited to, an apartment unit, house, cottage, condominium or a furnished accommodation that is not a hotel, motel, boarding or lodging house, or guesthouse, inn or bed and breakfast establishment, where at least one room or unit is rented to an occupant or occupants for 1-31 consecutive days at a time. STRs are characterized as transient in nature and not rented to the same occupant month to month. TIME SHARE, FRACTIONAL AND INTERVAL OWNERSHIP UNIT - Any Dwelling Unit which is owned by a limited liability company, corporation, partnership, or other joint ownership structure in which unrelated persons or entities own, sell, purchase or otherwise, for consideration, create or acquire any divided property interest including co-ownership or fractional or divided estates, shares, leaseholds, or memberships which are subject to, or subsequently bound by any agreement limiting the right or functional ability of interest holders or their designees to occupy or use the property to their respective interests or any other agreement which limits interest holders’ or their designees’ use of the property to fractional reservations through stay limitations of any duration. Such use is established by one or more of the following elements: 1) co-ownership or fractional or divided estates, shares, leaseholds, or memberships which are openly advertised, marketed, or offered for sale and sold individually at STR Article 1 – General Bylaw Draft #5 – October 2, 2026 Page 1 of 5 separate times; 2) centralized or professional management; 3) reservation systems; 4) maximum or minimum day limits on each interest holder’s occupancy or use of the property; or 5) management agreements or fees reflective of interval use or ownership, irrespective of whether the agreement may be cancelled individually or by any party. § 110-3. Ineligible Units. The following are not eligible to be rented as STRs. 1. Dwellings designated as income restricted or which are subject to affordability covenants or restrictions. 2. Approved Accessory Apartments, Accessory Dwelling Units, and Protected Use Accessory Dwelling Units, as defined in, and approved under, the Zoning Bylaw. 3. Dwelling units on a property containing an Accessory Apartment, Accessory Dwelling Unit or Protected Use Accessory Dwelling Unit. 4. Dwellings developed under the MU Zoning District bylaw and the VCOD, ROAD, HMOD1, HMOD2, and MOD Overlay District Bylaws. 5. Dwelling units with Time Share, Fractional and Interval Ownership. 6. Dwellings subject to any unresolved outstanding building, sanitary, zoning, conservation, or fire code violations. 7. As of right Duplexes created and approved under G.L. c. 40A, §3. § 110-4. Registration & Inspections. 1. All Short-Term Rentals shall be registered annually through the Yarmouth Health Department in accordance with General Bylaw Chapter 108 – Occupancy of Buildings; and shall be inspected annually by the Building Commissioner, or his/her designee, in accordance with 780 CMR – MA State Building Code; and shall adhere to all health and safety requirements. Overnight occupancy limitations shall be set by the Health Department based on inspections and septic capacity. 2. Rental Occupancy Certificate and Certificate of Inspection shall be displayed on the property in a prominent location and shall include 24-hour local contact information. All Certificates expire on December 31st of each year. 3. The Town reserves the right to post rental locations and contact information on the Town Website per MGL Ch. 64G, Section 14. § 110-5. Limitations on Short-Term Rentals. 1. Except as otherwise noted in this section, the following limitations shall apply to STR: a. No Owner shall register more than one (1) dwelling unit as a Short-Term Rental in the Town of Yarmouth. b. No person shall have legal or equitable title or beneficial interest in more than one (1) dwelling unit used for Short-Term Rentals in the Town of Yarmouth. For the purposes of this Section, a STR shall not be permitted if the Owner thereof, or any STR Article 1 – General Bylaw Draft #5 – October 2, 2026 Page 2 of 5 entity that has a substantial relation to the Owner, has any direct or indirect interest or control in another Owner that possesses a registered STR. 2. Owners who held a valid 2025 or 2026 Rental Certificate on more than one STR may continue to register more than one STR until the property is sold or transferred, and continues to hold a valid annual Rental Occupancy Certificate. § 110-56. General Provisions. 1. Trash Removal: All household trash shall be removed from the premises immediately after occupancy is concluded, and at a minimum once per week. 2. Parking: On-site parking area shall be provided and will be determined by the Health or Building Departments at time of inspection. There shall be no parking on lawns at any time and no expansion of parking into green space areas in front of the dwelling. No overnight street parking from 11:00PM to 7:00AM, and no street parking that impedes traffic or traffic safety at any time. 3. Duration: Renting for less than two (2) consecutive nights is prohibited. 4. Occupancy: Maximum overnight occupancy from 11:00PM to 7:00AM shall be the occupancy limit set by the Health Department in accordance with state and local laws, regardless of the number of bedrooms or places to sleep (i.e., beds, sofas, cots, bunk beds, etc.) provided in the STR. 5. Noise: All occupants of Short-Term Rentals shall adhere to General Bylaw Chapter 104 – Noise and shall respect quiet hours from 11:00PM to 7:00AM. 6. Type of Rentals: a. STRs are for Residential uses only. No large-scale events including, but not limited to, weddings; corporate events; graduation, fraternity/sorority, bridal or bachelor parties; and class/family reunions may take place in a STR or on a STR property. b. No events that include tents or amplified music may take place on a STR property. c. STRs shall not be used in a manner that adversely affects the residential character of the neighborhood or substantially and unreasonably interferes with any a reasonable person’s use and enjoyment of their residence and property. An adverse effect may occur when, for example, an STR is used in a manner that results in the production of excessive noise, vibration, light, glare, trash, fumes, odors, traffic, parking congestion, or any other nuisance at any time beyond that which normally occurs in the immediate residential area. 7. Pets: Adherence to any and all state and local regulations regarding pets. 8. Use of RVs, campers or sleeping tents as STRs or sleeping spaces is prohibited. 9. Short Term Rentals shall meet all local and state regulations, including but not limited to building and fire codes, health codes, water supply and wastewater disposal. § 110-67. Northern Middlesex Regional Housing Services Office (NMRHSO) Intermunicipal Agreement Approval This is an Intermunicipal Agreement with the Northern Middlesex Council of Governments (NMCOG) to participate in a shared Regional Housing Services Office (NMRHSO). Through this agreement, the Town will receive administrative and technical assistance for affordable housing matters, including monitoring affordable housing units, supporting housing initiatives, and assisting with compliance and reporting requirements. The agreement is for one year (FY27) with an annual cost based on services provided, and allows the Town to share resources and expertise with other participating communities. Jennifer Raitt, Executive Director of the Northern Middlesex Council of Governments (NMCOG), presented the proposed inter-municipal agreement to establish the Northern Middlesex Regional Housing Services Office (NMRHSO). She explained that the program has been piloted over the past year and is intended to provide regional support for tracking and managing affordable housing inventories, as well as offering technical assistance to participating communities. Ms. Raitt outlined that the service would provide more detailed, localized, and continuous technical assistance than what is currently available through the State, including maintaining a curated regional inventory, monitoring deed-restricted units, and assisting with compliance and reporting requirements. Town Manager Chris Dillon noted that the pilot program identified additional deed-restricted units that were not previously counted by the State and highlighted that the program includes approximately 30 hours of local project support as part of its base services. Member Rosa inquired about the value of the proposed $22,400 fee compared to services already provided by the Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD). Ms. Raitt clarified that while the State 4 Page 5 of 12 provides general data and reporting, the proposed service offers more detailed, community-specific support and monitoring. Member Favreau confirmed that the agreement represents a new service separate from the Town’s existing NMCOG membership assessment and that the associated fee would be an additional cost beginning in Fiscal Year 2027. She also asked whether services would extend to public housing, to which Ms. Raitt responded that public housing units are included within the affordable housing inventory and would be covered under the base scope of services. Vice Chair Burrows asked questions regarding the fee structure, including the differences in opt-in costs among participating communities and potential additional service charges. Ms. Raitt explained that the fee structure was developed based on a regional analysis of housing inventories and comparable programs, and that additional services beyond the base scope would be optional and billed separately as needed. Board members expressed general support for the regional approach and the benefits of enhanced tracking and technical assistance for affordable housing compliance. MOTION Secretary Darris-O’Connor moved to approve the Northern Middlesex Regional Housing Services Office inter-municipal agreement and to authorize the Town Manager to execute the agreement on behalf of the Town. Member Rosa seconded the motion. Darris-O’Connor Yea Favreau Yea Burrows Yea Rosa Yea Pavidis Yea b. Discussion and Vote on prior MOA regarding healthcare Request to approve a Memorandum of Agreement related to employee health insurance changes, including contribution adjustments and implementation of a cost share assistance program, which was previously agreed upon by all bargaining units but not formally approved by the Select Board. Approval is expected to result in cost savings to the Town. Town Manager Chris Dillon explained that a prior Memorandum of Agreement (MOA) had been negotiated with various bargaining units approximately two years ago to implement modifications to employee health insurance. He noted that the agreement was never formally approved by the Select Board at that time and is now being brought forward for formal approval. Mr. Dillon stated that one component of the agreement includes the implementation of a cost-share assistance program administered by PillarRx, which is expected to provide cost savings to the Town. He requested Board approval to move forward with the agreement. Secretary Darris-O’Connor expressed strong support for the agreement and acknowledged the cooperation of the Town’s bargaining units in negotiating the MOA, particularly in light of rising healthcare costs. 5 Page 6 of 12 Member Rosa also supported the measure and inquired about anticipated cost savings. It was noted that estimated savings are approximately $23,000 in the first year. Vice Chair Burrows indicated his support for the agreement as well. MOTION Secretary Darris-O’Connor moved to approve the Memorandum of Agreement regarding employee health insurance changes and to authorize the Town Manager to execute the agreement. Member Rosa seconded the motion. Darris-O’Connor Yea Favreau Yea Burrows Yea Rosa Yea Pavidis Yea c. SOI Approval-Kerry Cleary & Sean Bartlett Authorization to submit MSBA Statements of Interest for Locke (priority) and Marshall (non-priority) Middle Schools to address facility deficiencies and maintain eligibility for future funding opportunities. This is just the first step to keep Billerica eligible for potential state funding, no commitment to build anything. Superintendent Kerry Cleary, accompanied by Sean Bartlett, Director of Facilities, presented two Statements of Interest (SOIs) for submission to the Massachusetts School Building Authority (MSBA), one for the Locke Middle School (priority site) and one for the Marshall Middle School (non-priority site). Dr. Cleary explained that while the primary focus is the Locke Middle School, the Marshall Middle School must also be submitted as a non-priority site due to potential impacts associated with future planning scenarios, including a possible middle school consolidation. She noted that the School Committee unanimously approved the SOIs in March and requested Select Board approval in advance of the April 17 submission deadline. Members of the Board expressed support for the proposal: Member Favreau voiced strong support and relayed feedback from residents regarding interest in a combined middle school and the potential return of eighth-grade students to the middle school level. Member Rosa supported the inclusion of the Marshall School as a secondary site and emphasized the importance of maintaining flexibility for a centralized middle school option. Secretary Darris-O’Connor highlighted the SOI as a critical first step in entering the MSBA pipeline and emphasized the importance of transparency and long-term planning for school facilities. Vice Chair Burrows expressed appreciation for the work completed to date and indicated support for moving the project forward. Chair Pavidis stated her full support and looked forward to future phases of the project. The Board acknowledged that submission of the SOIs does not guarantee acceptance into the MSBA program but represents the initial step in a multi-phase process. 6 Page 7 of 12 MOTIONS Locke Middle School (Priority Site) Secretary Darris-O’Connor moved to authorize the Superintendent to submit a Statement of Interest to the Massachusetts School Building Authority for the Locke Middle School, 110 Allen Road, identifying deficiencies under Priority Categories 4, 5, and 7, and acknowledging that submission does not guarantee acceptance or funding. Member Rosa seconded the motion. Darris-O’Connor Yea Favreau Yea Burrows Yea Rosa Yea Pavidis Yea Marshall Middle School (Non-Priority Site) Secretary Darris-O’Connor moved to authorize the Superintendent to submit a Statement of Interest to the Massachusetts School Building Authority for the Marshall Middle School, 15 Floyd Street, as a nonpriority site, identifying deficiencies under Priority Categories 4, 5, and 7, and acknowledging that submission does not guarantee acceptance or funding. Member Rosa seconded the motion. Darris-O’Connor Yea Favreau Yea Burrows Yea Rosa Yea Pavidis Yea 9. New Business a. AFSCME Contract-Review of Ratified Contract Town Manager Chris Dillon presented a redlined tentative agreement between the Town and the AFSCME Union, noting that negotiations began in late summer/early fall. He explained that the agreement updates the union representation from IUPE to AFSCME and includes various administrative and clerical corrections throughout the document. Mr. Dillon highlighted several key changes, including the removal of four positions from the union contingent upon Town Meeting approval: Payroll Coordinator, Veterans Head Clerk, DPW Administrative Clerk, and Police Head Clerk. He also noted that the Senior Clerk position would be removed from the wage classification and that the wage scale has been streamlined to eliminate outdated or unused positions. The agreement includes title updates for several classifications and introduces additional steps within the wage scale to address compression issues and better align salaries with market rates. Mr. Dillon explained that a significant portion of the union had previously reached the top step, limiting opportunities for wage progression. 7 Page 8 of 12 The proposed contract includes cost-of-living adjustments (COLA) of 2% effective July 1, 2026; 2% effective July 1, 2027; and 2% effective July 1, 2028. Additional updates include clarifications to vacation and sick leave provisions, with revised language and examples intended to improve consistency in interpretation. SUMMARY This proposed law would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. This proposed law would exempt documents related to the development of public policy and communications between legislators and their constituents, if those communications are reasonably related to a constituent's request for assistance in obtaining government-provided benefits or services or interacting with a government agency. A YES VOTE would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. A NO VOTE would make no change to the Massachusetts Public Records Law. QUESTION 2: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would specify that employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services ("CPCS") are pennitted to engage in collective bargaining with their employer. It would also require CPCS, after executing a collective bargaining agreement, to request the appropriation necessary to fund such agreement from the Governor. A YES VOTE would specify that Committee for Public Counsel Services employees may form a union to collectively bargain with their employer. A NO VOTE would make no change to the law governing labor relations for Committee for Public Counsel Service employees. QUESTION 3: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would eliminate political party primaries for state elections and instead establish a system where there would be a single, all-party primary in which all candidates, regardless of their party affiliation, would be listed on one ballot, and voters could vote for any candidate on the ballot. The two candidates receiving the most votes in the primary would advance to the general election ballot. This proposed law would require candidates for governor and lieutenant governor to run and be listed jointly on the ballot in the primary. This proposed law would provide political party status to any group whose candidates for any statewide office received at least 3% ofthe ballots cast in the state primary. A YES VOTE would eliminate separate party primaries for state elections and require a single primary in which all candidates appear on one ballot, voters could vote for any candidate, and the top two candidates would advance to the general election. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing primary elections. QUESTION 4: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would permit eligible individuals to register to vote or update their voter registration address on Election Day. An individual who is eligible to vote could register to vote on Election Day by going to the polling place in the precinct where they live during voting hours and presenting proof of residency and signing a written oath. Proof of residency could be a valid photo identification, or documentation showing the individual's name and the address where the individual resides, such as a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, residential lease, wireless telephone statement, paycheck, current student fee statement or other document from a post-secondary school, or another government document or correspondence. The written oath would require the individual to certify that they are a citizen of the United 2 States, are at least 18 years old, are not legally prohibited from voting, and have not and will not vote in the same election at another location. The oath would require the individual to acknowledge that providing false infonnation is a felony punishable by not more than 5 years imprisonment or a fine of not more than $10,000, or both. If an individual did not present proof of residency, they would be allowed to cast a provisional ballot, which would be counted only if the individual returned to provide the required infonnation before the close of polls for a municipal election; within two days after a state primary; or within six days after a state election. Individuals who register to vote on Election Day would be registered to vote in future elections as well as in the election taking place that day. Individuals who are already registered to vote would not be able to change their political party affiliation on Election Day. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028. A YES VOTE would permit eligible citizens to register to vote or to update their voter registration address at their polling place on Election Day. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing voter registration. SUMMARY This proposed law would change the limit on how much revenue the state can collect in a given year. The proposal would limit state revenue in a given year to the net amount of state revenue from the year before, increased by a rate equal to the average growth of wages and salaries in Massachusetts over the most recent three years. If revenue collected by the state in a given year exceeds the limit, the excess amount would be refunded to taxpayers the following year. The proposed law would include all revenue from the surtax on incomes over $1 million when calculating the revenue limit and when detennining whether state revenue exceeds the limit. The provisions of the proposed law would all be effective as of July 1, 2027. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect. A YES VOTE would change the limit on state revenue collection, tying it to prior year collections plus average wage and salary growth, and provide for a rebate of revenue exceeding that limit. A NO VOTE would make no change in the law relative to state revenue collection. text: FITCHBURG CITY CLERK Oct 15 2026 3:37 pm WELCOME TO THE FITCHBURG CITY COUNCIL October 20, 2026 Fitchburg Legislative Building 700 Main Street Fitchburg MA 01420 7:00 PM This meeting can also be viewed live on FATV. Go to www.fatv.org/watch-fatv for more information on accessing this meeting. This is intended to help you understand the meeting format and assist you with the rules of the Council as they pertain to your participation. All meetings of the Fitchburg City council are open to the public. This does not mean that the public participates in all aspects of the meeting. It simply means that the meeting itself, including all discussions and votes, is open for public view. Executive Session The only time a Council meeting can be closed to the public is when the Council votes for Executive Session in order to discuss sensitive matters in private, such as pending litigation. Any votes taken however, must be taken in open session. OPPORTUNITIES FOR THE PUBLIC TO SPEAK DURING A COUNCIL MEETING: Public Forum The Public Forum occurs immediately following the Pledge of Allegiance. The President will ask if anyone in the audience wishes to speak on any matter appearing on the Agenda. If you wish to address the Council, you must stand and be recognized and follow these rules before speaking: 1. 2. 3. 4. State your name and city of residence. Approach the center table and either stand or sit. This allows you to be seen and heard clearly by everyone in attendance. You may speak only on items appearing on the agenda for no more than (2) minutes. Copies of the agenda are available on the center table prior to the meeting. Please state the petition, order, ordinance, or resolution number to which you refer. Public Hearings Public hearings are held on various issues such as Special Permits and Zoning changes. The same rules apply with the following exceptions: 1. You must stand and be recognized either “in favor” or “in opposition” when asked by the Council President. 2. You need not refer to the petition number. If you have any questions or comments either before or after the meeting, any Councilor would be happy to assist you. Thank you for your interest! I. PUBLIC FORUM This meeting will be open to the public. text: City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of October 5, 2026 Minutes of the Regular Meeting Monday, October 5, 2026 – 7:30 P.M City Council Chamber Roll Call Members Present: ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● President George Tyros Councillor Calvin Brooks Councillor Alek Dernalowicz Councillor Dana Heath Councillor Brad Heglin Councillor Elizabeth Kazinskas Councillor Judy Mack Councillor Paul Tassone Members Absent: ● ● ● Councillor Craig Cormier Councillor Karen Hardern Councillor David Thibault-Muñoz Open Meeting Law Announcement President Tyros announced that any person wishing to make an audio or video recording of the meeting, or transmit the meeting through any medium, was required to notify the Chair pursuant to Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 30A, §20. READING OF MINUTES OF PRIOR MEETINGS September 21, 2026 Informal Meeting Minutes Councillor Mack moved to waive the reading of the minutes and accept them as presented. Councillor Tassone seconded the motion. The motion passed by voice vote. September 21, 2026 Executive Session Minutes Consideration of the minutes was deferred to a later meeting. Page 1 of 10 PAGE 3 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of October 5, 2026 September 21, 2026 Regular Meeting Minutes Councillor Dernalowicz moved to waive the reading of the minutes and accept them as presented. Councillor Kazinskas seconded the motion. The motion passed by voice vote. With no objection from the Council, President Tyros took the reports of the Appointments Committee out of order. Item 11910 – A Measure Confirming the Mayor's Appointment of Darrell Sweeney to the Position of Inspector of Wires for a Term Expiring July 24, 2027 Councillor Kazinskas reported that the Appointments Committee had unanimously recommended confirmation and moved to confirm the appointment. Councillor Heglin seconded the motion. Councillor Kazinskas discussed Mr. Sweeney's service as Gardner's electrical inspector since April 2011, his experience in other communities, and his commitment to the City. She noted that he was recovering from an injury and intended to return to work when medically cleared. The motion passed by voice vote. Item 11916 – A Measure Confirming the Mayor's Appointment of Peter Kettle to the Airport Commission for a Term Expiring July 24, 2029 Councillor Kazinskas moved to confirm the appointment. Councillor Heglin seconded the motion. Councillor Kazinskas discussed Mr. Kettle's extensive experience in airport engineering and management, including his service as manager of Fitchburg Municipal Airport and as a member and chair of its Airport Commission. She noted his interest in improving Gardner Municipal Airport and working toward financial self-sufficiency. Councillor Brooks expressed support for the appointment, noting that he had previously worked with Mr. Kettle in Fitchburg. The motion passed by voice vote. Page 2 of 10 PAGE 4 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of October 5, 2026 Item 11917 – A Measure Confirming the Mayor's Appointment of Shaunesy Dame to the Position of Alternate Inspector of Wires for a Term Expiring July 24, 2029 Councillor Kazinskas moved to confirm the appointment. Councillor Heglin seconded the motion. Councillor Kazinskas reported that Mr. Dame had served as Gardner's alternate electrical inspector for several years and had extensive experience operating his own electrical business. She noted that the Building Commissioner had recommended his appointment. The motion passed by voice vote. Item 11924 – A Measure Confirming the Mayor's Appointment of Tanner Dumas to the Position of Police Officer Councillor Heath reported that the Appointments Committee had unanimously recommended confirmation and moved to confirm the appointment. Councillor Kazinskas seconded the motion. Councillor Heath reported that the Committee had met with the Mayor, Deputy Chief Maroni, and Mr. Dumas. He discussed Mr. Dumas's recent graduation from the police academy, his performance during training, and his commitment to community policing. The motion passed by voice vote. Item 11925 – A Measure Confirming the Mayor's Appointment of Justin Johnson to the Position of Police Officer Councillor Heath moved to confirm the appointment. Councillor Kazinskas seconded the motion. Councillor Heath reported that Mr. Johnson was a Gardner native and United States Navy veteran who had recently graduated from the police academy. He discussed Mr. Johnson's dedication during field training and expressed personal pride in his accomplishments, having previously coached him as a student-athlete. Councillor Mack also expressed support, noting that she had served as Mr. Johnson's guidance counselor. Councillor Kazinskas discussed the benefits of changes to civil service requirements that allowed the City to recruit qualified local residents. The motion passed by voice vote. Page 3 of 10 PAGE 5 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of October 5, 2026 Item 11926 – A Measure Confirming the Mayor's Appointment of Kimberly Shea, DNP, RN, to the Board of Health for a Term Expiring July 24, 2029 Councillor Heath moved to confirm the appointment. Councillor Kazinskas seconded the motion. Councillor Heath reported that Dr. Shea was a Dean of nursing and health sciences at Mount Wachusett Community College and a registered nurse with extensive experience in population health and healthcare policy. He expressed confidence that her professional background would benefit the Board of Health. The motion passed by voice vote. Item 11931 – A Measure Confirming the Mayor's Appointment of Dane Arnold to the Position of Public Works Director for a Term Expiring September 10, 2029 Councillor Heath moved to confirm the appointment. Councillor Kazinskas seconded the motion. Councillor Heath discussed Director Arnold's 25 years of service to the City, his institutional knowledge, and his leadership on major infrastructure projects, including water main replacements and wastewater treatment improvements. Additional appreciation was expressed for Director Arnold's responsiveness to Councillors and residents and his dedication to the City. The motion passed by voice vote. Following consideration of the appointments, the Council briefly recessed while the City Clerk administered oaths of office to the appointees. PUBLIC HEARINGS Item 11843 – Petition of National Grid and Verizon New England, Inc. for the Installation of One Jointly Owned Pole on Betty Spring Road Council President Tyros opened the public hearing, and the Clerk read the hearing notice. Representatives of National Grid appeared and explained that the proposed work involved the installation of a pole associated with the company's Advanced Metering Infrastructure project. Discussion arose concerning whether the proposed work constituted a pole relocation or a new installation and whether the language in the hearing notice accurately described the work. Page 4 of 10 PAGE 6 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of October 5, 2026 Due to the discrepancy in the description of the proposed installation, President Tyros closed the public hearing and announced that the matter would be rescheduled with corrected language and notice to abutters. Item 11908 – Petition of National Grid for the Installation of One Jointly Owned Pole on Park Street Council President Tyros opened the public hearing, and the Clerk read the hearing notice. A representative of National Grid explained that the petition sought authorization to install a new pole and transformer to provide electrical service to a new building at 69 Park Street. Councillor Mack clarified that the installation was associated with the City's Greenwood Pool pavilion project. No members of the public spoke in favor of or opposition to the petition. There being no further questions or comments, President Tyros declared the public hearing closed. Item 11836 – A Measure Adopting the City's Hazard Mitigation Plan Councillor Dernalowicz reported that the Finance Committee had reviewed the City's Hazard Mitigation Plan over several meetings while awaiting the completion of the federal and state review process. He explained that the City had received a $40,000 grant to prepare the plan and that the proposed plan and subsequent revisions had undergone review by the Federal Emergency Management Agency and the Massachusetts Emergency Management Agency. He reported that the required federal approval had been received. Councillor Dernalowicz moved to adopt the measure. Councillor Mack seconded the motion. The motion passed by voice vote. Item 11884 – An Ordinance to Strengthen Oversight and Transparency of Capital Improvement Planning and Projects Council President Tyros temporarily relinquished the chair to participate in discussion of the item. Page 5 of 10 PAGE 7 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of October 5, 2026 Councillor Heglin reported that the Finance Committee had reviewed the proposed ordinance over several months. He explained that the ordinance, introduced by President Tyros with the support of the Mayor, was intended to strengthen oversight of municipal capital projects, improve communication, and establish clearer procedures for project approval. He reported that revisions had been made following discussions with the Mayor, including adjustments to financial thresholds and exemptions for certain projects and emergencies. The Committee had also incorporated a requirement to identify a designated project lead. Councillor Heglin further reported that the Finance Committee had recommended an amendment entitled “An Amendment to Strengthen Enforcement of Section 40 of the City Charter.” He explained that the amendment would establish documentation and notification requirements for School Department capital projects while preserving the School Committee's existing authority. He noted that the School Committee had voted 6–1 to endorse the amendment. Councillor Heglin moved to adopt the amendment. President Tyros seconded the motion. President Tyros spoke in support of the amendment, citing concerns arising from the Gardner High School C-Wing project and the importance of ensuring that elected officials have an opportunity to review proposed capital improvements before significant public funds are committed. He emphasized that the amendment was intended to strengthen transparency and accountability without interfering with the School Committee's authority or the day-to-day administration of school projects. Councillor Kazinskas expressed support, discussing previous concerns regarding the availability of financial information and project planning for the middle school roof, high school auditorium, C-Wing improvements, and renovations to School Department administrative offices at Elm Street School. She stated that clearer procedures were necessary to ensure that elected officials understood project costs and funding before expenditures were authorized. Councillor Mack also expressed support, raising concerns regarding previous School Department capital expenditures and emphasizing the importance of respecting the oversight responsibilities of the School Committee and City Council. Councillor Heglin reiterated that the amendment had been developed in cooperation with members of the School Committee and was intended to address concerns shared by both governing bodies. The motion to adopt the amendment passed by voice vote. The Council then returned to consideration of the underlying ordinance, as amended. Page 6 of 10 PAGE 8 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of October 5, 2026 Councillor Heglin reviewed the principal provisions of the ordinance, including reforms to the Capital Improvements Committee, the establishment of financial thresholds for additional project oversight, designation of project leads, and requirements for final project plan review. Councillor Heglin moved to send the ordinance, as amended, to its first printing. President Tyros seconded the motion. President Tyros discussed the need for greater transparency in municipal capital projects, particularly regarding project scope, estimated costs, management responsibilities, and changes made after initial approval. He explained that the ordinance would provide the Council with final project plans before procurement for certain projects and establish advisory committees for larger projects while preserving appropriate administrative flexibility. Councillor Kazinskas expressed support for the ordinance and commended President Tyros, Councillor Heglin, and the Mayor for their work developing the proposal. She discussed the Council's responsibility to oversee public expenditures and cited the Macki Park project as an example of the need for improved accountability between project authorization and completion. The motion to send the ordinance, as amended, to its first printing passed by voice vote. President Tyros resumed the chair. Item 11927 – A Measure Declaring Property Taken Through Tax Title, Located at 35–39 Graham Street, as Surplus Councillor Mack reported that the Finance Committee had favorably recommended the measure and moved its adoption. Councillor Dernalowicz seconded the motion. Councillor Mack explained that the Massachusetts Land Court had foreclosed on the property for delinquent taxes and interest, which totaled approximately $666,895 when the tax-title proceedings began in 1991. She stated that the measure would authorize the Mayor and City Treasurer to proceed with disposition of the property in accordance with Massachusetts law and require notification to the Council following the sale. Councillor Tassone questioned whether the City would need to invest additional funds in the property before selling it. Mayor Nicholson explained that changes to state law in 2024 established new procedures for disposing of tax-title properties, including appraisal and marketing requirements. He stated that the City would be required to determine whether to retain the property for municipal purposes or proceed with a sale and that he recommended selling the property given its condition and history. Page 7 of 10 PAGE 9 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of October 5, 2026 The Mayor further explained that proceeds exceeding the outstanding taxes, interest, and eligible costs would be returned to the former property owner under the revised law. The motion passed by voice vote. Item 11928 – A Measure Declaring Property Taken Through Tax Title, Located at 67 Sawyer Street, as Surplus Councillor Mack reported that the Finance Committee had favorably recommended the measure and moved its adoption. Councillor Dernalowicz seconded the motion. Councillor Mack explained that the Massachusetts Land Court had foreclosed on the property for delinquent taxes and interest, which totaled approximately $92,755 when proceedings began in 2009. She stated that the measure would authorize the Mayor and City Treasurer to proceed with the sale in accordance with state law. Councillor Mack discussed the competitive bidding requirements applicable to municipal property dispositions and emphasized that the process was governed by state law. Councillor Kazinskas reiterated that the City was required to follow the procedures established by the Commonwealth. Councillor Brooks discussed the financial implications of tax-title foreclosures, including the City's ability to recover eligible costs associated with property disposition. He noted that tax-title enforcement was an important component of maintaining compliance with municipal property tax obligations. The motion passed by voice vote. Item 11929 – An Order to Designate a Certain Intersection as “Walsh Square” Councillor Dernalowicz reported that the order had been jointly proposed by Council President Tyros and Mayor Nicholson to designate the intersection of City Hall Avenue and Pleasant Street as Walsh Square. He explained that the designation would recognize the contributions of Martin Walsh, who served as City Councillor, Council President, State Representative, and Postmaster, and his son, Attorney James Walsh, who served as City Councillor, Council President, City Solicitor, and Acting Mayor. Councillor Dernalowicz reported that the Finance Committee had recommended approval and moved to adopt the order. Councillor Mack seconded the motion. Page 8 of 10 PAGE 10 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of October 5, 2026 The motion passed by voice vote. UNFINISHED BUSINESS AND MATTERS FOR RECONSIDERATION Item 11841B – An Ordinance to Amend Attachment F of Chapter 8 of the Code of the City of Gardner, thereof entitled “Primary Non-Union Compensation Schedule,” to Add the Position of Golf Administrative Assistant Councillor Mack moved to send the ordinance to its second and final printing. Councillor Heglin seconded the motion. There being no discussion, the motion passed by voice vote. Item 11870 – An Ordinance to Increase Financial Transparency, Financial Governance, and Budget Preparedness Councillor Heglin moved to send the ordinance to its second and final printing. Councillor Dernalowicz seconded the motion. Councillor Heglin thanked the Council for its support and discussed the importance of improving the City's long-term financial planning. He specifically referenced the proposed five-year financial forecasting requirement, noting that other communities, including Winchendon, were already undertaking similar forecasting efforts. Councillor Brooks expressed support for the ordinance and requested that the monthly expenditure reports required under the ordinance be distributed to all members of the City Council, rather than solely to the Finance Committee, so that all Councillors would remain informed regarding the City's financial condition. Councillor Dernalowicz noted that the Finance Committee had recently received a financial update from the City Auditor and encouraged Councillors to review that discussion. The motion to send the ordinance to its second and final printing passed by voice vote. Item 11891 – An Ordinance to Amend the Code of the City of Gardner to Create a Regular Review Schedule for Various Rates and Fees to Ensure Financial Viability and Responsibility Councillor Heglin moved to send the ordinance to its second and final printing. Councillor Dernalowicz seconded the motion. Page 9 of 10 PAGE 11 City of Gardner City Council - Regular Meeting of October 5, 2026 There being no discussion, the motion passed by voice vote. COUNCIL COMMENTS AND REMARKS Councillor Heglin reported that he had attended the annual vigil organized by the Domestic Violence Prevention Task Force at Monument Park earlier that evening, along with Mayor Nicholson. He stated that he had offered remarks on behalf of the City Council and recognized individuals affected by domestic violence. He encouraged residents needing assistance to utilize available community resources, including the Task Force, the Police Department, and the Department's domestic violence advocate. Councillor Mack recognized October as Breast Cancer Awareness Month and encouraged residents to obtain recommended mammograms and take advantage of available screening resources, including services for individuals without health insurance. Councillor Kazinskas offered birthday wishes to Caleb Michael Budwick on his ninth birthday and recognized the birthday of her late grandfather. There being no further Council comments or remarks, the Council proceeded to adjournment. ADJOURNMENT Prior to the closing prayer, Councillor Tassone moved to adjourn following the prayer. Councillor Heglin seconded the motion. The closing prayer was then offered. Is that too late to approve these? If so, I could convene the SB just before the Special town meeting on October 20th to do this approval. SusanMary On Oct 6, 2026, at 4:12 PM, Aaron Farber-Chen <afarberchen01434@gmail.com> wrote: Hi SusanMary, 1 The AAFWG has voted to recommend funding for 2 new mini-grant proposals. Could we add both to the agenda for the next Select Board meeting for approval? Brief summaries are below, and I'm happy to send the full applications ahead of time. 1. Harvard Public School (HPS) & Cartwheel Youth Mental Health and Substance Use Prevention Partnership: $9,975 Applicant: Harvard Public Schools (Michelle DellaValle) HPS will partner with Cartwheel to offer students school-connected telehealth: therapy, psychiatric care, parent guidance, and care coordination. The aim is to address mental health concerns early, before they lead to substance misuse, and to connect students with substance use concerns to specialized care. Targets include first appointments within about 7 days and measurable symptom improvement for 75% of participating students. The project runs for 1 year and is open to roughly 1,000 HPS students. 2. "What Families and Communities Should Know About Fentanyl, Addiction, and Recovery": $3,000 Applicant: Warner Free Lecture (Michael Kilian) This is a free public lecture and Q&A for families, educators, and residents of Harvard and surrounding towns. It will cover fentanyl risks, overdose prevention, treatment, recovery, and reducing stigma. The speaker is addiction medicine physician Dr. Sarah Wakeman of Mass General Brigham. Michael amended the budget after confirming Dr. Wakeman's fee at $2,000, which lowered the request from $4,500 to $3,000. The remaining funds cover other expenses (e.g., outreach, materials, refreshments). The event is planned for January–May 2027, with a target of 150–200 attendees. I'd be glad to attend the meeting to present both proposals and answer any questions. Just let me know the date. Thanks so much! Best, Aaron Farber-Chen 2

Those wishing to speak regarding a specific agenda item shall register to speak in advance of the meeting by sending an email to dricker@lowellma.gov, pcutrumbes@lowellma.gov AND mbrundage@lowellma.gov indicating the agenda item and a phone number to call so that you may be issued zoom link to the meeting. If no access to email, you may contact Development Services at 978-6744144. All requests must occur prior to 4:00PM on the day of meeting. The subject property is located in the Traditional Mixed-Use (TMU). The proposal requires Variance approval per Section 6.1 for relief from the minimum off-street parking requirement, and for any other relief required under the Lowell Zoning Ordinance. *PLEASE NOTE: THE ABOVE APPLICATION IS REQUESTING A WITHDRAWAL WITHOUT PREJUDICE* ZBA-2026-36 Petition Type: Special Permit and Variance Applicant: Jeffrey Ciccone Property Located at: 37-39 Roberts Street, 01854 Applicable Zoning Bylaws: Sections 4.3, 4.5, and 4.5 Petition: The Lowell Zoning Board of Appeals will hold a public hearing to hear all interested persons relative to an application by Jeffrey Ciccone to retain the existing three-family home at 37 Robert Street; and to construct a singlefamily home and Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU) at 39 Robert Street. The subject property at 37 Robert Street is located in the Traditional Two-Family (TTF) zoning district. The subject property at 39 Robert Street is located in the Traditional Single-Family (TSF) zoning district. The proposal at 37 Robert Street requires a Variance per Section 5.1 for relief from minimum lot size, minimum lot area per dwelling unit (LA/DU), minimum side yard setbacks; a Variance per Section 4.3.5 (4) for relief from garage side yard setback; a Variance per Section 6.1.4 for relief from minimum off-street parking spaces; and any other relief required under the City of Lowell Zoning Ordinance. The proposal at 39 Robert Street requires a Variance per Section 5.1 for relief from minimum lot size, minimum lot area per dwelling unit (LA/DU), minimum frontage, maximum Floor-Area-Ratio (FAR), minimum lot width; and any other relief required under the City of Lowell Zoning Ordinance. The regulations took effect on February 27, 2026, and mandatory municipal participation began on October 1, 2026. Municipalities have 12 months to review and decide on a complete application for a small clean energy project. The application must include the materials required for all applicable land-use permits—such as those issued by the Planning Board or Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA)—and environmental permits, such as those issued by the Conservation Commission. If no decision is issued within 12 months, the application receives constructive approval. Under this process, individual application components cannot be appealed separately before all boards have completed their reviews and the Local Government Representative has issued a decision on the application. The application’s approval, denial, or constructive approval may be appealed for de novo adjudication before the Director of the Energy Facilities Siting Board (EFSB), pursuant to 980 CMR 14.00. WHAT ARE THE RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT REPRESENTATIVE? Zoning Bylaw: 225 CMR 29.00 does not necessitate Local Governments to update their zoning bylaws. Local Governments may elect to adopt the model permitting bylaw to be made available by DOER. The permitting model bylaw may be used to customize the consolidated permitting process to meet the unique needs of cities and towns. Local Governments should always consult their local municipal counsel when considering adopting a bylaw. Local Governments may also consider adopting DOER’s updated model solar bylaw, and new model storage bylaw. Please be advised that neither DOER’s model solar bylaw nor model storage bylaw are offered under the regulatory umbrella of 225 CMR 29.00, nor are they related to the 2024 Climate Act. Please note, the Town of Montague has amended its Zoning Bylaw to include Section 8.9 Solar Energy Installations & Facilities and Battery Energy Storage Facilities. Local Government Representative: Before implementing the consolidated local permitting process, the Town of Montague should identify a Local Government Representative. Purpose: This Policy is adopted to facilitate orderly and efficient public comment periods at meetings of Town public bodies. It will protect the ability of the residents of Nantucket, and other persons, to provide feedback or information to pertinent public bodies regarding matters of public interest, Town initiatives, operations, services, and programs. To allow speakers a fair opportunity to address a public body, and to ensure the public body may accomplish its stated business in an efficient manner, these guidelines seek to ensure compliance with the Open Meeting Law and meet other legal and constitutional obligations. Meetings of public bodies in the Town of Nantucket should be places to engage in orderly and peaceable discourse. B. Authority: Principles of free speech and freedom to petition the government, fundamental rights protected by the United States and Massachusetts Constitutions, prohibit public bodies from preventing all speech that may be upsetting or offensive. As such, this Policy establishes reasonable time, place, and manner restrictions sufficient to facilitate orderly and peaceable public comment periods at meetings of elected and appointed public bodies of the Town. C. Legal Standards: Meetings of public bodies are subject to the requirements of the Open Meeting Law, G.L. c. 30A, §§ 18-25. The Open Meeting Law empowers the chair of a public body to preside at and regulate the proceedings of meetings. Pursuant to G.L c. 30A, § 20(g), no person shall address a meeting of a public body without permission of the chair, and all persons shall, at the request of the chair, be silent. Any person wishing to speak at an open meeting must first be recognized by the chair. All questions raised and all comments made by a duly-recognized speaker must be directed to the chair of the public body alone, not to individual members of the public body, staff, or the public. The chair is authorized to maintain order, and, although a rare occurrence, has authority, after appropriate warnings are ignored, to take action up to and including removal of a person who is disrupting a meeting. D. Application: To secure the rights of the public to participate in public comment periods in the Town of Nantucket in a manner consistent with law, and, to thereby protect the Town and members of elected and appointed bodies from civil rights claims, this policy shall apply to all public bodies in the Town of Nantucket. E. Procedures: 1. All agendas of multiple-member bodies in the Town of Nantucket shall include a period for Public Comment, subject to the limitations set forth in paragraph 3. Where to place Public Comment on the agenda is at the discretion of the chair. If public comment is invited during a separate agenda item, this Policy shall govern. 2. While statements made during a Public Comment period are not required to address an agenda item for that particular meeting, such comments must relate to a matter within the public body’s jurisdiction. Public comments on matters outside the public body’s jurisdiction may be ruled out of order by the chair. To avoid due process issues, a person seeking to provide comments on a matter appearing on the same agenda will be asked to defer until the specific agenda item is reached. 3. Each speaker will be allowed to speak once for up to 3 minutes. The chair will curtail verbal comments exceeding the allotted time. 4. A recognized speaker may not cede or assign their time to another unless such an assignment is required as reasonable accommodation for such person because of a disability. All speakers who may need an accommodation are strongly encouraged to contact Town staff or the chair of the public body at least 48 hours prior to the meeting. That said, to facilitate an efficient public comment period, groups that have multiple speakers with the same viewpoint may consider consolidating their comments or designating one person to speak on their individual behalf’s. F. Disruptive Conduct/Unprotected Speech: Disruptive conduct and engaging in other unprotected speech, including but not limited to the following, may be grounds for the chair of a public body to curtail speech and take other action as appropriate: 1. Speaking without being recognized; 2. Continuing to speak after the chair has curtailed additional verbal comment; 3. Interrupting a recognized speaker; 4. Speaking about matters not within the jurisdiction of the public body; 5. Engaging in conversations while another person is speaking; 6. Making true threats of violence directed toward a particular individual; and 7. Making comments inciting imminent lawlessness. G. Public Body Response: 1. A public comment period is a listening session, and the public body is there to listen. The public body, in fact, should not respond to matters raised at the meeting unless they are on the agenda for the same meeting. 2. Matters raised during public comment periods are not required to, and are unlikely to, be addressed or resolved by the public body at the same meeting. Such matters may be appropriately deferred to a noticed-agenda item at a future meeting due to Open Meeting Law considerations. 3. At the sole discretion of the chair of the public body, matters raised during public comment may or may not appear on a future agenda or be referred to the Town Administrator for appropriate action, if any. 4. A public body cannot demand that persons attending meetings or participating in public comment be civil to one another. Nevertheless, the Town, or the members of the public, and those that appear before them are encouraged to make any/or all residents of the Town feel welcome, including listening to them speak, and acknowledging that speakers may have a different viewpoints. Disclaimer: A Public Comment period is not a time for debate or response to comments by the public body. Comments made during the Public Comment period do not reflect the views or the positions of the public body. Because of constitutional free speech principles, the public body does not have the authority to prevent all speech that may be upsetting and/or offensive during the public portion of the meeting. H. Enforcement: Concerns about Public Comment Periods may be brought to the attention of the Town Manager, who will discuss the concerns with the chair of the public body, and take appropriate action. Failure to comply with this Policy may be deemed a violation of the Town’s Code of Conduct, and grounds for the removal of an appointed official. Because the subject layout is located on private property, the general public is prohibited from entering the site due to property owner liability, active site safety hazards, and trespassing regulations. The purpose of this field walk is to allow Planning Board members to observe the physical characteristics of the land. This includes evaluating topography, slopes, sight lines, proposed drainage basin locations, and vegetative buffers. These observations help the board understand the design plans submitted. In compliance with Massachusetts Open Meeting Law, the town maintains complete transparency throughout this administrative review process. Please note the following structural rules governing the visit: e No Deliberations: Board members will not debate the merits of the project, express personal opinions, or negotiate with the developer while on-site. e No Decisions or Votes: No formal actions, choices, or votes will be taken during the site visit. e No Official Public Testimony: No public comments or official statements will be heard or recorded during the field walk. While the public is not allowed on the private property boundaries, residents and interested parties may observe the board from the public right-of-way or abutting property with permissions to do so. At the next regularly scheduled public meeting (Tuesday, November 10, 2026, 7:05PM -Town Hall), the Planning Board will offer for the record, their observations made at the site visit.
