KOCH CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-139 ORDERED: October 19, 2026 The Quincy City Council hereby confirms the Mayor’s At-Large appointment of Timothy Baker of 54 Ocean Street to the Quincy Housing Authority Board. His appointment is for five years, effective February 2, 2026 thru the first Monday in February 2031. INTRODUCED BY: WARD FIVE COUNCILLOR – MAGGIE MCKEE CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-123 ORDERED: September 22, 2026 WHEREAS in 2024 the previous city council passed ordinances for 79% and 50% pay raises for the mayor and councillors – without debate or public input; and WHEREAS in 2025 the previous council passed an ordinance setting additional annual raises for the mayor and councillors based on the consumer price index, again without debate or public input; and WHEREAS in June 2026 the current council deleted all of those raise ordinances over concerns about the way they were enacted; BE IT ORDERED that the City Council begin rigorous discussions on politicians’ raises, with the goal of proposing and passing ordinances for fair, data-driven salaries for elected officials; and BE IT FURTHER ORDERED that this process include a public hearing on politicians’ pay so that community members can weigh in on both the amount and the process by which that pay is increased. INTRODUCED BY: WARD SIX COUNCILLOR – DEBORAH A. RILEY WARD FOUR COUNCILLOR – VIRGINIA M. RYAN COUNCILLOR AT LARGE – ZIQIANG SUSAN YUAN CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-140 ORDERED: October 19, 2026 DISCLOSURE OF THE CITY OF QUINCY CHRISTMAS FESTIVAL COMMITTEE, QUINCY FOUNDATION, QUINCY RELIEF FUND, QUINCY MAYOR’S CUP FINANCES AND OVERSIGHT REVIEW WHEREAS, The City of Quincy Christmas Festival Committee whose most recent reported place of business is One Merrymount Parkway, Quincy, MA, a city-owned municipal building; and WHEREAS, the organization’s federal tax ID is 04-3249190 and Massachusetts Attorney General account number is 034296; and WHEREAS, the organization was established in 1995 in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts filing with the Secretary of State as a 501c(4) entity under M.G.L. Chapter 180 Articles of Organization; and WHEREAS, the purpose of the organization, according to the most recent 2023 IRS filing, is stated: “The committee manages and promotes the City of Quincy Christmas Festival including the Christmas Parade, tree lighting ceremony, Santa’s arrival, as well as other ancillary activities within the city.”; and WHEREAS, during the FY 2027 budget reviews, specifically, on June 17, 2026 during the review of the Mayor’s budget and Celebrations line item, the Council had questioned the transfers to The Quincy Foundation in prior years; and WHEREAS, the revenue for the organization is received, in part, from the annual “Mayor’s Cup Golf Tournament”, as part of compensation to the City of Quincy, stated in the “2002 Amended and Restated Quarry Hills Lease”; and WHEREAS, prior to 2018, those funds were received into, and disbursed from, the City of Quincy Office of Municipal Finance; and ORDER NO. 2026 – 140 Page 2 of 3 WHEREAS, beginning in fiscal year 2018, the funds from the “Mayor’s Cup” golf tournament ceased to be deposited into the city’s general fund and instead were directed to The Quincy Foundation, aka The City of Quincy Christmas Festival Committee; and WHEREAS, in April, 2020, in response to the Covid-19 pandemic, the Mayor announced the Quincy Relief Fund would be used for the purpose of receiving donations from the public to aid local community members and stated that the donations were tax deductible as a recognized 501c(3) organization; and WHEREAS, it appears that the terms “Quincy Foundation”, “Mayor’s Cup”, “Quincy Relief Fund” and “City of Quincy Christmas Festival Committee” organizations have all been used interchangeably to refer to the same non-profit entity referenced above; and WHEREAS, city officials, including the City Solicitor and Mayor’s Chief of Staff, have stated that the entity is a private, non-profit, and therefore not accountable to the Quincy City Council or city taxpayers. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDERED, that the Quincy City Council hereby calls for the above-named organization(s) to provide a full accounting of the organization(s) finances including revenue, expenses, donors, and charitable versus non-charitable activities of the organization(s) within 30 calendar days of this date; and BE IT FURTHER ORDERED, that the board member(s) of the organization(s) appear before the City Council to answer questions relative to the work of the organization(s), the process for evaluating/approving expenditures from the fund, and the use of taxpayer funds by a private, non-profit entity; and BE IT FURTHER ORDERED, that this review includes federal tax returns including IRS form 990 Schedule B, Schedule of Contributors since 2017, annual Secretary of the Commonwealth filings, and annual Attorney General filings for the organization(s); and BE IT FURTHER ORDERED, that this review include publicly disclosable federal tax returns and schedules since 2017, annual Secretary of the Commonwealth filings, and annual Attorney General filings for the organization(s), subject to legally required redaction of protected contributor information; and BE IT FURTHER ORDERED, that the City Auditor, Treasurer, Finance Director, and all applicable City departments provide to the City Council, within thirty (30) calendar days, a year-by-year accounting of all municipal funds appropriated, transferred, paid, or otherwise directed to each of the named organizations, or to any related entity, from January 1, 2017 through the date of this Order. The accounting shall identify the date, amount, fiscal year, funding source, appropriation account, payee, stated purpose, approving official, and supporting vouchers, invoices, contracts, and payment records; and BE IT FURTHER ORDERED, that the City administration provide the 2002 Amended and Restated Quarry Hills Lease, relevant amendments and agreements, and a year-by-year reconciliation of amounts due and paid in connection with the Mayor’s Cup Golf Tournament or related lease obligations, identifying who received each payment and whether any amount was received by or deposited into the City treasury. For amounts paid directly to another entity, the City shall identify the agreement and asserted legal authority permitting that arrangement; and ORDER NO. 2026 – 140 Page 3 of 3 BE IT FURTHER ORDERED, that the City provide all records in its possession identifying each named organization’s exact legal name, federal employer identification number, tax-exempt classification, officers or directors where publicly available, and relationship to other named organizations or programs; and BE IT FURTHER ORDERED, that the City provide any grant or funding agreements, expenditure restrictions, required financial reports, reconciliations, receipts, and other available records demonstrating how public funds transferred to these entities were used for the purposes for which those funds were authorized; and BE IT FURTHER ORDERED, that the City Solicitor provide a written legal opinion identifying the authority for the City’s payments or transfers, the applicable requirements governing municipal receipts under Massachusetts law, the reporting obligations applicable to recipients of municipal funds, and the City Council’s authority and available procedures for obtaining additional records or testimony from private organizations; and BE IT FURTHER ORDERED, that each responding City department provide, within thirty (30) calendar days, the records then available and a written list of records not produced, stating whether they do not exist, cannot be located, are held by another custodian, or are withheld under an identified legal basis; and that the Council schedule a public follow-up review of the materials provided. RYAN CITY OF QUINCY IN COUNCIL ORDER NO. 2026-142 ORDERED: October 19, 2026 An Ordinance Regulating Intrusive Surveillance Technology Section 1. Purpose The purpose of this ordinance is to protect the privacy, civil liberties, and constitutional rights of Quincy residents while allowing the City to use ordinary cameras for legitimate traffic management, public safety, and property security. Intrusive surveillance technology can collect, analyze, retain, and share sensitive information about individuals. It can track people’s movement, reveal their associations, and create records that may be accessed or shared beyond the City’s knowledge or control. Its use must be transparent, limited, and subject to meaningful public oversight. Section 2. Definitions and Exemptions A. Surveillance Technology. “Surveillance Technology” means electronic equipment, software, or systems used by the City that can identify, track, monitor, or analyze individuals, vehicles, or their activities in ways that materially affect privacy or civil liberties. Covered technology includes, but is not limited to: 1. Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) and systems that collect or analyze vehicle-location data; 2. Facial recognition and other biometric identification systems; 3. Technologies used to track individuals’ locations, movements, or associations over time; 4. Audio surveillance and gunshot detection systems that collect or analyze information beyond ordinary emergency reporting; 5. Software that combines data from multiple sources to identify, profile, predict, or monitor individuals; and 6. Other technologies with comparable surveillance capabilities. ORDER NO. 2026 – 142 Page 2 of 3 B. Exemptions. This ordinance does not apply to: 1. Ordinary traffic cameras used solely to monitor traffic flow or record traffic violations as authorized by law; 2. CCTV cameras used solely for basic security at City-owned or controlled buildings, public facilities, or infrastructure; or 3. Other ordinary cameras that do not have the surveillance capabilities described in subsection These exemptions do not apply if a camera or system is equipped with or used for facial recognition, automated license plate recognition, individual tracking, biometric identification, or other covered surveillance capabilities. C. Material Expansion. Adding covered surveillance capabilities to an existing camera or system, or materially expanding its data collection, retention, analysis, or sharing, constitutes a new use subject to this ordinance. Section 3. Prior Approval and Public Hearing Before the City acquires, enters into an agreement for, or begins using any covered Surveillance Technology, the City must: 1. Submit the proposed use to the City Council; 2. Provide the impact report and proposed use policy required by Section 4; 3. Make these documents available to the public at least 30 days before the public hearing; and 4. Obtain City Council approval following a public hearing. The same requirements apply before materially expanding an existing system’s surveillance capabilities or permitted uses. These requirements apply regardless of whether the technology is obtained through a vendor, contractor, grant, pilot program, or agreement with another government agency. Section 4. Impact Report and Use Policy Before approval, the responsible department must provide a plain-language report explaining: 1. Why the technology is needed and how it will be used; 2. What information it collects, analyzes, and retains; 3. Who can access the information and with whom it may be shared; 4. How long the information is retained and when it is deleted; 5. How the vendor can access or use the information; 6. The technology’s limitations, risks, and potential for errors or misuse; 7. The safeguards and audit procedures that will protect the information; and 8. The estimated costs and available alternatives. The department must also submit a proposed use policy specifying permitted purposes, access restrictions, data retention and deletion, and information-sharing limits. ORDER NO. 2026 – 142 Page 3 of 3 Section 5. Data Protection and Vendor Accountability The City and its vendors may collect, access, use, retain, and share information only as authorized by law and the City Council-approved use policy. The City must maintain appropriate access controls and audit records. Vendors may not independently use, sell, disclose, or retain City data for their own purposes, except as authorized by law and the approved agreement. Any material change to a vendor’s technology or data practices that expands surveillance capabilities or materially increases privacy risks must be reviewed under Section 3 before implementation. Section 6. Emergencies and Annual Reporting A. Emergencies. A department may use covered technology without prior approval only when reasonably necessary to respond to an imminent threat to life or serious bodily harm, and only as permitted by law. The department must notify the City Council and provide a written explanation as soon as practicable. Emergency use may not become routine use without approval under Section 3. B. Annual Reporting. Each department using approved Surveillance Technology must submit an annual public report to the City Council describing how the technology was used, the categories of information collected and shared, compliance with retention rules, and any known misuse or significant errors. Reports must protect information that is lawfully confidential. Section 7. Severability and Effective Date If any provision of this ordinance is held invalid, the remaining provisions shall remain in effect. This ordinance shall take effect as provided by applicable law. text: CITY OF SALEM OCTOBER 19, 2026 JOINT PUBLIC HEARING OF THE CITY COUNCIL AND THE PLANNING BOARD AMENDED Due To Correction From Ten (20) Feet To Twenty (20) Feet The Salem City Council will hold a Joint Public Meeting with the Planning Board in-person in the City Council Chambers, City Hall, 93 Washington Street, 2ndfloor, Salem, MA on Monday, October 19, 2026 at 6:00 PM. in accordance with Chapter 40A, Section 5, of the Massachusetts General Laws for the purpose of discussing Ordinance relative to Zoning - Roof-Mounted wind Energy Systems Ordinance. Depends on size and quantity of zoning ordinance if in full or summarized Below are summaries of each zoning ordinance amendments. SUMMARY Ordinance relative to Zoning - Roof-Mounted wind Energy Systems Ordinance Section 1. Section 3.1 Table of Principal and Accessory is hereby amended by inserting a new use in section E. ACCESSORY USES as follows: Use RC R1 R2 R3 B1 B2 B4 B5 BPD I NRCC Wind Energy System, Y Y Y Y Y Y Y Y Y Y Y Roof-Mounted Section 2. Section 4.1.2 Notes to Table of Dimensional Requirements is hereby amended by inserting the line “and roof-mounted wind energy systems” after “medium-scale ground mounted solar energy systems” in subsection 8 and by inserting a new subsection 10: CITY OF SALEM OCTOBER 19, 2026 JOINT PUBLIC HEARING OF THE CITY COUNCIL AND THE PLANNING BOARD “The limitations on height of buildings shall apply to roof-mounted wind energy systems with an additional allowance of 5 feet over the maximum height of the building.” Section 3. Section 10.0, "Definitions," is hereby amended by inserting the following definitions in alphabetical order: Wind Energy: Energy received from the conversion of wind to electricity. Wind Energy System: A device or structural design feature, a substantial purpose of which is to provide for the collection, storage, and distribution of wind energy for lighting, space heating or cooling, electricity generation, or water heating. Wind Energy System Rated Nameplate Capacity: The maximum rated output of electric power production equipment for a Wind Energy System. Wind Energy System Height: The height of the Wind Energy System is measured from the base of the system to the tip of the blade at its highest point. Wind Energy System, Roof-Mounted: An Active Wind Energy System that is structurally mounted to the roof of a building or structure; shall be considered those with a rated nameplate capacity less than or equal to 10 kilowatts per turbine, and a height up to twenty (20) feet. Section 4. Section 6.9.1, is hereby amended by adding the phrase “Wind Energy System, Roof-Mounted, as defined in Section 10.0, are not considered wind energy facilities as defined in this section (Section 6.9).” at the end of the section, so that it shall read as follows: 6.9.1 Purpose. The purpose of this section is to accommodate wind energy facilities in appropriate locations, while minimizing any adverse visual, safety, and environmental impacts of the facilities. Wind Energy Systems, RoofMounted, as defined in Section 10.0, are not considered wind energy facilities as defined in this section (Section 6.9). This ordinance shall take effect as provided by city charter. Data Center: A facility or campus consisting of one or more buildings primarily used for housing, operating, and co-locating networked computer systems, servers, data storage systems, and telecommunications equipment. The primary land-use intent of the facility is the remote processing, continuous management, physical storage, and global dissemination of digital data, information, or high-performance artificial intelligence model training and machine learning computation. This definition explicitly applies to hyperscale data centers, enterprise data centers, co-location facilities, edge data centers, server farms, modular or containerized data systems, and cryptocurrency or blockchain mining operations (only where such activity constitutes the principal use of the premises.) This definition excludes standard, localized IT rooms, server closets, or computer infrastructure that is secondary, subordinate, and customarily incidental to an otherwise permitted use on the property (e.g., standard server rooms supporting an individual office building, medical complex, school, or retail store) Amendments to the Town of Southbridge Zoning Bylaw Section 8, Special Regulations by adding a new section 8.11 Temporary Moratorium for Data Centers. First Reading: September 21, 2026 Second Reading: October 5, 2026 Third Reading: October 19, 2026 Section 8, Special Regulations, is hereby amended by adding the following new section 8.11: 8.11 TEMPORARY MORATORIUM FOR DATA CENTERS 8.11.1 Moratorium. There shall be a 365-day moratorium on the permitting, construction, expansion, conversion, establishment, or operation of any Data Center in the Town. This moratorium shall begin on the first day following the Town Council’s adoption of this zoning by-law. 8.11.2 No applications. During the moratorium, no application, permit, special permit, site plan, variance, building permit, zoning permit, or other land use approval shall be accepted, processed, or approved for a Data Center. 8.11.3 Pending applications. Any pending application for a Data Center shall be stayed during the moratorium. 8.11.4 Purpose, The Town Council hereby finds that the rapid development, expansion, and high-density operational characteristics of Data Centers and Data Center Campuses present unique, unprecedented, and accelerating demands on municipal infrastructure, public utilities, and the local environment. As such, the purpose of this temporary moratorium is to establish a reasonable, defined, and limited period during which the Town can pause the review and approval of new Data Center applications. This pause is vital to enable the Town Planning Board, Conservation Commission, and local utility authorities to: (a) Conduct independent studies on the cumulative impacts of data center resource consumption on the local aquifer, municipal water networks, and electrical grid capacity; (b) Develop comprehensive performance standards regarding multi-frequency sound emissions, low-frequency hum mitigation, visual screening, and architectural integration; (c) Review and update the Town Master Plan to ensure that future data center sitings are confined to appropriate zoning overlays that protect residential neighborhoods and natural resources; and (d) Formulate specific ratepayer and environmental protections to ensure that any future data center developments do not impose unfair fiscal burdens or resource degradation upon the residents and businesses of the Town. Town Council Agenda Page 3 of 5 24. 8.11.5 Extension. The moratorium may be extended twice for up to 180 days each by the Town Council if it determines that additional time is necessary to complete studies, develop performance standards, review and update the Town Master Plan, or adopt appropriate regulations and zoning by-laws to ensure the protection of residents, businesses, natural resources and the environment. The moratorium may be extended by the Town Council if presented with evidence-based justification from the Board of Health, Planning Board, Conservation Conmnittee-Commission*, Water Department, or utility authorities. (*Amended First Reading) 8.11.6 Severability. If any section, subsection, paragraph, sentence, clause, phrase, or provision of this Temporary Moratorium By-Law is for any reason held to be unconstitutional, unlawful, invalid, or unenforceable by a court of competent jurisdiction, such decision shall be confined strictly to the specific provision directly involved in the controversy and the remaining portions of this By-Law shall continue in full force and effect. To the Constables of the Town of SWANSEA GREETINGS: In the name of the Commonwealth, you are hereby required to notify and warn the inhabitants of said town who are qualified to vote in Elections to vote at: PRECINTS ONE, TWO, THREE, FOUR & FIVE JOSEPH CASE HIGH SCHOOL 70 SCHOOL STREET SWANSEA, MA 02777 On TUESDAY, THE THIRD DAY OF NOVEMBER, 2026, from 7:00 A.M. to 8:00 P.M. for the following purpose: To cast their votes in the State Election for the candidates for the following offices and questions: SENATOR IN CONGRESS For this Commonwealth GOVERNOR and LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR For this Commonwealth ATTORNEY GENERAL For this Commonwealth SECRETARY OF STATE For this Commonwealth TREASURER For this Commonwealth AUDITOR For this Commonwealth REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS FOURTH DISTRICT COUNCILLOR FIRST DISTRICT SENATOR IN GENERAL COURT FIRST BRISTOL & PLYMOUTH DISTRICT REPRESENTATIVE IN GENERAL COURT FOURTH & FIFTH BRISTOL DISTRICT DISTRICT ATTORNEY BRISTOL DISTRICT REGISTER OF PROBATE BRISTOL COUNTY COUNTY TREASURER BRISTOL COUNTY COUNTY COMMISSIONER BRISTOL COUNTY QUESTION 1: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. This proposed law would exempt documents related to the development of public policy and communications between legislators and their constituents, if those communications are reasonably related to a constituent’s request for assistance in obtaining government-provided benefits or services or interacting with a government agency. A YES VOTE would make most records held by the Legislature and the Office of the Governor public records under the Massachusetts Public Records Law. A NO VOTE would make no change to the Massachusetts Public Records Law. QUESTION 2: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would specify that employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services (“CPCS”) are permitted to engage in collective bargaining with their employer. It would also require CPCS, after executing a collective bargaining agreement, to request the appropriation necessary to fund such agreement from the Governor. . A YES VOTE would specify that Committee for Public Counsel Services employees may form a union to collectively bargain with their employer. A NO VOTE would make no change to the law governing labor relations for Committee for Public Counsel Service employees. QUESTION 3: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would eliminate political party primaries for state elections and instead establish a system where there would be a single, all-party primary in which all candidates, regardless of their party affiliation, would be listed on one ballot, and voters could vote for any candidate on the ballot. The two candidates receiving the most votes in the primary would advance to the general election ballot. This proposed law would require candidates for governor and lieutenant governor to run and be listed jointly on the ballot in the primary. This proposed law would provide political party status to any group whose candidates for any statewide office received at least 3% of the ballots cast in the state primary. A YES VOTE would eliminate separate party primaries for state elections and require a single primary in which all candidates appear on one ballot, voters could vote for any candidate, and the top two candidates would advance to the general election. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing primary elections. QUESTION 4; LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would permit eligible individuals to register to vote or update their voter registration address on Election Day. An individual who is eligible to vote could register to vote on Election Day by going to the polling place in the precinct where they live during voting hours and presenting proof of residency and signing a written oath. Proof of residency could be a valid photo identification, or documentation showing the individual’s name and the address where the individual resides, such as a current utility bill, bank statement, government check, residential lease, wireless telephone statement, paycheck, current student fee statement or other document from a post-secondary school, or another government document or correspondence. The written oath would require the individual to certify that they are a citizen of the United States, are at least 18 years old, are not legally prohibited from voting, and have not and will not vote in the same election 2 at another location. The oath would require the individual to acknowledge that providing false information is a felony punishable by not more than 5 years imprisonment or a fine of not more than $10,000, or both. If an individual did not present proof of residency, they would be allowed to cast a provisional ballot, which would be counted only if the individual returned to provide the required information before the close of polls for a municipal election; within two days after a state primary; or within six days after a state election. Individuals who register to vote on Election Day would be registered to vote in future elections as well as in the election taking place that day. Individuals who are already registered to vote would not be able to change their political party affiliation on Election Day. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028. A YES VOTE would permit eligible citizens to register to vote or to update their voter registration address at their polling place on Election Day. A NO VOTE would make no change to the laws governing voter registration. QUESTION 5: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would change the limit on how much revenue the state can collect in a given year. The proposal would limit state revenue in a given year to the net amount of state revenue from the year before, increased by a rate equal to the average growth of wages and salaries in Massachusetts over the most recent three years. If revenue collected by the state in a given year exceeds the limit, the excess amount would be refunded to taxpayers the following year. The proposed law would include all revenue from the surtax on incomes over $1 million when calculating the revenue limit and when determining whether state revenue exceeds the limit. The provisions of the proposed law would all be effective as of July 1, 2027. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect. A YES VOTE would change the limit on state revenue collection, tying it to prior year collections plus average wage and salary growth, and provide for a rebate of revenue exceeding that limit. A NO VOTE would make no change in the law relative to state revenue collection. QUESTION 6: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would establish a Nature for All Fund that, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, would receive 50% of state taxes collected from the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses for the first year of its operation. After July 1, 2028, the Nature for All Fund would begin receiving, subject to appropriation by the Legislature, 100% of state taxes collected on the sale and use of sporting goods, recreational vehicles, and golf courses. The sales tax revenue received by the Nature for All Fund would exclude sales tax revenue transferred to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority State and Local Contribution Fund and the School Modernization and Reconstruction Trust Fund. The proposed law would allow the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to spend the money in the Nature for All Fund for natural resource conservation. 3 The proposed law would allow public and private donations to the Nature for All Fund. The proposed law would prevent the state comptroller from transferring surplus funds in the Nature for All Fund at the end of the fiscal year. It would also allow state agencies, municipalities, public charities involved in natural resource conservation, tribal governments, and other regional public entities to receive money from the Nature for All Fund. Natural resource conservation would include the conservation or restoration of land to protect drinking water, streams, rivers, lakes, coasts, farms, forests, connectivity between open spaces, and lands and natural resources of indigenous cultural significance. Natural resource conservation would also include the creation, improvement, and management of parks, trails, greenspaces or outdoor recreation access. The proposed law would establish a 15-member Nature for All Board that consists of five state officials and ten members of the public appointed by the Governor. The proposed law would require the ten members of the public to include representatives of underserved communities and indigenous peoples and at least one person with expertise or experience in natural resource conservation. The proposed law would allow the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to spend money from the Nature for All Fund to hire staff to manage the fund. The proposed law would also require the Nature for All Board to establish rules about how the money in the Nature for All Fund should be spent, including rules regarding alignment with environmental justice principles, access to and restoration of lands and natural resources of indigenous cultural significance, promotion of affordable housing development, and other matters regarding spending and bond issuance. The proposed law would require the state Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs to submit an annual report to various state committees regarding the funds spent to buy or improve land in cities and towns containing environmental justice populations. The proposed law would take effect on July 1, 2027. A YES VOTE would create a fund that could be utilized for natural resource conservation that would receive some state taxes collected on the sale and use of sporting goods and recreational vehicles, and the use of golf courses. ANO VOTE would not create this natural resource conservation fund or change how sales and use taxes are spent. QUESTION 7: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY This proposed law would allow single-family homes to be built in a residentially zoned area as long as the land on which it is to be constructed is at least 5,000 square feet, has at least 50 feet of land bordering the street, road, or public way that it faces, and has access to public sewer and water services. The proposed law would allow cities and towns to reasonably regulate certain aspects of those single-family homes, including their height, distance from neighboring buildings, open space, parking requirements, and whether they can be rented out on a short-term basis. The proposed law would also allow the Executive Office of Housing aid Livable Communities to issue guidance or regulations to administer the proposed law. A YES VOTE would allow single-family homes to be built on lots of 5,000 square feet or more in residential areas, subject to reasonable local regulation of certain, aspects of those homes., A NO VOTE would make no change to the law relative to building single-family homes. QUESTION 8: LAW PROPOSED BY INITIATIVE PETITION Do you approve of a law summarized below, on which no vote was taken by the Senate or the House of Representatives before May 6, 2026? SUMMARY The proposed law would change the type and amount of marijuana that may legally be possessed in Massachusetts by repealing the laws that legalize, regulate, and tax the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana in Massachusetts. The proposed law would also permit persons 21 years of age and older to possess 1 ounce or less of marijuana including no more than 5 grams in the form of concentrate, and to gift or transfer to another person 21 years of age and older 1 ounce or less of marijuana including no more than 5 grams in the form of concentrate. The proposed law would also impose a civil penalty of $100 and forfeiture of the marijuana for the possession of marijuana between the weight of 1 and 2 ounces. For persons 21 years of age and younger, the proposed law would make the possession of 2 ounces or less of marijuana a civil infraction subject to a $100 fine, forfeiture of the marijuana, completion of a drug awareness program and community service, and notification to their parents or legal guardian of the offense and penalties. The proposed law would allow currently licensed adult recreational marijuana businesses to apply on an expedited basis to become a licensed medical marijuana dispensary and to sell their remaining inventory of adult recreational marijuana to medical marijuana dispensaries. The proposed law would retain the Cannabis Control Commission but modify its authority so it would regulate only the medical marijuana market. The proposed law states that, if any of its parts were declared invalid, the other parts would stay in effect. The proposed law would take effect on January 1, 2028. A YES VOTE would prohibit the legalization, regulation, and taxation of the retail sale of adult recreational use marijuana, and change the penalties for possession of marijuana. A NO VOTE would make no change to the law relative to marijuana. QUESTION 9: REFERENDUM ON AN EXISTING LAW Do you approve of a law summarized below, which was approved by the House of Representatives on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 124 to 33, and approved by the Senate on July 18, 2024 by a vote of 35 to 5? SUMMARY This law makes a number of changes to Massachusetts laws governing firearms. The law adds school administrators and licensed healthcare providers as parties permitted to ask a court to issue an Extreme Risk Protection Order — requiring an individual to surrender or relinquish their firearm licenses, permits, and firearms - if an individual is a present danger to self or others. The law also provides that, when issuing an Harassment Prevention Order, a court may also order the surrender of firearms licenses, permits, and firearms. The law imposes penalties for possessing, creating, and transferring untraceable “ghost gun” firearms and requires all firearms except antiques and relics, including unfinished frames and receivers that can be readily made into a finished product, to have serial numbers. The law includes privately-made guns like 3D-printed guns within the provisions governing untraceable “ghost gun” firearms. The law changes firearms licensing requirements to: (1) allow local licensing authorities to request prior license and permit information from the state, as well as access petitions for involuntary mental health commitments denied by a court in addition to prior involuntary commitments, as a part of their review of applications for licenses to carry firearms, firearm ID cards, and licenses to sell firearms; (2) require an individual to be 21 years of age to own semiautomatic rifles or shotguns; (3) add the possibility of incarceration of up to six months for a second offense of failing to report a firearm loss or theft; and (4) enable 12-15 year olds to apply for a self-defense spray permit with parental permission, and 15 to 18 year olds to apply independently.

text: Whately Conservation Commission To: Town Hall 4 Sandy Lane Whately, MA 01037 From: Date: Berkshire Design Group September 29, 2026 Project: Re: 299 River Rd, Whately, MA Chang Farm Solar Array Notice of Intent To Whom This May Concern, Enclosed are the following materials included in the Notice of Intent application for a proposed large-scale, ground-mounted, elevated, dual-use solar energy system at 299 River Road, Whately, MA on parcel # 33-0-09. Included in this application are the following materials: 1. DEP Form 3 2. Notice of Intent Project Narrative 3. USGS Locus Map 4. 100-foot Abutters List Report 5. Wetland Delineation Report Thank you, Doug Serrill, R.L.A. Berkshire Design Group 4 Allen Place • Northampton, Massachusetts 01060 • t 413.582.7000 • f 413.582.7005 • Berkshire Design Group September 29, 2026 Whately Conservation Commission Whately Town Offices 4 Sandy Lane Whately, MA 01373 RE: 299 River Road - Chang Farm Solar Array Notice of Intent Dear Members of the Whately Conservation Commission, On behalf of Hyperion Solar Systems and Chang Farm, we respectfully submit the enclosed Notice of Intent application for a proposed 400.00 kW ac (590.40 kW dc) large-scale, ground-mounted, elevated, dual-use solar array located at 299 River Road. Existing Conditions Chang Farm spans several parcels, including specifically parcel #33-0-09, located at 299 River Road, which contains approximately 47.01 acres. The parcel is located within the Agricultural Residential district; the portion of the site that borders River Road is zoned as A/R1, while the land west of the A/R1 district is zoned as A/R2. The parcel is bound by River Road to the east, and agricultural residential parcels to the north, south, and west. The parcel contains a mix of agricultural buildings on the eastern side near River Road, land in agricultural use on the eastern side, and forested lands on the western side. The parcel contains several regulated resource areas including, Bordering Vegetated Wetlands (BVW) associated with a drainage ditch along the southern edge of the parcel, Riverfront Area from Sugarloaf Brook located in the adjacent parcel to the east, and Bordering Land Subject to Flooding identified in the recently updated FEMA Preliminary Flood Hazard Data. Proposed Conditions The project, as it is currently designed, proposes to install a 400.00kW ac (590.40kW dc) large-scale, groundmounted, elevated, dual-use solar array within an overall area of 2.14-acres, within land in agricultural use. The proposed array includes 960 panels configured in 10 rows, spaced 27’ on-center, with a north-south orientation with the southernmost rack post located approximately 42.5’ from the BVW located along the southern edge of the farm field. The panels are mounted to a single axis tracker (SAT) racking system that enables the panels to rotate in an east-west orientation throughout the day. When horizontal, the panels are 10’ above the surface. The elevated panel height and wider row width allows typical agricultural field operations to function without interruption and with a negligible loss of space in the field. The racking system is mounted onto I-beam posts that are pile-driven into the ground to provide a very secure foundation without the need for large concrete footings. The I-beam posts contain a very small footprint of approximately 10 square inches (0.07 S.F.) Four (4) inverters mounted on fence posts are proposed within a 6’ tall chainlink fence with locked gate northeast of the array. Electrical conduit will be trenched underground and run to the southwest corner of the new barn building expansion currently under construction. Wiring will run within the building to an area of electrical equipment in the southeast corner of the building and then finally will run to a utility service transformer that has already been installed as part of the barn building expansion project. The solar array installation is proposed within land in agricultural use. No site grading is proposed, and no soil disturbance is proposed beyond the levels of soil disturbance that occur from regular agricultural activities. 4 Allen Place, Northampton, MA 01060 (413) 582-7000 bdg@berkshiredesign.com September 29, 2026 299 River Road - Chang Farm Solar Array Notice of Intent Page 2 of 3 However, filter sock erosion control barriers are proposed along the southern side of the project outside of the 25’ wetland buffer during the period of construction to provide appropriate preventative measures. Resource Areas 310 CMR §10.55 Bordering Vegetated Wetlands The proposed array is located within the 100’ wetland buffer with the closest post located approximately 42.5’ from the edge of the BVW. A total of 20 I-beam posts, containing a total area of approximately 1.4 S.F., are proposed within the 100’ wetland buffer. 310 CMR §10.57 Bordering Land Subject to Flooding The majority of the proposed array falls within the 100-year floodplain identified in the 2025 FEMA preliminary flood hazard data. The preliminary 100-year floodplain has no base flood elevation (BFE) associated with it. However, the nearest BFE identified on Sugarloaf Brook north of the site is 146.00’. A total of 187 racking posts are proposed within the preliminary 100-year floodplain. The cumulative impact to flood storage below 146’ in elevation from the racking posts is approximately 17 cubic feet. As shown in the chart below, the array posts within the flood plain have a negligible impact on the overall flood storage. No work is proposed within the 200’ Riverfront Area. Stormwater Management MassDEP has issued Wetlands Program Policy 17-1 (https://www.mass.gov/info-details/massdep-wetlandsprogram-policy-17-1-photovoltaic-system-solar-array-review) to provide guidance on the application of the Wetlands Protection Act Regulations to ground-mounted solar array projects. Under Standard of Review #4, DEP provides recommendations for measures to control peak runoff, provide recharge, and treat TSS. The proposed project incorporates all measures identified in the policy: • Slopes less than 33.5%: The site is flat with slopes generally less than 2%. • Erosion Control Plan: Erosion controls are proposed during construction. The flat agricultural field is low risk for significant levels of erosion and continuous perimeter controls are proposed between the work 4 Allen Place, Northampton, MA 01060 (413) 582-7000 bdg@berkshiredesign.com September 29, 2026 299 River Road - Chang Farm Solar Array Notice of Intent Page 3 of 3 and the adjacent resource areas. • Phased/selective land disturbance: Large-scale land disturbance is not proposed, no tree clearing is required. Foundations will be installed from track-mounted equipment that creates similar level of disturbance to farm equipment and outside of trenching of electrical conduit, all existing vegetation will remain. • Post-construction measures: The proposed site will continue to operate as agricultural field meeting the strict requirement of DOER/MDAR to operate as a dual-use agrivoltaic project. Groundcover is unchanged from the existing agricultural fields and stormwater BMPs are not necessary to control runoff. • Topsoil preservation: No topsoil will be removed from the site, and soils will be de-compacted in accordance with DOER/MDAR requirements. • Panel spacing to allow vegetation: Panels are spaced to allow sufficient sunlight for continued agricultural production. • Panel orientation relative to slope: The site is flat and this measure is not applicable. • Drip edge high 10 feet or less: Panels will be installed at a 10-foot height when horizontal to meet DOER/MDAR requirements. Drip edge of tilt panels will always be at 10-foot height or lower. • No conveyances or outfalls are constructed: None proposed. • No work impacting habitat: The listed areas are not present at the site. The project proposes to use existing farm access roads. No new impervious or compacted gravel surfacing is proposed. The existing agricultural field will remain in production, and groundcover is unchanged from the existing condition. Based on these factors, and the MassDEP policy guidance, the proposed project is in compliance with the Massachusetts Stormwater Standards and additional stormwater BMPs are not necessary. We find that the proposed project complies with the requirements of the state’s wetland regulations and stormwater standards as outlined above and look forward to discussing this project with the Whately Conservation Commission at the next available hearing. Abutters List Report - Whately, MA Page 1 of 1 Wendell Wetland Services 105 Montague Road Wendell, MA 01379 (978) 544-5607 ward.ves@gmail.com March 19, 2026 Mr. Jake Marley Hyperion Systems, LLC Via electronic mail Re: Wetland delineation for a potential solar project, 299 River Road, Whately Dear Mr. Marley: As requested, Wendell Wetland Services (WWS) visited the above referenced property today in order to identify and delineate the outer boundary all wetlands in the project area that are protectable under the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act (M.G.L. chapter 131, section 40) and Regulations (310 CMR 10.00). All wetlands in this area have been marked in the field with consecutively numbered pink “wetland delineation” flagging tape and stake-flags. While the wetland boundary has been accurately identified, only the Whately Conservation Commission, or the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) on appeal, can make the final determination of the extent of the wetland resource areas. Delineation Methodology The general methodology employed in evaluating the site for wetlands utilized both vegetation and hydrology as outlined in the Regulations at 310 CMR 10.55 and in the DEP handbook Massachusetts Handbook for the Delineation of Bordering Vegetated Wetlands, Second Edition (2022). Hydrophytic Vegetation was based upon the US Fish and Wildlife Service’s National List of Plant Species that Occur in Wetlands (2020), as well as all plant species listed in the Act. Wetland hydrology includes a high water table, waterstained leaves, and hydric soils. Hydric soils were determined based upon the interagency document Field Indicators for Identifying Hydric Soils in New England, Version 5 (2025). On this site, much of the wetland boundary was delineated using the criteria for disturbed sites at 310 CMR 10.55 (2)(c-3) given that the project area is an agricultural field. Although wetland indicators plants were used to aid in the delineation where available, the existence of hydric soils and/or the existence of saturated soils was primarily used to determine the wetland boundary. Site Description The site is located to the west of River Road, and to the south of an old tobacco barn. Access to the project would be via an existing agricultural road between the farm buildings fronting River Road. To the south of the field, there is an intermittent stream that flows from west to east within a deep channel that has been excavated by agricultural activities over the years. There are small fringe wetland areas along this channel that are vegetated by red maple (Acer rubrum), silky dogwood (Swida amomum), sensitive fern (Onoclea sensibilis), jewel weed (Imaptiens spp.), and skunk cabbage (Symplocarpus foetidus). The wetland boundary extends into the agricultural field. There is a manmade channel connecting the wet portion of the filed with the intermittent stream. The delineated field contained areas of shallow standing water at the time of my site visit. Most of the project site is mapped by the Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) as the non-hydric Winooski silt loams, while the hydric Limerick silt loams are shown as intruding into the southwestern part of the field. Our soils investigation is in general agreement, although the actual hydric/non-hydric soil boundary is somewhat different than mapped. Wetland Resource Areas Under the state Regulations (310 CMR 10.00), wetlands are broken up into different “resource areas,” each of which is regulated in a slightly different manner. The delineated wetlands contain the following resource areas, to which there is a 100 foot buffer zone: * Bank (10.54) – the banks of the intermittent stream; * Bordering Vegetated Wetland (10.55); * Land Under a Waterway (10.56) – the intermittent stream. The stream is not shown on the most recent USGS quadrangle. Therefore, as required by the Regulations, the USGS Streamstats Program was run. According to Streamstats, the watershed for this stream at the eastern edge of the site is only 0.05 square miles. This is well below the 0.5 square mile threshold that is required for a potentially perennial stream. Therefore, there should not be any “Riverfront Area” (10.58) on the site. Project Planning I have attached a sketch of the approximate location of my wetland flags. These flags should be surveyed and plotted onto the Site Plan, along with all work. It is my understanding that you would like to construct a large-scale solar array on the Lot. Any work within 100 feet of the wetlands will require a filing with the Conservation Commission. Limited work in the buffer zone may be approved by the Commission through the filing of a Request for Determination of Applicability (WPA form 1). More extensive buffer zone work, or any work that will “alter” wetlands, will require the filing of a Notice of Intent (WPA form 3). In addition, a 35 foot setback from wetlands has generally been required for projects in Whately when they are located in 2 agricultural fields such as this. The site does not fall within the Estimated Habitats of Rare Wildlife or Priority Habitats of Rare Species according to the most recent online mapping. Therefore, unless new information becomes available, you should not have to make any filing with the Natural Heritage and Endangered Species Program. Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions regarding the delineation. Sincerely, Wendell Wetland Services Ward W. Smith, SPWS Senior Professional Wetland Scientist 3

Existing Conditions Currently, the site consists of an equipment building, weather station, telescope structure, carport storage canopy, shed, and associated gravel driveway. Parking for these facilities is separated from the site to the south of the project. There are no proposed changes to the existing parking area and therefore it is not included in the proposed project site. East of the project site is Bording Vegetated Wetlands associated with Jimmy Nolan Brook. The 100-foot buffer associated with the BVW extends into the east side of the project site. Wetland flagging was completed by Wendell Wetland Services on September 08, 2026. The associated report provided by Wendell Wetland Services notes the Brook as an intermittent stream, not considered Riverfront Area under 310 CMR 10.00. Proposed Conditions The proposed work includes improvements to the existing equipment building, construction of a new garage addition, and removal of the telescope structure and storage canopy. To accommodate these changes, the existing gravel driveway will be replaced in kind with an adjusted footprint. The existing weather station and shed will remain as it is. The proposed work does not include any new utility connections. Sanitary and water services are not needed for the proposed use, and the existing electric service will be maintained. The limit of work was minimized as much as feasible to keep the proposed work farther from the wetland than the existing conditions. All work will be outside of the 50’ wetland buffer. Standard erosion and sediment control measures will be in place during construction to minimize construction impacts on the wetland and other surrounding areas. Disturbed areas will be stabilized with a native seed mix. Resource Areas 310 CMR §10.55 Bordering Vegetated Wetlands As noted above, there is an existing Bordering Vegetated Wetland east of the project site. All the proposed work is outside of the 50-foot wetland buffer. Work proposed within the 100-foot buffer includes improvements to the existing equipment building, removal of the telescope building and carport, and replacement of the gravel driveway with an adjusted footprint. text: Town of Yarmouth Per M.G.L.: All town and school boards, committees, commissions, and authorities shall post a notice of every meeting at least 48 hours prior to such meeting, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays. Zoning Bylaw Amendments and General Bylaw: Review input from Town Counsel and consider minor amendments on the following Draft Zoning Articles and General Bylaw related to Short-Term Rentals, and Draft Zoning Article for Accessory Dwelling Units: a. Short Term Rental Articles: i) Article 5 - General Bylaw Chapter 110 – Short Term Rentals (1): New General Bylaw to regulate Short-Term Rentals, which would ultimately replace the regulatory provisions currently within Zoning Bylaw Section 418. ii) Article 6 - Short Term Rentals (2) – Zoning Amendment: Continue the STR Use in the Zoning Bylaw and extend the sunset clause to the effective date of the General Bylaw. This Article would be withdrawn if the General Bylaw does not pass. iii) Article 7 - Short Term Rentals (3) – Zoning Amendment: Extend Sunset Clause in Section 418 – Short-Term Rentals. This Article would be withdrawn if the other STR Articles pass. b. Article 8 - Accessory Dwelling Units: Amendments to the Accessory Apartment Zoning Bylaw to match the mandated changes from The Affordable Homes Act (Section 8 of Chapter 150 of the Acts of 2024) and regulations 760 CMR 71.00: Protected Use Accessory Dwelling Units, while maintaining as many existing provisions as allowed by the state regulations. c. October 27, 2026 – Meet with Select Board – Execution of Special Town Meeting Warrant b. November 4, 2026 c. November 16, 2026 – Special Town Meeting d. November 18, 2026 12. Posted By (Name): Signature: Kathleen D. Williams Kathy Williams ARTICLE #5: General Bylaw Chapter 110 – Short-Term Rentals (1): To see if the Town will vote to add to the Town of Yarmouth General Bylaws Chapter 110 – Short Term Rentals, or take any other action relative thereto, as follows: Chapter 110 SHORT-TERM RENTALS § 110-1. Purpose. To provide for the orderly operation of short-term rentals for residential properties that balance private, neighborhood and public interests, and will: 1. Protect and maintain the residential character of existing neighborhoods. 2. Protect public health and safety. 3. Protect and preserve year-round housing stock. 4. Inhibit the commercialization of housing for use as Short Term Rentals. 5. Enable residents to better afford to live in Yarmouth, maintain their properties and contribute to the community. 6. Ensure the continued revenues to the Town from the short-term rental excise tax. § 110-2. Definitions. OWNER – Any person, corporation, LLC, trust or other entity that, alone, or severally with others, directly or indirectly, has legal or equitable title or beneficial interest in any dwelling unit. OPERATOR – A person or entity who is designated by an Owner to be responsible for the dayto-day operations of the Short-Term Rental and who serves as the local 24-hour emergency contact person with the Town of Yarmouth. An Owner may also be an Operator provided they are available 24 hours a day during the rental period to address operational issues at the Short-Term Rental. SHORT-TERM RENTALS (STR) - defined as owner-occupied, tenant-occupied or non-owner occupied residential property including, but not limited to, an apartment unit, house, cottage, condominium or a furnished accommodation that is not a hotel, motel, boarding or lodging house, or guesthouse, inn or bed and breakfast establishment, where at least one room or unit is rented to an occupant or occupants for 1-31 consecutive days at a time. STRs are characterized as transient in nature and not rented to the same occupant month to month. TIME SHARE, FRACTIONAL AND INTERVAL OWNERSHIP UNIT - Any Dwelling Unit which is owned by a limited liability company, corporation, partnership, or other joint ownership structure in which unrelated persons or entities own, sell, purchase or otherwise, for consideration, create or acquire any divided property interest including co-ownership or fractional or divided estates, shares, leaseholds, or memberships which are subject to, or subsequently bound by any agreement limiting the right or functional ability of interest holders or their designees to occupy or use the property to their respective interests or any other agreement which limits interest holders’ or their designees’ use of the property to fractional reservations through stay limitations of any duration. Such use is established by one or more of the following elements: 1) co-ownership or fractional or divided estates, shares, leaseholds, or memberships which are openly advertised, marketed, or offered for sale and sold individually at STR Article 1 – General Bylaw Draft #6 – October 14, 2026 Page 1 of 5 separate times; 2) centralized or professional management; 3) reservation systems; 4) maximum or minimum day limits on each interest holder’s occupancy or use of the property; or 5) management agreements or fees reflective of interval use or ownership, irrespective of whether the agreement may be cancelled individually or by any party. § 110-3. Ineligible Units. The following are not eligible to be rented as STRs. 1. Dwellings designated as income restricted or which are subject to affordability covenants or restrictions. 2. Approved Accessory Apartments, Accessory Dwelling Units, and Protected Use Accessory Dwelling Units, as defined in, and approved under, the Zoning Bylaw. 3. Dwelling units on a property containing an Accessory Apartment, Accessory Dwelling Unit or Protected Use Accessory Dwelling Unit. 4. Dwellings developed under the MU Zoning District bylaw and the VCOD, ROAD, HMOD1, HMOD2, and MOD Overlay District Bylaws. 5.4.Dwelling units with Time Share, Fractional and Interval Ownership. 6.5.Dwellings subject to any unresolved outstanding building, sanitary, zoning, conservation, or fire code violations. 7.6.As of right Duplexes created and approved under G.L. c. 40A, §3. § 110-4. Registration & Inspections. 1. All Short-Term Rentals shall be registered annually through the Yarmouth Health Department in accordance with General Bylaw Chapter 108 – Occupancy of Buildings; and shall be inspected annually by the Building Commissioner, or his/her designee, in accordance with 780 CMR – MA State Building Code; and shall adhere to all health and safety requirements. Overnight occupancy limitations shall be set by the Health Department based on inspections and septic capacity. 2. Rental Occupancy Certificate and Certificate of Inspection shall be displayed on the property in a prominent location and shall include 24-hour local contact information. All Certificates expire on December 31st of each year. 3. The Town reserves the right to post rental locations and contact information on the Town Website per MGL Ch. 64G, Section 14. § 110-5. General Provisions. 1. Trash Removal: All household trash shall be removed from the premises immediately after occupancy is concluded, and at a minimum once per week. 2. Parking: On-site parking area shall be provided and will be determined by the Health or Building Departments at time of inspection. There shall be no parking on lawns at any time and no expansion of parking into green space areas in front of the dwelling. No overnight STR Article 1 – General Bylaw Draft #6 – October 14, 2026 Page 2 of 5 3. 4. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. street parking from 11:00PM to 7:00AM, and no street parking that impedes traffic or traffic safety at any time. Duration: Renting for less than two (2) consecutive nights is prohibited. Occupancy: Maximum overnight occupancy from 11:00PM to 7:00AM shall be the occupancy limit set by the Health Department in accordance with state and local lawsbylaws and regulations, regardless of the number of bedrooms or places to sleep (i.e., beds, sofas, cots, bunk beds, etc.) provided in the STR. Noise: All occupants of Short-Term Rentals shall adhere to General Bylaw Chapter 104 – Noise and shall respect quiet hours from 11:00PM to 7:00AM. Type of Rentals: a. STRs are for Residential uses only. No large-scale events including, but not limited to, weddings; corporate events; graduation, fraternity/sorority, bridal or bachelor parties; and class/family reunions may take place in a STR or on a STR property. b. No events that include tents or amplified music may take place on a STR property. c. STRs shall not be used in a manner that adversely affects the residential character of the neighborhood or substantially and unreasonably interferes with a reasonable person’s use and enjoyment of their residence and property. An adverse effect may occur when, for example, a STR is used in a manner that results in the production of excessive noise, vibration, light, glare, trash, fumes, odors, traffic, parking congestion, or any other nuisance. Pets: Adherence to any and all state and local regulations regarding pets. Use of RVs, campers or sleeping tents as STRs or sleeping spaces is prohibited. Short Term Rentals shall meet all local and state regulations, including but not limited to building and fire codes, health codes, water supply and wastewater disposal. § 110-6. Rental Listings, Advertisements and Booking Platforms. The following information shall be provided on all Rental Listings, Advertisements and Booking Platforms for STRs in the Town of Yarmouth: 1. Town Issued Rental Occupancy Certificate number. 2. MA Department of Revenue STR Certificate ID number. 3. Maximum number of cars a property can accommodate on-site as set by the Health or Building Departments. 4. No overnight street parking is allowed from 11:00PM to 7:00AM. 5. Maximum overnight occupancy from 11:00PM to 7:00AM as set by the Health Department. Number of sleeping spaces advertised shall not exceed this number. 6. Minimum booking of two (2) consecutive nights. 7. No large-scale events or parties. § 110-7. Penalties and Enforcement. Enforcement of this bylaw shall be the responsibility of the Health, Building, and Police Departments. STR Article 1 – General Bylaw Draft #6 – October 14, 2026 Page 3 of 5 1. The Town may seek to enjoin violations thereof through any lawful process, and the election of one remedy by the Town shall not preclude enforcement through any other lawful means. 2. Non-Criminal Disposition: Any person violating any provisions of this bylaw may be penalized by the non-criminal disposition process as provided in G.L. c. 40, §21D. Owners will be provided notification of the violation, with the first notice being a warning. If not promptly resolved after the warning, they may be fined three hundred dollars ($300.00) for each offense. Each day that such violation continues shall constitute a separate offense. 3. Civil Penalty: In accordance with MGL CH 64G, §14(v), the Town may assess a civil penalty not to exceed $5,000, or as determined by the Select Board, for any violation of this bylaw. Each day a violation continues shall be considered a separate offense. 4. Suspension/Revocation/Non-Renewal of Certificates: Three (3) or more material violations of any state or local bylaws or regulations verified by the appropriate Town official(s) within a calendar year, shall be grounds for revocation, suspension or nonrenewal of the Rental Occupancy Certificate for up to two (2) years as determined by the Building Commissioner. The violations shall be from three separate rental engagements and not a single event or renter. Applicants may appeal this determination to the Select Board. § 110-8. Severability. The provisions of this chapter are severable. The invalidity of any portion or provision of this bylaw shall not invalidate any other portion or provision thereof. § 110-9. Effective date. The provisions of this bylaw shall take effect as of January 1, 2028. EXPLANATION: This Article would modify and fine-tune current regulations related to Short Term Rentals and convert regulatory provisions currently located within the Zoning Bylaw to a separate General Bylaw. At the 2022 Annual Town Meeting, Section 418 of the Zoning Bylaw was approved to allow for Short-Term Rentals while incorporating general provisions to regulate their use. This was done to codify the historic use of homes on Cape Cod as vacation rentals in response to 2021 case law that questioned this type of use unless expressly allowed in the Zoning Bylaw. The original STR bylaw was prepared expeditiously to ensure continued economic benefits and revenues to the Town from the short-term rental tax. STRs are a vital revenue stream for the Town, bringing in over $2.375 Million in Fiscal Year 26, with 75% going towards funding our wastewater program to improve our estuaries and water quality. As the bylaw was developed in an expedited manner, a sunset clause was included in the bylaw to allow time for further studies or analysis, with the STR provisions currently expiring on November 30, 2026, unless amended at Town Meeting. Subsequent studies conducted included a detailed Short-Term Rental Report by UMass Donahue Institute dated February 2026. This study analyzed demographics, the housing market, STRs in Yarmouth, impacts and benefits of STRs, reviewed existing regulations and identified potential new regulations. This study was presented to the Select Board at their March 3, 2026 meeting and STR Article 1 – General Bylaw Draft #6 – October 14, 2026 Page 4 of 5 recommended a multi-faceted strategy. In addition to looking at various ways to incentivize yearround housing, the study discussed tailoring regulations to inhibit future commercialization of STRs, strengthen compliance, and further address quality of life issues. The Planning Board used this study to start developing draft language and holding public meetings to garner community input. Some key provisions and modifications contained within the General Bylaw include:  further restrictions on types of dwellings that can be used as a STR  further clarifications on occupancy, parking, noise, and type of rentals  identification of specific information to be included within all STR listings, and  enhanced penalties and enforcement including the potential revocation of a Rental Occupancy Certificate related to verified violations. In addition to these bylaw enhancements, other administrative procedures will be enacted for the 2027 season, such as:  an on-line STR complaint form  improved education of the regulations to STR owners, and  collection of additional information in the application process including Department of Revenue Registration number. Town Planner Kathy Williams will give a brief presentation highlighting the main changes to the STR provisions included in this General Bylaw.
